communication:
"Your 401(k) at a Crossroads" - Seminar Script (v3)
Foxhaven Financial Services LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC
Presenter: Hannah Osei, Registered Representative

SLIDE 1 - Welcome
HANNAH: Thanks for coming out tonight. I'm Hannah Osei with Foxhaven Financial Services. Over the next 45 minutes we'll cover what you can do with a 401(k) when you leave a job, and we'll finish with a quick look at the markets.

SLIDE 2 - Your Four Options
HANNAH: You generally have four choices: leave the money in your former employer's plan if it allows; move it to your new employer's plan; roll it to an IRA; or cash it out. Each has trade-offs. Plans often offer lower-cost institutional share classes and strong federal creditor protection; an IRA usually offers a wider range of investments but may cost more depending on what you choose. Cashing out generally triggers income tax and, before age 59 1/2, a possible 10% penalty. There's no single right answer; it depends on your costs, your needs and the options in your plan.

SLIDE 3 - Market Snapshot
HANNAH: People always ask what we're seeing in the markets. Our research department's January 2026 Strategy Outlook sets a year-end 2026 target of 7,100 for the S&P 500. The analysts get there by applying a 21.5 times multiple to their $330 earnings-per-share estimate for 2027. The same report lists the main risks to that view - slower earnings growth, sticky inflation that keeps rates higher, and geopolitical shocks - and notes the index could finish the year well below the target. A price target is an analyst's opinion, not a promise, and it isn't by itself a reason to make a rollover decision. Copies of the full report are on the back table.

SLIDE 4 - Questions
HANNAH: I'm happy to take questions now, or you can book a free one-on-one review at the sign-in table.

[Footer on every slide: Foxhaven Financial Services LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC. Investing involves risk, including loss of principal. Indexes are unmanaged and cannot be invested in directly.]

Subject: Market volatility update: staying on course with your mutual fund portfolio

Dear Copperline Client,

Yesterday's global selloff was one of the sharpest single-day declines in several years, and many of you saw the value of your mutual fund holdings drop noticeably. We want to reach you quickly, before the opening bell, with some context and a reminder of the resources available to you.

Market declines of this size are unsettling, and no one can say whether the volatility will ease this week or continue for some time. What we can say is that most of the portfolios we oversee were built around a long-term plan that already assumed periods like this one would happen. Selling after a sharp drop locks in losses and can leave you out of the market if prices later recover - though there is no assurance that they will.

Diversification across stock, bond and cash funds is designed to soften, not eliminate, the impact of a selloff. Diversification does not ensure a profit or protect against loss in a declining market, and mutual funds are subject to market risk, including possible loss of principal.

If your goals, time horizon or comfort with risk have changed, this is a good moment to talk with your financial professional. Your Tulsa and Wichita advisors have opened extra appointment slots today and tomorrow; call (918) 555-0164 or reply to this email to schedule.

Sincerely,
The Copperline Investment Services Client Team
Copperline Investment Services, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC

Hi Rosalind,

communication:
RETIREMENT STILL ON THE HORIZON? LET'S TALK ABOUT YOUR MIX.

Whether you're 28 or 61, the same question comes up sooner or later: how should my mix of stocks and bonds change as I get older? Target-date funds are one way people approach it. A target-date fund holds a blend of investments designed to shift gradually toward a more conservative allocation as a chosen year, usually an expected retirement year, gets closer.

They are not the only approach, and they are not right for everyone. Funds with the same target year can hold very different mixes and charge different fees, and the target date is not a date when the fund stops changing or when you must retire. The principal value of a target-date fund is not guaranteed at any time, including at or after the target date.

Bring your workplace plan statement to a no-cost, no-obligation conversation with Ramon Echeverria at our Westlake office. We'll look at what you own today and talk through whether it still fits your timeline and your other savings.

Call (512) 555-0118 or stop by 2200 Bee Cave Road, Suite 140, Austin, TX 78746. Weekday and Saturday-morning appointments are available.

Investors should consider a fund's investment objectives, risks, charges and expenses carefully before investing. The prospectus contains this and other information and should be read carefully. All investing involves risk, including possible loss of principal.

Ramon Echeverria, Registered Representative. Securities offered through Pecan Hollow Securities, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC.

metadata.subject: Your question about fixed annuity rates

communication:
Hi Mrs. Abernathy,

It was nice meeting you at the library workshop on Saturday. You asked why fixed annuity rates looked so much better in 2023 than they did a few years earlier. The short answer is that insurers price fixed annuity rates largely off bond yields, and when the Federal Reserve raised short-term rates sharply through 2022 and into 2023, the yields insurers could earn rose too, so the guaranteed rates they offered on new contracts climbed with them. That was a specific response to that rate cycle, not a pattern you should expect to repeat: rates have already moved around since then and could be lower by the time you buy, and nobody can tell you where they will be next year.

A fixed annuity's rate is guaranteed for the term you choose, but the guarantee depends on the claims-paying ability of the issuing insurance company. Most contracts have surrender charges if you take out more than the free-withdrawal amount (often 10% a year) during the surrender period, typically 5-7 years, and withdrawals before age 59½ may also face a 10% IRS penalty on top of ordinary income tax on the gains. If it would help, I can put together current quotes from two or three carriers so you can compare terms side by side - no obligation.

Warm regards,
Hannah Oduya
Registered Representative, Pinecrest Brokerage Services, LLC, member FINRA/SIPC
Annuities offered through Pinecrest Insurance Agency, LLC, an affiliate
(503) 555-0147

Sam Whitlock, Registered Rep

COBALT RIDGE SECURITIES, LLC — Public Seminar Script
"Income in Retirement: Understanding Municipal Bond Funds"
Version for use at library and community-center sessions, Spring 2025

[SLIDE 4 — What is a municipal bond fund?]

PRESENTER: Let's step back from the jargon for a minute. When a city builds a water treatment plant or a county repaves its roads, it often borrows money by issuing bonds. A municipal bond fund is simply a mutual fund that pools investor dollars and buys a diversified basket of those bonds — hundreds of issuers instead of the one or two you might be able to buy on your own. The fund's managers handle the research, the reinvestment of maturing bonds, and the paperwork.

[SLIDE 5 — Why retirees look at them]

PRESENTER: So why do so many people in this room ask us about these funds? One word: taxes. The income these funds pay is tax-free, which means more of every distribution stays in your pocket instead of going to the government at filing time. For someone drawing a pension and Social Security, that can make a real difference in monthly cash flow. Of course, the value of your shares will move up and down with interest rates, and if rates rise, the share price generally falls. Bond funds are not insured and you can lose money. Funds also carry sales charges and ongoing expenses, which we'll walk through on the next slide, and you should read the prospectus before investing.

[SLIDE 6 — Costs and share classes]

Cobalt Ridge Securities, LLC, member FINRA/SIPC. Investors should consider a fund's investment objectives, risks, charges and expenses carefully before investing; the prospectus contains this and other information.

Why We Like Kessling Aerostructures at Today's Valuation
Rook Harbor Securities | Investment Insights Blog | February 11, 2026
By Simone Achebe, Registered Representative

Kessling Aerostructures Inc. (KSAE), which supplies fuselage panels and wing assemblies to commercial and defense aircraft makers, has spent two years working through supply-chain bottlenecks, and its latest results suggest the effort is paying off: the company reported a $4.1 billion backlog at year-end 2025, operating margins recovered to 9.8% from 6.2% a year earlier, and the shares trade at roughly 15 times trailing earnings versus a peer median near 19. Based on that backlog visibility and margin repair, we recommend that long-term investors consider building a position in Kessling Aerostructures.

The risks are real. Roughly 60% of revenue comes from two airframe customers, so a production slowdown at either would hit results quickly; the company carries $1.3 billion of debt that matures between 2027 and 2029; and titanium and labor costs could squeeze margins again. Aerospace suppliers are also cyclical, and the stock could decline significantly in a downturn. This position may not be suitable for every investor, and you should discuss it with your financial professional before investing.

Rook Harbor Securities LLC, member FINRA/SIPC. This article is provided for informational purposes. Investing involves risk, including possible loss of principal.

communication:
What Our Research Team's 2026 S&P 500 Target Does - and Doesn't - Mean for Your Index ETFs
Posted January 22, 2026 by Elaine Kovac, Branch Manager, Grantham Hill Securities - Tucson

Our Research department's 2026 Equity Outlook (published January 12) sets a year-end target of 7,250 for the S&P 500. The analysts reach that number by applying a forward price-to-earnings multiple of 21x to their 2027 earnings estimate of $345 per share, roughly in line with the index's five-year average multiple. The report is just as clear about what could derail it: earnings could disappoint if tariff costs squeeze margins, valuations could compress if long-term Treasury yields rise, and the index's heavy weighting in a handful of large technology companies leaves it exposed to a reversal in that group. The report also lays out a bear case of 5,900 under a recession scenario.

For clients who hold broad-market index ETFs, a target is one research team's reasoned estimate, not a number to plan your finances around. Index ETFs track their benchmark minus fees, can lose value, and the index has finished well above and well below published year-end targets in recent years. If you want the full report - including valuation methodology, risk discussion and analyst disclosures - ask your advisor or download it from the Research Library in your client portal.

Grantham Hill Securities, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC. This post summarizes a research report prepared by Grantham Hill's Research department; see the full report for important disclosures. Investing involves risk, including possible loss of principal. Past performance does not guarantee future results.

THE CANYON VIEW QUARTERLY | Spring 2024
From Rafael Quintero and the Quintero Wealth Group at Saguaro Peak Securities, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC

Hello friends!

What a first quarter. Stocks shrugged off a hotter-than-expected January inflation print, the S&P 500 notched a string of record closes in March, and bond yields drifted higher as the market pushed back its timeline for Fed rate cuts. Under the surface, leadership broadened a bit beyond the handful of mega-cap tech names that dominated last year, with industrials and energy joining the party.

WHY CLIENTS CHOOSE US
There's a reason our phones keep ringing! The Quintero Wealth Group is the #1 wealth management team in Arizona, and our market calls are simply the best in the business - nobody in the Valley reads the market like we do. If you have friends or family who deserve this level of service, send them our way.

WHAT WE'RE WATCHING
We're keeping an eye on three things this spring: whether services inflation keeps cooling, how consumer spending holds up as excess savings run down, and first-quarter earnings season, which kicks off in mid-April. None of these tell us where the market is headed next, but they shape the conversations we'll be having with you at your reviews.

HOUSEKEEPING
Spring review season is here! Use the scheduling link in your client portal to grab a time, and remember that IRA contributions for 2023 are due by April 15. Our Scottsdale office will be closed Friday, March 29.

Cheers,
Rafael Quintero, Registered Representative
Saguaro Peak Securities, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC | 7150 E. Camelback Road, Scottsdale, AZ 85251 | 480-555-0122

From the Mariner Glen Internal Sales Desk

Sleeping Better in Choppy Markets
This spring's volatility had a lot of you asking how to stay invested without losing sleep. And the results speak for themselves: GSHO has returned 6.1% from its October 1, 2024 inception through June 13, 2025, while the S&P 500 swung through a 19% drawdown.

As with any fund, read the prospectus before investing; it describes the outcome period, cap, buffer and the fund's 0.79% management fee. Ask your advisor whether GSHO fits your plan.

Mariner Glen Securities LLC, member FINRA/SIPC | 1 Harborview Plaza, Portland, ME 04101

• Interest adds up every month whether your stocks go up or not.

Derek Asante

communication:
Hi Dev,

Following up on our call - here are the two bonds I mentioned for the $150,000 coming due on the 1st. The first is an Ohio Water Development Authority revenue bond, 4.00% coupon maturing 2039, offered at a yield to worst of 3.62%. Because you live in Ohio, its interest is generally exempt from both federal and Ohio income tax. At your 37% federal bracket plus Ohio's top rate, that works out to a taxable-equivalent yield of roughly 6.0% - a number I'm comfortable calling attractive, but it's just math on today's price, not a prediction of what you'll earn if you sell before maturity.

The second is a Texas airport revenue bond yielding 4.05% to worst. It pays more, but two catches: interest is federally tax-exempt but fully taxable by Ohio, and because it's a private activity bond, the interest is a preference item for the federal alternative minimum tax. You're not in AMT territory today based on last year's return, but that can change. Both bonds are callable at par in 2033, so you could get your principal back early when rates are lower, and both will fall in price if rates rise. Please run this past Meera at your CPA's office before we decide; happy to send the official statements.

Best,
Alana Whitford
Registered Representative
Cinderhill Securities Corp., member FINRA/SIPC
(614) 555-0168 | Columbus, OH

Hi everyone,

A lot of you asked after our spring client night how an ETF actually works, so here's the short version. An exchange-traded fund holds a basket of securities - stocks, bonds or both - and trades on an exchange throughout the day like a single stock. Most track an index, which tends to keep costs lower than many actively managed funds, but you still pay an expense ratio, you may pay a commission or a bid-ask spread when you trade, and the value of your shares will go up and down with the underlying holdings. An S&P 500 ETF, for example, fell along with the index in 2022.

When we build ETF portfolios at Cobalt Ridge, we screen every fund for expense ratio, tracking difference, trading volume and how its index is constructed. That discipline is why our ETF portfolios have outperformed every other advisory program in the state for the last five years. If you'd like to see how your current holdings stack up, reply to this email and I'll set up a 20-minute review.

Best,
Anika Sorensen
Registered Representative
Cobalt Ridge Financial Services, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC
1450 Commerce Street, Suite 300, Dayton, OH 45402

Meet Rosa Delgado-Whitfield, CFP(R)
Financial Advisor | Registered Representative and Investment Adviser Representative | Tucson, Arizona

Hi, I'm Rosa. For nearly fifteen years I've helped Tucson families and retirees build income from bonds, CDs and Treasuries. Most of the people I work with are a few years from retirement or already there, and what they want is a plan they can understand: where the income comes from, when each piece matures, and what could go wrong.

How I work. We start with your cash-flow needs, then look at which mix of Treasuries, brokered CDs, municipal and corporate bonds fits your tax situation and timeline. For many clients that means a ladder, with maturities spread out so that something comes due every year. I'll show you the yield, the call features, the credit rating and the costs of every bond or CD before you buy.

What to keep in mind. Bond prices move opposite to interest rates, so a bond sold before maturity can be worth less than you paid. Callable bonds and CDs can be redeemed early, usually when rates have fallen. Corporate and municipal bonds carry credit risk, and brokered CDs are FDIC insured only up to applicable limits. No ladder removes those risks; it just spreads them out.

Outside the office you'll find me hiking Sabino Canyon or coaching my daughter's softball team. Give me a call at (520) 555-0142 or [book a time](https://www.copperlinefs.com/rosa/book) and let's talk.

Dear Clients,

Several of you wrote to me after the market decline in early August to point out that my July 26 commentary described near-term volatility as "likely to remain subdued." As of the close on August 16, the index had regained most of that decline; I mention this only as a description of what has happened, not as a forecast of what markets will do next.

I have made no changes to any of your accounts in response to these events, and I will not make any without discussing them with you first. Respectfully,

Nathaniel Ostrowski

communication:
Wait, is anything actually "safe"? A plain-English take from our compliance desk
Posted March 11, 2025 by Renee Okonkwo, Compliance Officer, Tidewell Brokerage Services, LLC

Ok, real talk. We get this one a lot: "I want to buy stocks but my cash is just sitting there. Is it safe?" Short answer: stocks are never safe in the guaranteed sense. Shares of any company can drop, sometimes a lot, and you can lose some or all of what you put in. Nobody (not us, not FINRA, not SIPC) guarantees a stock's price.

Where "guaranteed" is literally true: if you park cash in an FDIC-insured brokered CD while you decide what to buy, principal and interest are insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per issuing bank, per ownership category, if that bank fails. Two catches tho. (1) The guarantee comes from the FDIC and is tied to the issuing bank, not to Tidewell, and anything over the limit at the same bank isn't covered. (2) If you sell the CD before it matures, you sell at the market price, which can be less than you paid, and FDIC insurance doesn't cover that. SIPC is a different animal: it protects up to $500,000 of customer securities and cash (including a $250,000 limit for cash) if a member brokerage firm fails and customer assets are missing. It does not protect you from a stock going down. tl;dr: CD held to maturity at an insured bank = insured. Stocks = not insured, not guaranteed, can lose value. This post is general education, not a recommendation of any stock or CD.

Tidewell Brokerage Services, LLC | Member FINRA (www.finra.org) / SIPC (www.sipc.org)
Check the background of our firm and investment professionals on FINRA's BrokerCheck: https://brokercheck.finra.org

required_actions: Approve for use
label.rationale: Public blog post, so a retail communication. 'Guaranteed' and 'insured' are used only for FDIC coverage of brokered CDs, with the per-bank limits, the issuer-bank backing and the secondary-market price caveat, while stocks are expressly described as not safe or guaranteed. The SIPC description is accurate and disclaims market-loss protection, so nothing implies regulator or SIPC endorsement under 2210(e).

Ok, real talk. We get this one a lot: "I want to buy stocks but my cash is just sitting there. Is it safe?" Short answer: stocks are never safe in the guaranteed sense. Shares of any company can drop, sometimes a lot, and you can lose some or all of what you put in. Nobody (not us, not FINRA, not SIPC) guarantees a stock's price.

Where "guaranteed" is literally true: if you park cash in an FDIC-insured brokered CD while you decide what to buy, principal and interest are insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per issuing bank, per ownership category, if that bank fails. Two catches tho. (1) The guarantee comes from the FDIC and is tied to the issuing bank, not to Tidewell, and anything over the limit at the same bank isn't covered. (2) If you sell the CD before it matures, you sell at the market price, which can be less than you paid, and FDIC insurance doesn't cover that. SIPC is a different animal: it protects up to $500,000 of customer securities and cash (including a $250,000 limit for cash) if a member brokerage firm fails and customer assets are missing. It does not protect you from a stock going down. tl;dr: CD held to maturity at an insured bank = insured. Stocks = not insured, not guaranteed, can lose value. This post is general education, not a recommendation of any stock or CD.

CEDAR HOLLOW QUARTERLY | Spring 2025
From the desk of Marcus Delgado, Financial Professional

Changing Jobs? Bring Your 401(k) Home!

Every spring I hear from clients who are starting new roles, and almost all of them have the same question: what do I do with the old 401(k)? My answer is almost always the same. Roll it into an IRA here at Cedar Hollow, and put every retirement dollar you own under one roof.

Think about what you get. Instead of the 15 or 20 funds on your old plan's menu, you open the door to thousands of stocks, bonds, ETFs and mutual funds. You get one statement, one login, one beneficiary form, and one advisor who actually knows your whole picture. And when the money moves as a direct rollover, there is no tax due on the transfer.

Old plans get forgotten. Former employers change recordkeepers, statements go to old addresses, and before long you are not sure what you own. A rollover IRA puts you back in control, with a personalized allocation built around your goals and reviewed with you every year.

With that kind of flexibility and attention, rolling over simply makes sense for nearly everyone who leaves a job. If you or someone in your family has an old plan sitting idle, call our office this month and we will handle the paperwork from start to finish.

Marcus Delgado | Cedar Hollow Securities, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC
310 Grand Avenue, Des Moines, IA 50309 | (515) 555-0176

Subject: Re: Is a crash coming? Should I move everything to the annuity?

Gloria,

Short answer: I can't tell you whether the market will drop next year. Nobody can predict that reliably, and I won't pretend to.

What I can tell you is what the Quillmark Life 5-year fixed annuity we discussed actually does. It credits 4.85% a year for five years, and that rate is guaranteed by Quillmark Life, so it depends on the insurer's claims-paying ability. It isn't FDIC insured. You can take out 10% a year free; anything beyond that in the first five years carries a surrender charge starting at 7%. Putting everything in it would tie up money you may need, so I'd suggest we size it to what you won't touch for five years.

Call me Monday and we'll look at the numbers.

Nate
Nathaniel Ojo, Financial Advisor
Silverthorn Mesa Financial, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC
(505) 555-0110

metadata.recipient_description: three retail client households with young children, sent by BCC
metadata.subject: 529 vs. custodial (UTMA) account: the follow-up I promised

communication:
From: Caleb Northrup <cnorthrup@hollowaycreek.com>
To: Caleb Northrup
Bcc: [3 client households]
Date: August 27, 2025
Subject: 529 vs. custodial (UTMA) account: the follow-up I promised

Hi all,

A few of you asked the same question after our back-to-school calls, so here's one note instead of three. Both a 529 plan and a UTMA custodial account let you invest for a child, but they work differently. Taxes: 529 earnings grow tax-deferred and are free of federal income tax when used for qualified education expenses; state tax treatment depends on your state and plan, and earnings on non-qualified withdrawals are subject to income tax plus a 10% federal penalty. UTMA earnings are taxed each year, partly at the child's rate and partly at the parents' rate under the kiddie tax rules, but the money can be used for anything that benefits the child. Control and liquidity: you keep control of a 529 and can change the beneficiary within the family; UTMA assets legally belong to the child, who takes control at the age set by state law (often 18 or 21), and gifts to a UTMA can't be taken back. Costs: 529 portfolios carry program and underlying fund expenses, and advisor-sold plans may add sales charges; a UTMA's costs depend on what you hold in it. Financial aid: a parent-owned 529 is generally treated more favorably than a UTMA, which counts as the student's asset.

Neither account is guaranteed or insured, and in both you can lose money if the investments decline. Which one fits depends on your goals, so let's look at your numbers together, and please read the plan's offering document before investing in any 529.

Caleb Northrup, Registered Representative
Holloway Creek Securities, LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC

Dear Dr. Abernathy,

Thank you for meeting with me on Thursday to talk about your retirement from St. Brendan's Medical Center next spring. As promised, I am writing to summarize the approach we discussed for the approximately $640,000 in your 403(b).

For someone in your position the appeal of a target-date fund is simplicity. The fund holds a diversified mix of U.S. and international stocks and bonds, rebalances automatically, and gradually shifts toward bonds and cash as 2030 approaches. As you approach 2030, that glide path takes the market-timing worry off your plate entirely, which means one less decision in the years when you would rather be traveling than watching markets.

On cost, the fund's Class A shares carry a maximum front-end sales charge of 5.25%, reduced at breakpoints; at your investment level the sales charge would be 2.00%, and the fund's total annual operating expense ratio is 0.71%. Respectfully,

Subject: ok bond people, let's talk ladders

Hey everyone!

GLEN: Money Minute. Glen Archuleta, Mesa Verde Securities. Let's go.

Grab a coffee and hang out with the Bluehaven Tacoma team for a no-pressure, plain-English session. We'll walk through how dividend-focused ETFs are built, what they cost, and where they can let you down.

We'll use one real fund as our example, the Cedar Arc Dividend Growth ETF (CADG), so here are its numbers, straight up:

Average annual total returns as of 6/30/2025 (standardized)

metadata.subject: Duration, Rate Cuts and Your Bond Allocation

communication:
Dear Client,

With the Federal Reserve having begun to lower its policy rate, many of you have asked whether now is the time to revisit the bond side of your portfolio. History offers a useful perspective. According to our review of Federal Reserve and Treasury data, the price of the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond rose in the twelve months following the first rate cut in six of the last seven easing cycles since 1984. Longer-maturity bonds have historically been the most price-sensitive to changes in interest rates, and investors who held them through easing cycles have generally seen the largest price gains in fixed income.

For clients who have kept their bond holdings in short-term Treasuries and CDs, we are offering complimentary reviews this month to discuss extending maturities into the 20- to 30-year range. Please call our office at (317) 555-0148 to schedule.

Past performance is no guarantee of future results. All investments involve risk.

Sincerely,

Nadia Brennan-Hale
Senior Vice President - Investments
Whitlock Hartley & Co., Member FINRA/SIPC

violations.excerpt: investors who held them through easing cycles have generally seen the largest price gains in fixed income
violations.explanation: The email frames long-bond price sensitivity only as upside and urges extending to 20-30 year maturities, omitting that the same sensitivity produces the largest losses when long rates rise, even during easing cycles, and saying nothing about the cycle that broke the pattern.

required_actions: Return for revision
Add balanced disclosure that long-maturity bonds can suffer large price declines when long-term rates rise, including during or after Fed easing, and describe the exception cycle
label.rationale: As a template to 338 retail clients this is a retail communication. Its historical statistics may be accurate and it carries a generic risk legend, but by presenting interest-rate sensitivity solely as a source of gains while soliciting clients to lengthen maturities, it omits the corresponding risk required by (d)(1)(A).

FOXGLOVE FINANCIAL SERVICES BLOG
Target-Date Fund or CD Ladder? How to Choose Your Retirement Savings Engine
By Simone Arkwright, Registered Representative | March 3, 2025

If you've been putting off a decision about your retirement savings, here's some good news: you don't need a complicated plan to get started, and both a target-date fund such as our Foxglove Pathway 2050 Fund and a laddered set of bank CDs can do real work for you. A target-date fund gives you a diversified mix of stock and bond funds that automatically shifts toward bonds as 2050 approaches, you can buy or redeem shares any business day, and it charges an ongoing expense ratio (0.58% for the Pathway 2050 Investor class). Its value is NOT guaranteed, it is not FDIC-insured, it can lose money including near or after the target date, and in a taxable account its distributions are taxed each year. A CD ladder, by contrast, offers a fixed rate with principal FDIC-insured up to $250,000 per depositor per bank, has no expense ratio, but locks your money up until each CD matures (early withdrawal usually costs a penalty), its interest is taxed as ordinary income each year, and its fixed rate may not keep pace with inflation over a multi-decade horizon.

Which is better depends on your timeline, your comfort with market swings and when you'll need the money; many savers use both. Let's talk it through: book a free 20-minute call on our website. Investors should consider the fund's investment objectives, risks, charges and expenses carefully before investing; the prospectus, which contains this and other information, is available at foxglovefs.example/prospectus and should be read carefully.

Foxglove Financial Services, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC | Investing involves risk, including possible loss of principal.

Dear Clients,

On Monday, March 10, 2025, between approximately 9:41 a.m. and 11:05 a.m. ET, our online trading platform and mobile app were unavailable while markets were moving sharply, and many of you contacted us; several of you have filed formal complaints. Here is what we know. The outage was caused by a failed software update at our third-party order-routing vendor. You may also contact FINRA or your state securities regulator directly. We regret the disruption and are reviewing our vendor arrangements and backup procedures.

Sincerely,
Theresa Lindqvist, CFP

communication:
Subject: Our take: healthcare looks too cheap to ignore

Hi there,

Quick one from the Ferncliff Investment Committee: we think healthcare stocks deserve a fresh look. Here's why. As of January 31, 2025, the S&P 500 Health Care sector traded at about 16.8x expected 12-month earnings versus roughly 21.9x for the S&P 500 overall (source: Ferncliff Research, using S&P Dow Jones Indices data), one of the widest gaps in the past ten years, and the number of Americans over 65 keeps growing. That's our opinion, not a promise, and there are real reasons the sector is cheap: drug-pricing rules, patent expirations on big-selling drugs and failed clinical trials can all hit share prices hard, and any single sector can lag the broader market for years. Cheap can stay cheap.

For clients in our Balanced and Growth models, we've added a modest position in the Tidewater Health Sciences Fund (Class A). Sector funds tend to be more volatile than diversified funds, and you can lose money. COPPERLINE FINANCIAL ADVISORS BLOG

Why Municipal Bonds Deserve a Fresh Look in 2026

If you're in a high tax bracket and tired of handing a big slice of your bond income to the IRS, municipal bonds may deserve a spot on your radar. Interest from most municipal bonds is exempt from federal income tax, and if you buy bonds issued in the state where you live, the interest is often exempt from that state's income tax too. That's where the "tax-free" label comes from, but read the fine print with us: interest on bonds from other states is generally subject to your home state's income tax, interest on certain private activity bonds can be subject to the federal alternative minimum tax, and any gain when you sell a bond for more than you paid is taxable as a capital gain. Municipal interest can also affect the taxation of Social Security benefits.

Munis are not risk-free. Prices fall when interest rates rise, issuers can be downgraded or default, many bonds can be called before maturity, and some issues trade infrequently, so you may get less than you hoped if you need to sell early. Whether munis make sense depends on your bracket, your state, and the rest of your portfolio. Our team will run a taxable-equivalent yield comparison using your actual numbers. Book a call, and talk with your tax advisor before you invest.

Securities offered through Copperline Securities LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC. Advisory services offered through Copperline Financial Advisors LLC, an SEC-registered investment adviser and affiliate of Copperline Securities LLC. Copperline does not provide tax or legal advice.

# What Today's Chip Selloff Means for Your Portfolio
*Posted June 11, 2024 by Owen Castellano, Registered Representative*

*Editor's note: Compliance is still looking at this post, but given how quickly markets are moving we went ahead and published it this morning.*

Semiconductor stocks fell sharply at the open after a major chipmaker cut its revenue outlook, and the selloff spread across the sector within minutes. If you own individual chip stocks, or funds heavy in technology, you've likely seen a noticeable drop in your account today. Moves like this are a reminder that sector concentration cuts both ways: the same holdings that drove gains can drive losses just as quickly, and individual stocks can fall further and stay down longer than the broader market. Before reacting, look at how much of your portfolio sits in one sector and whether that still matches your goals and timeline. If you'd like to talk it through, call me at 571-555-0146.

*Brambleton Securities, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC. This post is for general information and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security. All investing involves risk, including loss of principal.*

Subject: Lock in a 5-year guaranteed rate — here's how a fixed annuity works

Hi there,

If you've got CDs or savings coming due this summer and you're wondering what to do next, I want to put one option on your radar: a multi-year guaranteed annuity, or MYGA. It's one of the simplest products I offer, and right now it's getting a lot of attention.

Here's the headline: the Ironvale Life SecureTerm 5 currently credits 5.15% a year, guaranteed for the full five-year term. That rate is set when you buy and doesn't move with the stock market. Interest grows tax-deferred, so you don't pay tax on it each year while it stays in the contract.

communication:
Bond ETFs vs. Brokered CDs: Quick Take

A brokered CD's principal and interest are FDIC-insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, and the full face amount is paid if you hold it to maturity. Sell it early and the secondary-market price can be below what you paid. That insurance guarantee doesn't extend to bond ETFs: they aren't insured or guaranteed, have no maturity date, trade at prices that rise and fall with rates and credit, and charge an ongoing expense ratio, while CDs carry a markup built into the price. Interest from both is generally taxable as ordinary income; CDs are FDIC-insured bank deposits with a fixed rate, while ETF distributions vary month to month.

- Kenji Morrow, Registered Representative, Saltmarsh Point Securities, LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC

communication:
Hi Ms. Gallardo,

It was great meeting you after Saturday's workshop at the Elmhurst library. You asked some good questions about exchange-traded funds, so here's the fuller explanation I promised.

An ETF is a basket of securities (stocks, bonds or both) that trades on an exchange like a single stock. You can buy or sell shares whenever the market is open, and most ETFs publish their holdings daily, so you can see exactly what you own. That transparency is one reason they've become popular with people building their first portfolio.

You mentioned you were worried about fees eating into your savings. Good news there: ETFs don't have any annual fees or expenses at all. The only cost is the trade commission, and at Lindqvist & Pell we waive that for new accounts.

For the conservative portion of your savings, I'd look at a defined-maturity bond ETF, such as one holding investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2030. Because the fund winds down and returns its assets when those bonds mature, your original investment is guaranteed to come back to you in 2030 as long as you hold until then.

On the stock side, a broad market fund such as VTI gives you exposure to thousands of U.S. companies in a single trade. Its price will move up and down with the market, sometimes sharply, so it belongs with money you won't need for at least five to ten years.

Once your account is open I can put together a sample allocation for you to review. I'm in the office Monday through Thursday.

Warm regards,

Henrik Solberg
Registered Representative
Lindqvist & Pell Securities, LLC | Member FINRA/SIPC
Rockford, IL | 815-555-0176

communication:
Subject: That wild April, one year later

Hi all -

Remember last April? Stocks dropped hard in a matter of days after the tariff headlines, and plenty of you called me wondering if it was time to sell everything. By the end of the summer the S&P 500 had recovered those losses. I'm bringing it up not because I think that'll happen the same way next time - it might not, and some downturns take years to recover from - but because it's a good reminder of why we built your plans around your timeline instead of the headlines.

If your mutual fund mix still matches your goals, there's usually nothing to do when markets get choppy. If your situation has changed, or if last April made you realize you're less comfortable with swings than you thought, let's talk - adjusting your risk level is a totally reasonable move. Past performance doesn't guarantee future results, and all investing involves risk, including loss of principal.

Talk soon,
Marcus Delacroix-Yee
Registered Representative, Sandpiper Coast Investments, member FINRA/SIPC
Sarasota, FL | 941-555-0108

Elliot Nakashima

metadata.subject: Re: Settlement delay on the agency ladder - our apologies

communication:
Dear Ms. Farouk,

Please accept my apology for the settlement delay on Cedar Valley Community Bank's agency ladder purchase last week. Our operations desk mis-keyed the CUSIP on two of the nine positions, which pushed settlement on those lots from March 12 to March 15, 2024. We have absorbed the accrued-interest difference of $4,318.60, and the corrected confirmations went to your custodian this morning.

To make this right going forward, I've asked Jonah Pretorius on our fixed income desk to personally oversee your account. I'm also confident the ladder as now constructed will produce a total return of 6.1% for the bank over the next twelve months, comfortably ahead of your 4.75% budget hurdle, so the delay will not cost you anything on an annual basis. Please call me directly if anything else looks off.

Sincerely,

Renata Gilchrist
Branch Manager, Fixed Income Institutional Sales
Alder Crest Capital Markets, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC

violations.explanation: States a specific forward total return for the portfolio, which is a prohibited projection of performance; no (d)(1)(F) exception applies to institutional communications under the current rule.

YOU'RE INVITED
Building an Income Portfolio with ETFs
An evening seminar hosted by Ashgrove Investment Services, LLC

Thursday, April 17, 2025 | 6:30-8:00 p.m.
Lakeview Community Center, 1200 Shoreline Drive, Madison, WI
No cost to attend | Light refreshments served

Dear Neighbor,

If you're approaching retirement, or already there, you've probably wondered how to turn a lifetime of savings into income you can count on month to month. Exchange-traded funds have become one of the most popular tools for that job, and on April 17 our Madison team would like to show you how they fit into an income plan.

Over about 90 minutes we'll cover how dividend-focused and bond ETFs generate income, how they differ from owning individual stocks and bonds, what to look for in an ETF's holdings and costs, and how to think about withdrawals in the early years of retirement. Among the funds we'll walk through is the Silverpine Dividend Achievers ETF (ticker: SDAX), which returned 21.7% over the past 12 months and 64% over the last three years.

ETFs trade on an exchange like stocks, so their market prices fluctuate and you can lose money, including in income-oriented funds. Dividends are not guaranteed and can be reduced. Investors should consider an ETF's investment objectives, risks, charges and expenses carefully before investing; the prospectus contains this and other information and is available at the seminar or by calling us.

Seating is limited to 60 guests. Reserve your spot by calling (608) 555-0164 or replying to this invitation by April 10. Bring a spouse or friend - questions are welcome.

Warm regards,
Theodora Klasen
Branch Manager
Ashgrove Investment Services, LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC
2500 University Avenue, Madison, WI 53705

Hi everyone,

With the Fed holding rates where they are, a few of you have asked whether there's a fund that actually benefits from that instead of getting hurt by it. The one I keep coming back to is the Ashgrove Floating Rate Income Fund. It invests in bank loans whose interest payments reset every 30 to 90 days, so as rates stay elevated the income it pays out stays elevated too, and it pays monthly, which is nice if you're drawing on your account.

The other thing I like is that because the coupons float, the fund barely reacts when rates move, so it has been a steadier place to park money than a typical bond fund. For anyone holding a lot of cash or a long-term bond fund, this could be a smart swap. Reply and I'll pull together a quick proposal for your account.

Talk soon,
Heather Moravec
Registered Representative
Greenleaf Harbor Securities, member FINRA/SIPC

Subject: Re: should I sell VTI??

Hi Gwen,

I saw your message come in at 6:50 this morning and I know the headlines are unnerving — the market opened down sharply and the financial channels are in full crisis mode. Let me give you a straight answer first and the context second.

The straight answer is that I cannot tell you where the market goes from here — not this week, not this quarter — and anyone who says otherwise is guessing. What I can tell you is what we know: your holding in VTI is a broad U.S. total-market ETF, it trades on the exchange throughout the day, and it may trade at a premium or discount to its net asset value during volatile sessions like today's, which is one reason I would not use a market order in this environment.

Some history, offered as history and not as a forecast: declines of 10% or more from a recent high have occurred in a majority of calendar years going back several decades, and in some of those years the market finished higher and in others it finished lower. Past patterns do not tell us what happens this time.

The more useful question is whether your plan still fits. When we built it last spring, we set the VTI position at roughly 55% of the portfolio on the assumption that you would not need to draw from it for at least eight years, and we kept two years of planned withdrawals in the money market fund and the short-term Treasury ladder so that a bad stretch in stocks would not force a sale. Nothing in your life has changed that I know of; if it has, that is the thing we should talk about, because that would change the plan regardless of what the market does.

Selling today is an option, and it is your money. I would ask that we talk before any order is placed so you have the full picture, including the tax consequences of realizing gains in the taxable account. I have cleared 11:00 and 1:30 today — reply with one or call my cell.

Mike

Hi Ms. Delacroix, this is Renee Okafor in Operations at Prairie Crest Investments LLC, following up on the IRA transfer request you started on our portal yesterday (Sept. 9, 2025).

The main holding at your current firm is the Trellis Path 2045 Target Date Fund, Class R6. That share class is only offered through retirement plans and certain platforms, and our firm can't hold it in an individual IRA, so it can't come over 'in kind' as R6. That leaves two paths. One: your current firm sells the shares and sends us cash. Two: your current firm first exchanges the shares into a class we can hold (for this fund, that's usually Class A or Class I), and then the new shares transfer over. Your current firm controls whether option two is available, so it's worth a call to them.

A couple of things worth knowing either way. Because this is an IRA, selling inside the account does not create a current tax bill; the money stays tax-deferred and is taxed as ordinary income when you eventually withdraw it. If the shares are sold and sent as cash, the money is not invested while it's in transit, which is usually 5 to 7 business days, so you would not participate in any market gains or losses during that window. Different share classes of the same fund also have different expenses, so the class you end up holding will affect your costs.

I'm not able to tell you which option is better for you; that's a conversation for your representative, Alan Brooks, who can review the share-class costs with you. On the paperwork side, I still need a copy of your most recent statement from the other firm (dated within the last 90 days) and your signature on page 3 of the transfer form. You can upload both through the secure message center.

Thanks, and let me know if any of this is unclear.
Renee Okafor | Operations | Prairie Crest Investments LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC

Lakeview Harbor Financial, Member FINRA/SIPC | Presenter: Rosalind Achebe, Financial Advisor

[SLIDE 7 - "Your Retirement Paycheck"]
ROSALIND: So far we've talked about Social Security timing and how much you'll actually need each month. Now let's talk about where that monthly paycheck comes from. Many of our clients use a mix of three mutual funds, the Lakeview Core Bond Fund, the Lakeview Equity Income Fund and the Lakeview Balanced Allocation Fund, and set up a systematic withdrawal plan that deposits money into their checking account on the same day every month.

Before you invest, please read the prospectus for each fund, available at the table in the back. [PAUSE FOR QUESTIONS]

I've blocked Thursday and Friday afternoons for calls so we can go through your individual holdings. Thank you for your patience and for telling me directly.

Warm regards,
Bettina Lowery

Subject: A note from Gina on behalf of Mark - your target-date fund check-in

Hi all!

Gina here, Mark's client service associate. Mark asked me to send this to a few of you who've asked about the target-date funds in your IRAs over the last couple of months. He's out at a conference this week but wanted this in your inboxes before the end of the quarter.

First the boring-but-important stuff: every year around now Mark does a check to make sure the target-date fund you're in still matches when you actually expect to retire. A lot of you picked a 2035 or 2040 fund years ago, and life happens: retirement dates move, people go part-time, a spouse retires early. If your target date has shifted, the fund's glide path (how it moves from stocks to bonds over time) might not line up anymore, and that's worth a quick conversation. Target-date funds don't guarantee you'll have enough income in retirement, they can lose money including right around and after the target date, and their mix keeps changing after that date too. So the date on the label is a starting point, not a promise.

Second, Mark wanted to share something nice. One of his longtime clients, who said it was fine to pass along anonymously, wrote this after their review last spring:

"Mark took the time to explain what the 2030 fund actually holds and why it was too aggressive for when I planned to stop working. We moved to a more conservative option, and for the first time I understand my own retirement account."

Mark asked me to include these notes with it, and he means them: This is one client's experience and may not be representative of the experience of other clients. It is not a guarantee of future performance or success. The client was not paid or compensated in any way for this statement.

If you'd like to set up a 30-minute review, just reply to this email with a couple of times that work and I'll get it on Mark's calendar. Please don't send any trade instructions by email; Mark needs to speak with you directly about any changes.

Thanks so much and have a great week!

Gina Morales

Thornbury Hill Investments, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC

Subject: A quick lesson on compounding (and why time matters)

Hello everyone,

Several of you asked after our spring workshop why I keep harping on starting early, so here is the math, stripped of any particular investment. HYPOTHETICAL ILLUSTRATION ONLY: if $5,000 is set aside at the start of each year and grows at an assumed constant 6% annual rate, it would total about $69,900 after 10 years and about $419,000 after 30 years. Only $150,000 of that 30-year figure is contributions; the rest is growth earned on prior growth. Wait ten years and contribute for 20 years instead, and the same assumptions produce roughly $195,000. This example is purely mathematical. It does not represent any specific investment or the performance of any account, it ignores fees, expenses and taxes that would lower the results, and real investments do not earn a steady rate: returns fluctuate, can be negative, and you can lose money. It is not a prediction of what your portfolio will do.

If you would like to see how this applies to your own plan, just reply and Josie will set up a call.

Best,

Theo Lindqvist, CFP
Financial Advisor
Pemberton Hollis Securities, LLC, member FINRA/SIPC

Quick muni tax reminder before you buy anything this rate cycle 👇

Muni bond interest is generally exempt from FEDERAL income tax. That's not the whole story:
• Bonds from outside your home state are usually taxable by your state.
• Some munis (private activity bonds) can be subject to the federal AMT.
• Sell for a gain -> capital gains tax applies.
• Munis still carry interest-rate, credit and call risk. Prices can fall.

Talk to your tax advisor about your own situation.

Marcus Delacroix, Registered Representative
Lowfield Harbor Securities LLC | Member FINRA/SIPC
#MunicipalBonds #TaxSmartInvesting #FixedIncome

Subject: Your rollover — timeline and next steps

Dear Ms. Faraday,

Thank you for your email of June 3; I understand why you're frustrated. Here is what our records show: we submitted the direct rollover request to the Brennwood Corp. 401(k) plan administrator on April 22, the administrator issued the check on May 14, and it was deposited into your Driftstone IRA on May 19. Because this was a direct rollover, nothing was withheld for taxes; the plan will report it on Form 1099-R with code G, which identifies it as a non-taxable rollover, so the delay does not change your tax treatment. Your assets sat in the IRA's money market sweep until you approved the allocation on May 28, which matches the instructions on your rollover form.

You mentioned that the market rose during those weeks. I can't say how your account would have performed had the money been invested sooner, and I'm not in a position to offer an adjustment. Because you raised this concern in writing, I have forwarded your email to our compliance department, which reviews every written complaint, and you may hear from them directly. In the meantime I'm glad to go through the timeline with you by phone.

Sincerely,
Peter Lowe
Registered Representative
Driftstone Capital, member FINRA/SIPC
(608) 555-0193

Bond prices can move around in the short term like anything else, of course, but I'd be surprised if this one doesn't work out.

Let me know by 3:00 if you want me to place the order today. Otherwise we can talk tomorrow morning.

Best,

Subject: RE: Ridgeline Floating Rate Income Fund - quick answers

Carla,

Short version since I'm between meetings. Before you add the Ridgeline Floating Rate Income Fund (C shares) to the IRA, the risks: 1) Loans in the fund are mostly below investment grade, so defaults can and do happen and the share price can drop meaningfully in a credit selloff, as it did in 2020. 2) The fund borrows to buy more loans (up to about a third of assets), which magnifies losses as well as gains. 3) Leveraged loans trade less often than stocks or Treasuries; in a rough market the fund may have to sell at poor prices, which hits NAV. 4) C shares carry a 1% CDSC if you sell within 12 months, and the ongoing expenses are higher than A shares. 5) The income floats with short-term rates, so if the Fed keeps cutting, the payout will come down. None of this is guaranteed income and you can lose principal.

Jorge Villaseñor

Elmstead Annuity & Securities, LLC | Retirement Income | Fixed Annuities

Fixed Annuities: Predictable Growth for the Conservative Side of Your Plan

A fixed annuity is a contract with an insurance company. You make a lump-sum premium, and the insurer credits a fixed interest rate that is guaranteed for a set term, typically three to seven years. Those guarantees are backed by the claims-paying ability of the issuing insurer, so we only work with carriers rated A- or better by A.M. Best. And if the insurance company ever ran into financial trouble, don't worry: your entire account value is fully covered by your state's insurance guaranty association, no matter how large it is.

Before you buy, know the tradeoffs. Most contracts let you withdraw up to 10% a year without penalty, but larger withdrawals during the term incur surrender charges that can start at 7% and decline over time. Earnings grow tax-deferred, are taxed as ordinary income when withdrawn, and withdrawals before age 59 1/2 may also incur a 10% IRS penalty. Fixed annuities are not bank deposits and are not FDIC insured. Call me at 402-555-0112 to compare current rates.

STONEBRIDGE BROKERAGE LLC
Member FINRA/SIPC | 75 Front Street, Hartford, CT 06103

April 8, 2025

To my clients in the Evergreen Target Retirement 2027 Fund

Dear Client,

I am writing to each of you who hold the Evergreen 2027 Fund in the wake of the past four trading sessions, during which the S&P 500 has fallen roughly 11% and the fund has declined with it. I know that with a retirement date two years out, a week like this one is alarming, and I want to lay out why I am asking you to stay put.

First, what the fund is doing. The 2027 Fund is now about 48% equities and 52% bonds and short-term instruments, and the glide path continues to shift toward bonds every quarter until the target year. The bond sleeve has held its value this week; the equity sleeve is where the decline has come from. That is the design working as intended: the closer you get to 2027, the smaller the equity sleeve becomes.

Second, what I expect from here. The fund has recovered from every correction of this size since its 2012 launch within fourteen months, and with the glide path reducing equity exposure each quarter, I expect the current drawdown to be recaptured well before your 2027 date. Selling now would turn a temporary decline into a permanent one and forfeit that recovery.

Third, the practical point. The fund is built so that by 2027 the portfolio is positioned to deliver the income you planned around. The automatic shift to bonds is precisely what protects that outcome. I would rather you call me and we talk it through than see a redemption request come across my desk.

I am in the office all week and will make time for each of you.

Sincerely,

Robert Lindqvist
Registered Representative
Stonebridge Brokerage LLC, member FINRA/SIPC

ETF basics, part 3: the spread and the premium.

When you buy an ETF, you're usually trading with another investor on an exchange, not buying directly from the fund. That means two costs beyond the expense ratio deserve your attention. The bid-ask spread is the gap between what buyers are paying and sellers are asking; it tends to be narrow for heavily traded ETFs and can be wide for thinly traded ones or right at the open and close. The premium or discount is the difference between the ETF's market price and the value of the securities it holds (its NAV); in fast markets, especially for bond or international ETFs, that gap can widen. Limit orders can help you control the price you pay, though a limit order may not be filled.

ETFs can lose value, and diversification does not guarantee a profit or protect against loss. Questions? Send me a message.

Colin Ashworth, Registered Representative | Summit Path Wealth

metadata.recipient_description: Lucas Ferreira, existing retail client with a concentrated tech position
metadata.subject: Re: still bullish on semis?

communication:
Hey Lucas - following up on your question this morning about whether I'm still bullish on semis. Short answer: I still have a constructive view on semiconductor equipment specifically, and here's my reasoning so you can judge it for yourself.

The basis: the four largest cloud providers all raised their 2025 capital-spending guidance on their most recent earnings calls, and a big share of that money goes into data-center build-outs that need leading-edge chips. Equipment makers like Corvane Semiconductor (CVSM) sell the tools used to make those chips, and Corvane's latest 10-Q showed order backlog up about 30% year over year. Its balance sheet is solid too - net cash and no debt maturing before 2029. That's the case for owning some.

Now the other side, and it's a real one. This is one of the most cyclical industries in the market. When chipmakers pause spending, equipment orders can fall off quickly - Corvane's revenue dropped about 35% peak to trough in the 2019 and 2023 slowdowns, and the stock fell further than that. Export restrictions on China are a live issue, and roughly a quarter of Corvane's sales go there. And the stock already trades above its own 10-year average P/E, so a lot of good news is arguably priced in. None of this tells us what the stock does next.

Where that leaves you: semis plus other tech are now about 31% of your brokerage account after the run-up, so I would not add more here. If anything, I'd like to talk about trimming CVSM back toward the 8% single-stock cap in your investment policy statement.

Free for a call Thursday at 11?
- Nadia Okafor, Registered Representative, Westmarch Securities LLC, member FINRA/SIPC

Subject: Brokered CD offerings — November 2024

Dear Client,

This month Wexmoor Securities Corporation is offering brokered certificates of deposit issued by several FDIC-insured banks, with terms from six months to five years; current rates and the issuer list are attached. Because these CDs are deposits of the issuing banks, principal and interest are insured by the FDIC up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category, and that limit includes any deposits you already hold directly at the same bank. That federal insurance is the only guarantee involved: it is provided by the FDIC, not by Wexmoor, and it does not cover any premium you pay above face value in the secondary market or any loss in market value if you sell before maturity. Brokered CDs can be sold early only in the secondary market, where prices generally fall when interest rates rise and a buyer may not be readily available, so you could receive less than you invested. Several CDs on the list are callable by the issuing bank, which could end your interest payments before the stated maturity, typically when rates have fallen.

Please contact me to review which maturities fit your cash needs, and let me know about any other deposits you hold at the listed banks so we can keep you within insurance limits.

Sincerely,

communication:
[Mon 9:42 AM] Priya Raman (Copperline Investment Services): Hi all — a few of you asked after Thursday's call how ETFs actually work, so here's the quick version in one thread.

[9:43 AM] Priya Raman: An ETF is a pooled fund like a mutual fund, but it trades on an exchange all day at market prices. You buy and sell through your brokerage account just like a stock. The price can drift slightly above or below the value of the underlying holdings (that gap is called a premium or discount), and you pay the bid/ask spread when you trade.

[9:45 AM] Priya Raman: Most ETFs track an index. Our dividend sleeve uses the Copperline Dividend Leaders ETF (CDLX), which holds about 80 U.S. companies with long records of raising dividends. It's a good example of why people like the structure: it returned 21.6% over the past 12 months and is up 38% since we added it in October 2023. Diversified, low turnover, and it does what it says on the tin.

[9:47 AM] Priya Raman: A couple of practical points: ETFs generally distribute dividends quarterly, you can set them to reinvest automatically in your account, and capital gains distributions tend to be smaller than in many actively managed mutual funds because of how shares are created and redeemed.

[9:48 AM] Priya Raman: Happy to walk anyone through it live — just reply here or call me at 520-555-0193.
Priya Raman, Registered Representative | Copperline Investment Services, Member FINRA/SIPC | Tucson, AZ

Best,
Hannah Szabo

Dear Friends,

Several of you asked after our last conversation how much difference it makes to start education savings in the first year of a child's life rather than waiting. Here is a simple way to see the math. HYPOTHETICAL ILLUSTRATION: if a family set aside $250 every month for 18 years and those savings earned an assumed 6% annual return compounded monthly, the account would total roughly $96,800, of which $54,000 would be contributions and about $42,800 would be compounded growth. Actual returns vary year to year and can be negative, and you can lose money in a 529 plan.

A few points that matter when you choose a plan: earnings in a 529 grow tax-deferred, and withdrawals used for qualified education expenses are free from federal income tax. State tax treatment depends on your state and the plan you choose, and Georgia's deduction applies only to contributions to the Georgia plan. Earnings withdrawn for non-qualified purposes are subject to income tax and generally a 10% federal penalty. Plans differ in investment options, fees and risks, so please read the plan's offering document before investing. I am glad to walk any of you through the options one on one.

Warm regards,

Jenna Okafor
Financial Advisor
Saltmarsh Financial Group, LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC
(912) 555-0176

Subject: your old 401(k)s - a rollover idea

Hey everyone,

Sending this to the handful of you who mentioned at our reviews this spring that you still have 401(k)s sitting with former employers. I get it, they're easy to forget about, and the statements are confusing. I wanted to lay out the option a lot of my clients have been choosing.

The idea: roll the old plan into a traditional IRA here and put it in a single target-date fund, like the Meridian Path 2040 Fund if you're planning to retire around 2040. A target-date fund holds a mix of stock and bond funds and automatically shifts toward bonds as the target year gets closer, so you don't have to rebalance it yourself.

Two things people really like about this. First, everything that grows inside the IRA is tax-free, so you never have to think about capital gains or dividends again. Second, the Meridian Path funds don't charge an expense ratio at all; the only cost is a one-time $95 transfer fee on our side.

Now the honest part. Target-date funds can lose money, including close to and after the target date, and the 2040 fund still holds a big chunk of stocks. Two funds with the same target year can have very different mixes and glide paths, so the year on the label doesn't tell you everything. And a rollover isn't right for everyone: your old plan might have lower-cost institutional funds, certain protections, or loan features you'd give up, so we should compare before you move anything.

If you want to talk it through, just grab a time on my calendar link below or reply here.

Talk soon,
Ben Okafor
Registered Representative
Cobalt Mesa Securities, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC
(505) 555-0187 | calendar.cobaltmesa.example/bokafor

communication:
HALYARD POINT SECURITIES LLC
Member FINRA/SIPC
600 Market Street, Suite 1900, Pittsburgh, PA 15222

October 9, 2025

Dear Client,

Several of you asked about our research department's recent note on Vantorre Semiconductor Corp. (VNTR), which you hold in your accounts. I want to summarize what the report says and, just as importantly, explain what a price target is and what it is not.

On October 2, 2025, Halyard Point's equity research analyst reiterated an Outperform rating on VNTR with a 12-month price target of $64, compared with the stock's closing price of $51.20 that day. The analyst arrived at the target by applying a multiple of 18 times to an estimate of 2026 earnings per share of $3.55. The report explains that this multiple is close to the stock's five-year average and to the median of a peer group of analog chip makers.

The report is equally clear about what could keep the stock from reaching that level. VNTR's sales depend on industrial and automotive chip demand, which is cyclical; its two largest customers account for about 31% of revenue; export restrictions could limit its sales into China; and its new fabrication plant in Arizona could run late or over budget. If the earnings estimate turns out to be too high, or investors are willing to pay a lower multiple, the stock could trade well below $64 and could fall from today's price.

A price target is the analyst's opinion of where a stock could trade over a stated period if the analyst's assumptions hold. It is not a promise, and price targets are frequently missed in both directions. The report also discloses that Halyard Point makes a market in VNTR and received compensation for investment banking services from the company in the past 12 months. I have enclosed the complete report with all of its disclosures.

If you are considering adding to VNTR, I would want to look first at how much of your portfolio is already in technology stocks, and I would generally suggest keeping any single stock to a modest share of your holdings. Please call me with any questions.

Sincerely,

Bernard Kowalczyk
Registered Representative
(412) 555-0186

From: Priya Ramanathan <pramanathan@marloweteague.example.com>
Subject: Reading a cash flow statement - and one company where it caught my eye
Date: Monday, October 6, 2025

Hello everyone,

A question I hear often is why I spend more time on a company's cash flow statement than on its headline earnings. This month I want to explain my reasoning, then show how it plays out in one stock I am currently recommending to clients for whom it is suitable.

Earnings versus cash. Reported earnings include accounting estimates - depreciation schedules, the timing of revenue recognition, one-time charges - that can make profits look smoother or lumpier than the underlying business really is. Free cash flow, which is operating cash flow minus capital spending, shows how much money the business actually generated that management could use to pay down debt, buy back stock or pay dividends. When free cash flow consistently trails net income, I want to know why. When it consistently exceeds net income, that can point to conservative accounting or a business that does not need heavy reinvestment. Neither measure tells the whole story by itself, and any single year can be distorted by swings in inventory or receivables.

Applying it: Tamarind Logistics Inc. (NASDAQ: TMRD). Tamarind operates refrigerated warehouses and last-mile cold-chain delivery for grocers across the Southeast. In each of its last four fiscal years, free cash flow exceeded reported net income, and the company used that cash to reduce net debt from roughly $610 million to $380 million (source: company Form 10-K filings, fiscal 2021-2024). I recommend TMRD as a long-term holding for growth-oriented clients. It closed at $43.17 on October 3, 2025, the last trading day before this email was sent.

The risks are real. Tamarind's two largest customers account for about 31% of revenue, so losing either would hurt results. Cold storage is energy-intensive, and higher electricity costs can squeeze margins quickly. The company is smaller than its national competitors, and its shares have historically been more volatile than the broader market - TMRD fell more than 40% from peak to trough in 2022. You could lose money, and any single stock should be only one part of a diversified portfolio. Whether it fits you depends on your objectives, time horizon and other holdings, so please talk with me before acting.

Required disclosures. Marlowe & Teague Securities, Inc. makes a market in TMRD. Marlowe & Teague Securities, Inc. was a co-manager of Tamarind's secondary offering in March 2025. Officers of Marlowe & Teague, as a group, hold a long position in TMRD common stock, and I own shares personally. Supporting information for this recommendation is available on request; reply to this email or call (919) 555-0193.

Best,

Priya Ramanathan
Senior Registered Representative
Marlowe & Teague Securities, Inc. | Member FINRA/SIPC
4300 Six Forks Road, Suite 700, Raleigh, NC 27609

Riding Out the Noise: Why I Ask Clients to Wait 48 Hours Before Selling
By Hollis Grantham, Registered Representative | Sunderland Gate Financial, LLC | October 7, 2025

Every few months the headlines turn scary, and my inbox fills up with the same question: should I get out? My answer is almost always the same - let's talk first, and let's wait 48 hours before placing any sell order driven by the news. Selling in a panic locks in a loss you may never recover, and history is full of sharp drops followed by long recoveries, though no one knows how long the next one will take or whether it will come at all for a given holding. The 48-hour rule simply gives us time to revisit your goals, your time horizon and whether your mix of stocks and bonds still fits. As one longtime client put it: "When the market dropped in 2022, Hollis talked me out of selling and rebuilt my plan. My account is up more than 35% since then - best financial decision I ever made." - Ruth K., client since 2016.

If the latest headlines have you uneasy, call our Ann Arbor office at (734) 555-0181 and let's set up a review.

Sunderland Gate Financial, LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC | 301 E. Liberty St., Ann Arbor, MI 48104

A Colorado Water Revenue Bond Worth a Look
By Nathaniel Brooks, Senior Vice President, Kittredge & Lowe Securities, Inc. | October 2025

With short-term rates drifting lower, many of our Denver-area clients have asked where they might lock in tax-advantaged income for the next decade or more. Essential-service revenue bonds, which are repaid from user fees for water, sewer or electric service rather than from general taxes, are one area I think deserves attention from investors in higher tax brackets.

Specifically, I recommend that income-focused Colorado investors consider the City of Aurora Springs Water Enterprise Revenue Bonds, 4.00% coupon due December 1, 2041, rated AA- by one major rating agency. The system serves a growing customer base, has raised rates on a regular schedule and has maintained debt service coverage well above its bond covenant. Kittredge & Lowe currently has a limited block of these bonds available from our own inventory at a yield to worst of 3.85%.

Interest on these bonds is exempt from federal income tax and, for Colorado residents, from Colorado income tax. It may be subject to the federal alternative minimum tax, and any capital gain if you sell or the bonds are redeemed above your cost is taxable.

Like any bond, these carry risks. Their market value will fall if interest rates rise, and you may receive less than you paid if you sell before maturity. The bonds are callable at par beginning December 1, 2034, which means the city may redeem them early if rates fall, and you would then have to reinvest at lower rates. Revenue bonds depend on the system's ability to collect user fees, and ratings can be lowered. Municipal bonds can also be less liquid than other securities. Yields and availability change throughout the day.

If you would like to discuss whether these bonds fit your portfolio, call me at 303-555-0177.

Kittredge & Lowe Securities, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC | 1700 Larimer Street, Denver, CO 80202

[VIDEO SCRIPT: "Three Minutes on Industrials" | Bluewater Pass Securities LLC | Recording date 2025-03-11 | For firm YouTube channel and website video library]

[OPEN ON TOMAS REYES, SEATED, FIRM LOGO LOWER THIRD]

TOMAS: Hi everyone, Tomas Reyes with Bluewater Pass Securities. I get asked a lot which part of the market I actually have conviction about, so today I'm going to give you a straight answer: I'm an optimist on U.S. industrials, and I want to walk you through why, and what could make me wrong.

[CUT TO GRAPHIC: "Why I'm constructive" - three bullets appear as he speaks]

TOMAS: Three reasons. First, spending on new manufacturing construction in the U.S. has roughly tripled since 2021 according to Census Bureau data, and a lot of those plants still need equipment, automation and power infrastructure. Second, the infrastructure and energy programs passed in 2021 and 2022 are still being spent down, so order books at many machinery and electrical-equipment companies are fuller than they were a few years ago. Third, after the 2022 selloff a number of these companies cleaned up their balance sheets, and dividends across the sector have generally been growing.

[CUT TO GRAPHIC: "What could go wrong"]

TOMAS: Now the other side, because it matters just as much. Industrials are cyclical. If the economy slows, orders get cancelled fast and these stocks tend to fall harder than the overall market. Valuations are not cheap; the sector trades above its ten-year average price-to-earnings ratio, so a lot of good news is already priced in. Tariff and trade policy can change input costs almost overnight, and higher-for-longer interest rates raise the cost of exactly the capital projects that are driving the story. I cannot tell you where the sector is going over the next year, and anyone who says they can is guessing.

[BACK ON TOMAS]

TOMAS: So this is an opinion, with reasons, not a promise. Whether any of it belongs in your portfolio depends on your goals, your time horizon and how much of a swing you can stomach. If you want to talk it through, my number is on the screen. Thanks for watching.

[END CARD - ON-SCREEN TEXT]

YOU'RE INVITED
Tax Season Is Over. Next Year's Tax Bill Doesn't Have to Be a Surprise.
A free evening workshop on municipal bonds

Thursday, May 15, 2025 | 6:00-7:30 p.m.
Delmar Branch Library, Community Room B, 410 Kingsland Ave., St. Louis, MO
Light dinner served. Seating limited to 40.

Did April's tax bill sting? You're not alone, and if you're in a higher bracket, municipal bonds deserve a serious look. Join Financial Advisor Rafael Quintero of Bellwether Point Securities for a no-cost, no-obligation evening on how munis work and whether they belong in your plan.

Here's what we'll cover:
- Why interest on most municipal bonds is exempt from federal income tax, and why that isn't the whole story. Interest on bonds issued outside Missouri is generally subject to Missouri income tax, interest on certain "private activity" bonds can be subject to the federal alternative minimum tax, and any capital gain you realize when you sell a bond is taxable.
- How to compare a muni yield with a taxable yield on a "tax-equivalent" basis, and why the math favors munis only in certain tax brackets.
- The risks you need to understand before you buy: bond prices fall when interest rates rise, issuers can be downgraded or default, many bonds can be called before maturity, and some issues trade infrequently, so you may have to sell for less than you paid if you need cash early.
- Individual bonds vs. municipal bond funds vs. professionally managed bond ladders, and the costs and trade-offs of each.

Rafael has been helping St. Louis families build bond portfolios for 17 years, and he'll answer your questions in plain English. Bring a recent statement if you'd like a one-on-one conversation after the presentation.

RSVP by May 9: call (314) 555-0193 or reply to this invitation. Guests are welcome.

This is an educational seminar. No specific security will be recommended and nothing will be sold at the event. Bellwether Point Securities does not provide tax or legal advice; please consult your tax professional about your own situation.
