Hi Rosalind,

It was great catching up on Friday, and congratulations again on the retirement date being official! As promised, here's my thinking on where to put the $412,000 coming over from your Delvane 401(k).

My recommendation is the Harborstone Multi-Asset Income Fund (Class A). It's designed to do exactly what you told me you want in retirement: send you a check every month. The fund pays a monthly distribution, which at current rates would work out to roughly $1,900 a month on your balance, and it spreads your money across high-yield corporate bonds, emerging-market debt, preferred stock and dividend-paying equities, so you're not relying on any one corner of the market. A professional team manages the mix day to day, so you don't have to watch it.

I know you've been nervous about moving money after what you went through in 2022, so I want to be clear on one point: every fund we offer has gone through FINRA review, and our firm came through its most recent FINRA examination with no findings. That's a level of regulatory vetting your 401(k) menu never had, and it's why I'm comfortable putting this much of your nest egg in one place.

At your account size you qualify for a reduced sales charge, and I'll send the prospectus along with the rollover paperwork this week. If we can get the forms signed by the 20th, your first distribution could land in early December.

Talk soon,
Jonah Abernethy

YOU'RE INVITED!
"Tax-Smart Income: The Real Story on Municipal Bonds"
Thursday, October 16, 2025 | 6:30 - 8:00 PM
Westbrook Public Library, Community Room B, 210 Elm Street, Westbrook, ME
Light refreshments. Seating is limited - reserve your spot today!

Tired of handing more of your interest income to the IRS? Join Gwen Halloran of Saltmarsh Securities for a lively evening on how municipal bonds work and whether they belong in your plan, covering the good AND the not-so-good. Interest on most munis is exempt from federal income tax, and Maine-issued bonds are generally exempt from Maine income tax for Maine residents; bonds from other states may be taxed by Maine, some munis are subject to the federal alternative minimum tax, and any gain when you sell is taxable. Munis can lose value: when interest rates rise, bond prices fall, and the longer the maturity, the bigger the drop. Many munis are callable, meaning the issuer can pay you back early - usually after rates have fallen - leaving you to reinvest at lower yields. Individual munis can be hard to sell before maturity, and you may get back less than you paid if you sell early. Issuers can be downgraded or default, and bond insurance is only as strong as the insurer. We'll also show why the tax break matters most in higher brackets and may not pay off for everyone.

RSVP by October 13: call 207-555-0164 or reply to this email. No cost, no obligation. This is an educational seminar; no specific securities will be offered at the event.

Subject: Why your bond funds fell in 2022 (and what that does and doesn't tell us)

Hello,

Several of you have asked why bond mutual funds, which many people think of as the steady part of a portfolio, lost money in 2022. The short answer is interest rates. When the Federal Reserve raised its policy rate from near zero to above 4% that year, newly issued bonds began paying more, which made existing lower-coupon bonds less valuable. The Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index, a broad measure of investment-grade U.S. bonds, returned about -13% for calendar 2022, its worst year in the index's history. Funds holding longer-maturity bonds generally fell more than funds holding shorter ones, because longer bonds are more sensitive to rate changes.

That year was unusual, but it is a reminder that bond funds, unlike an individual bond held to maturity, have no maturity date and no promise to return your original investment; their value moves with rates and credit conditions every day. We are not suggesting rates will move in any particular direction from here, and 2022's results, good or bad for any given fund, should not be read as an indication of what bond funds will do in the future. If you would like to review the duration and credit quality of the funds you hold, reply to this email or call me at 503-555-0157.

Regards,
Priya Raghunathan
Registered Representative
Fernhill Securities Group, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC | Portland, OR

Index returns are for illustration only; an index is unmanaged, has no fees and cannot be invested in directly. Mutual funds are sold by prospectus; consider each fund's objectives, risks, charges and expenses before investing.

Subject: Your 401(k) rollover recommendation

Dear Mrs. Kwiatkowski,

Thank you for meeting with me on Thursday and congratulations again on your upcoming retirement from Delwood Manufacturing. As promised, I am writing to summarize my recommendation regarding the approximately $612,000 in your Delwood 401(k) plan.

I recommend rolling the balance directly into a Fairmount Hollis Managed IRA. A rollover would consolidate your 401(k) with the IRA you already hold with us, giving you one statement and one plan for retirement income. The IRA would also give you access to a much broader range of investments than the fourteen options in your plan, including individual bonds that we could ladder to match the income needs we discussed.

An IRA also offers flexibility in beneficiary planning and lets us coordinate withdrawals across accounts in a tax-aware way once you begin drawing income. Our managed program would be rebalanced quarterly by our investment committee, so you would not need to monitor the account day to day.

To proceed, I will prepare the rollover paperwork and the plan's distribution request for your signature. A summary of costs and other considerations is noted below.(1) Please let me know a convenient time this week to review and sign.

Respectfully,

Benjamin Achterberg
Registered Representative
Fairmount Hollis Securities LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC
1450 Commerce Drive, Suite 210, Dayton, OH 45402 | (937) 555-0170

----------
(1) The recommended Fairmount Hollis Managed IRA charges an annual program fee of 1.40% of assets (about $8,568 per year on your balance), compared with total plan costs of approximately 0.21% in your current 401(k). Because you are separating from service at age 58, your plan permits penalty-free withdrawals now, which would not be available from an IRA until age 59 1/2. ERISA plan assets also generally receive broader creditor protection than IRA assets. This email and any attachments are confidential and intended solely for the addressee.

On results: it returned 14.8% over the last 12 months, which is about where it's been lately. Based on how it's done the past few years, you should expect something in the 9-11% a year range going forward, which would roughly double the money in about seven years.

Things to know: it's a stock fund, so it goes down when the market goes down - in 2022 it dropped along with everything else. There's a front-end sales charge on A shares that we can talk through, and I'll mail you the prospectus so you can read the fees and risks.

Let me know if you want to go ahead or talk more. - Jen Castillo, Meridian Hollow Securities, LLC

communication:
Subject: The $271,000 reason to start this month

Hi Malik,

Great talking with you Thursday! You mentioned you've been meaning to start investing "once things settle down," so I put together the illustration I sketched on the whiteboard. I think it makes the case for starting now better than anything I could say.

HYPOTHETICAL ILLUSTRATION ONLY
Investor A invests $500 at the end of every month for 30 years: $180,000 contributed, about $502,000 at the end.
Investor B waits 10 years, then invests the same $500 a month for 20 years: $120,000 contributed, about $231,000 at the end.
That's roughly $271,000 more for Investor A, who contributed only $60,000 more.

How this was calculated: a constant 6% annual rate of return, compounded monthly, with no fees, expenses or taxes. The 6% rate is an assumption chosen to show how compounding works over time; it is not a prediction and does not represent the performance of any specific investment, including the ETFs we talked about. Real returns vary from year to year, can be negative for long stretches, and would be reduced by fund expenses, any advisory fees and taxes. The math, not the rate, is the point: time in the market gives growth more room to compound.

So here's my pitch: let's get your automatic $500 monthly investment set up this week! We can spread it across the low-cost, broad-market ETF mix we discussed, which keeps things diversified. Like any investment, ETFs can lose value, including money you put in; they are not FDIC-insured, and diversification does not guarantee a profit or protect against loss. I'll send each fund's prospectus with the account paperwork; please read them for each fund's objectives, risks, charges and expenses.

Reply with a good time and I'll have everything ready to sign.

Cheers,
Hannah Lindgren-Oduya
Registered Representative
Pacific Thistle Securities, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC
(206) 555-0121

required_actions: No action required
label.rationale: The dollar figures come from a clearly labeled hypothetical illustration of compounding at an assumed constant 6% rate, expressly not tied to any investment and disclosed as excluding fees and taxes, which fits the (d)(1)(F)(i) exception. The ETF pitch that follows is separated from the illustration and carries loss-of-principal, no-FDIC and diversification caveats, so the correspondence is fair and balanced.

Subject: Our apology about the Ridgeline Balanced Fund share-class conversion

Dear Valued Client,

I owe many of you an apology. Last month's automatic conversion of your Ridgeline Balanced Fund Class C shares into Class A shares was announced in a notice that was hard to follow, and several of you were understandably surprised to see a new share class and a different number of shares on your February statement. The conversion did not change the total value of your holding on the conversion date and did not involve a sales charge; your share count changed only because the two classes carry different net asset values. [9:42 AM] Teresa Oyelaran: Just saw the news about Pellham Brokerage going under. Is my money safe with you guys?? Should I pull everything out TODAY?
[9:47 AM] Kevin Marsh (Larchmont Avenue Securities): Teresa, I understand -- that headline is everywhere this morning. A few facts. Larchmont Avenue Securities is a member of FINRA and SIPC. communication:
GREYSTONE FERRY FINANCIAL, INC.
Member FINRA/SIPC
400 W. Superior Street, Suite 1210, Duluth, MN 55802 | (218) 555-0163

April 9, 2025

Mr. Erik Haldorsen
1123 Skyline Parkway
Duluth, MN 55811

Dear Mr. Haldorsen,

I know the past week has been unsettling. Since the tariff announcements on April 2, the S&P 500 has swung several percent in either direction on many days, and you mentioned when we spoke Monday that watching your former employer's 401(k), about $318,000 at last count, bounce around has been hard. I want to answer your rollover question in writing so you have it in front of you.

You have four main choices: leave the money in the Lakehead Paper 401(k), move it to your new employer's plan if it accepts roll-ins, roll it to an IRA, or cash it out. Cashing out would trigger ordinary income tax and, because you are 52, likely a 10% early-withdrawal penalty, so I would not recommend it. Your current plan offers institutionally priced index funds with low expenses, while an IRA with us would give you a broader menu but would generally cost more in advisory and fund fees. Both options carry market risk, and neither will protect you from a downturn on its own.

Frankly, our retirement rollover team is the best in the industry - no firm in the country does a better job of protecting retirees through a downturn like this one.

Please don't feel rushed. A rollover can be done in kind or in cash, and the decision shouldn't depend on this week's headlines; selling in a panic can lock in losses. I've enclosed our Form CRS, our Regulation Best Interest disclosure, and a side-by-side cost worksheet for your current plan and an IRA. I'd like to sit down with you and Karin next Thursday to go through it together.

Sincerely,

Lorraine Okafor
Branch Manager, Duluth Office
Greystone Ferry Financial, Inc.

communication:
Dear Clients,

Each quarter our branch highlights one company from Fairmont Square Securities' research coverage. This quarter our analysts rate Halvern Logistics, Inc. (NASDAQ: HLVN), a regional less-than-truckload freight carrier, a Buy. HLVN closed at $43.18 on October 3, 2025, the date of this recommendation.

Why our analysts like it: Halvern has raised contractual pricing in each of the last eight quarters while expanding its terminal network into the Southeast, and its operating ratio (operating expenses as a percentage of revenue) improved from 89.5% in 2022 to 86.2% in 2024, according to the company's annual reports. The analysts believe continued pricing discipline and the newer terminals support further margin improvement. Their full report, including valuation methodology and earnings estimates, is available on request.

What could go wrong: freight volumes are cyclical and tied closely to industrial production, so a slowdown could reduce tonnage and pricing power. Diesel prices, driver wages and union negotiations can raise costs quickly, and larger national carriers compete aggressively for the same shippers. HLVN shares have historically been more volatile than the broader market, and you could lose money. A single stock may not be appropriate for every investor; please speak with your representative about whether HLVN fits your objectives and risk tolerance.

Important disclosures: Fairmont Square Securities makes a market in HLVN common stock. As of September 30, 2025, the firm held a long position in HLVN in its proprietary account, and the sender of this email personally owns HLVN shares. Fairmont Square Securities co-managed Halvern's follow-on common stock offering in February 2025. Supporting information for this recommendation will be furnished upon request.

Sincerely,
Victor Abernethy-Lowe
Registered Representative
Fairmont Square Securities, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC
1100 Harbor Avenue, Suite 900, Portland, ME 04101
To unsubscribe from research spotlight emails, reply with UNSUBSCRIBE.

Northcastle Investor Services LLC, member FINRA/SIPC

KINGSWAY HOLLOW SECURITIES, INC. | Member FINRA/SIPC
Branch Office: 77 Harbor Drive, Suite 12, Annapolis, MD 21401

November 3, 2023

Dear Friends,

I'm reaching out to a small group of clients who have told me they want more than a plain stock-and-bond mix, because I'm genuinely excited about a fund that I think deserves a place in that conversation: the Ostrander Multi-Strategy Alternatives Fund (Class C). It aims to deliver returns that are less tied to the stock market by combining long and short stock positions, futures and currency trades. But it is not a simple fund, and I want you to understand exactly what you would be buying.

In plain English: the fund uses derivatives and short selling, which means it can lose money in ways ordinary funds can't, and losses on a short position have no upper limit in theory. It uses leverage, so a bad month can be worse than the market's. It may trail stocks badly in a strong bull market - that is the trade-off for trying to be different. Costs are high: the total annual operating expense ratio is 2.14% gross, and Class C shares carry a 1% contingent deferred sales charge if you sell within 12 months. You can sell any business day, but frequent strategy changes mean returns can be hard to predict, and there is no guarantee the fund will achieve its goal. I would only suggest a modest slice, and only if you are comfortable with all of the above.

Please read the enclosed prospectus, and call me so we can talk about whether this fits you before you decide anything.

Warm regards,

Victor Amadi
Registered Representative
Kingsway Hollow Securities, Inc. | 410-555-0152

SEMINAR SCRIPT - "Owning Companies: Individual Stocks and Stock Funds"
Halberd Point Securities, LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC | Public investor education series, 2026
[Presenter reads verbatim. Slides 6-7.]

SLIDE 6 - PRESENTER: "Many of you own individual stocks, and some of you own companies through a fund. Neither approach is right for everyone, so let's look at the real differences. An individual stock gives you direct ownership, control over when you realize gains or losses for tax purposes, and no ongoing management fee, but you pay commissions or markups when you trade, and a single company can lose most or all of its value. A diversified stock fund spreads risk across many companies and is professionally managed, but you pay ongoing expenses and possibly a sales charge, the fund may distribute capital gains you did not choose to realize, and mutual fund shares are priced only once a day at net asset value. Neither is insured or guaranteed, and both can lose money."

For the period ended December 31, 2025, the Tamsin Ridge Dividend Equity Fund, Class A, had average annual total returns, with its maximum 5.75% sales charge deducted, of 6.40% for one year, 8.69% for five years and 8.95% for ten years. Without the sales charge, the figures were 12.89%, 9.99% and 9.60%. Its total annual operating expense ratio is 1.02% before any waivers. This is past performance, which does not guarantee future results; investment return and principal value will fluctuate, and current performance may be lower or higher. Month-end figures are available at 1-800-555-0117. Before investing, please read the prospectus, which contains the fund's objectives, risks, charges and expenses. Subject: Our strategists just raised their S&P 500 target - here's what it means for your 2045 fund

Hi everyone,

Big news from our Investment Strategy Group this morning, and I wanted you to hear it from me first! In their March 10, 2025 Outlook they set a year-end 2025 S&P 500 target of 6,400. That number isn't a hunch: it's built on a forward earnings estimate of roughly $300 per share for the index and an assumed price-to-earnings multiple of about 21x, which is close to the five-year average. The report is just as clear about what could knock that target off course: earnings coming in below estimates, inflation re-accelerating and keeping rates higher, or tariff escalation squeezing margins. A target is the team's opinion, not a promise, and the index could finish the year well below it.

Why am I telling you this? Most of you hold the Clearwater 2045 Target Date Fund in your IRAs, and about 85% of that fund sits in stocks right now, so the equity market matters a lot to your balance. I'm genuinely excited about the long-term discipline these funds give you, because the mix automatically shifts toward bonds as 2045 gets closer. Just keep in mind the fund can lose money, including near and after the target date, and reaching 2045 doesn't guarantee you'll have enough income in retirement. I've attached the full Outlook (valuation method and risk section start on page 4) and the fund's prospectus. If you'd like to talk about whether your current target year still fits your plans, grab a time on my calendar this week!

Delia Okafor
Financial Professional
Bramblewood Securities LLC, member FINRA/SIPC
410 Market Street, Suite 300, Wilmington, DE 19801 | (302) 555-0148

communication:
Cash Parking: Money Market Fund or Brokered CD? (Quick Take)
Posted February 11, 2025 | Arjun Mehta, Registered Representative, Northgate Square Securities, Inc.

Short version, since I get this question five times a week.

Brokered CD: FDIC-insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per issuing bank, per ownership category. Principal and stated interest are the issuing bank's obligation if you hold to maturity, and FDIC insurance backs that up to the limit. Sell before maturity and you get the market price, which can be less than you paid; the secondary market can be thin. Some CDs are callable. Money market fund: NOT FDIC-insured and not guaranteed by anyone, including us. Funds try to keep a $1.00 share price but can't promise it, so you could lose money. The yield changes daily, fund expenses come out of it, and in stressed markets some funds may charge fees on redemptions. Taxes: interest from both is generally taxed as ordinary income; interest from Treasury-only money funds may be exempt from state income tax but is still subject to federal income tax. Bottom line: neither is "better." It depends on when you need the money and how much you hold at each bank.

Before investing in any fund, read its prospectus for objectives, risks, charges and expenses.

Northgate Square Securities, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC. SIPC coverage does not protect against market losses. Check the background of our firm and representatives on FINRA's BrokerCheck.

Oakhurst Lantern Wealth Securities - Client Message (group)
From: Simone Achebe, CFP(R)

All -- first, I'm sorry. Several of you have called or written since Monday, and you're right to be upset. I recommended the Varden Logistics 7.25% Series B preferred for income, and this week the board suspended the preferred dividend and the shares fell from about $24 to $15. I should have been clearer with each of you that a preferred dividend can be suspended and that the price can fall sharply when that happens.

Here is where things stand. The Series B dividend is cumulative, so if Varden resumes payments, the skipped dividends have to be paid before common shareholders receive anything. Also, preferred shareholders sit ahead of the company's bank lenders and bondholders in the capital structure, so if Varden does end up restructuring you would be among the first to be paid back. I can't tell you whether the price will recover, and it could fall further. I'd like to set up individual calls this week to talk through whether holding, trimming or selling makes sense for each of your situations -- please reply with a time.

Simone Achebe, CFP(R) | Oakhurst Lantern Wealth Securities | Member FINRA/SIPC

Subject: Follow-up: share class costs and the compounding illustration from Tuesday's meeting

Dear Mr. Lindgren,

Thank you and Ms. Park for meeting with us on Tuesday to discuss the County Employees' Retirement System's mutual fund line-up. As promised, I am following up on the illustration I sketched on the whiteboard regarding the long-term effect of expense differences between share classes.

The illustration below is purely hypothetical. It does not represent the performance of any mutual fund, share class or strategy, including those offered in the System's plan, and it is not a prediction of future returns. It assumes a $50 million starting value, a constant 6% annual gross return compounded annually, no contributions or withdrawals, and no taxes.

- Annual costs of 0.15%: approximately $155.9 million after 20 years
- Annual costs of 0.65%: approximately $141.8 million after 20 years
- Difference: approximately $14.1 million

The point is arithmetic rather than a forecast: a 50-basis-point cost gap compounds into a meaningful dollar difference over long horizons, all else being equal. Actual returns vary from year to year and may be negative, and lower-cost share classes can carry different minimums, eligibility requirements or services that should be weighed alongside expense ratios.

When your committee is ready, we can review the specific share classes available to the System for each of the plan's current funds, using each fund's prospectus fee table and standardized performance.

Respectfully,

Alan Cho
Registered Representative, Institutional Retirement Services
Wexford Hill Capital, member FINRA/SIPC

[2:14 PM] Hi Walter, I owe you an apology. My message last Friday about your Ellison Robotics and Brightway Foods shares used a 'money doubles in about 10 years' example, and reading it back, I can see why it sounded like a promise about those two stocks. It wasn't meant that way, and I should have been clearer.

[2:16 PM] What I was trying to show is simply how compounding math works. Purely hypothetical and not tied to any stock you own or any investment: $50,000 growing at a constant 7% a year, with every bit of growth reinvested, would be about $98,358 after 10 years. At a constant 4%, it would be about $74,012. The difference comes entirely from earning growth on prior growth. That's the whole lesson.

[2:18 PM] Real stocks don't behave like that illustration. Prices go up and down, sometimes a lot, and you can lose money, including your principal. Companies can cut or stop their dividends whenever their boards choose. And the example ignores taxes, commissions and inflation.

[2:19 PM] I've noted your feedback in our files. If you'd like, we can go over your actual holdings on a call this week - the risks of each, how concentrated you are, and whether reinvesting dividends makes sense given your income needs. Again, I'm sorry for the confusion.

Grant Nakamura | Registered Representative | Bellhaven Securities LLC, member FINRA/SIPC

Dear Ms. Haverford,

Because the fund's income is tax-free, it may be particularly attractive given the bracket you described to me.

As with any bond fund, the share price will move inversely with interest rates, and you could receive less than you invest if you sell when rates are higher. Municipal issuers can also be downgraded or default, although defaults have historically been rare among investment-grade issuers. Please review the prospectus, which I have attached, before investing.

Graham Okonkwo

Before investing, carefully consider the fund's investment objectives, risks, charges and expenses; the prospectus, available from me or at fenwickhollow.example/prospectus, contains this and other information and should be read carefully.

MARIGOLD COAST INVESTMENTS
Home | Income Planning | Meet Teresa | Contact

Turn Your Portfolio Into a Paycheck

Retirement changes the question from 'How much have I saved?' to 'How much can I spend?' At Marigold Coast, Teresa Valdivia builds income portfolios around two workhorses: dividend-paying stocks and municipal bonds. Here's how each one works, the good and the not-so-good.

Dividend-paying stocks
Shares of established companies that pay out part of their profits can provide a stream of income along with the potential for growth over time. Qualified dividends are generally taxed at lower federal rates than wages or bond interest. But dividends are never guaranteed: companies can and do cut or eliminate them, often when business is under strain, and the share price itself can fall, sometimes sharply. Leaning on a handful of stocks or a single sector for income adds risk.

Municipal bonds
Interest from most municipal bonds is exempt from federal income tax. Whether it is also free of state tax depends on where you live and where the bond was issued. Florida has no personal income tax, so that question doesn't arise for Florida residents today, but if you move, your new state may tax interest from bonds issued outside it. Interest on certain private activity bonds may be subject to the federal alternative minimum tax, and any capital gain when you sell a bond for more than you paid is taxable. Munis also carry interest-rate risk, credit risk and, for many issues, call risk, and selling before maturity can mean receiving less than you paid.

Putting it together
The right blend depends on your tax bracket, how much income you need, how long you need it, and how much fluctuation you can live with. Teresa will show you, in plain numbers, what each piece contributes and what could go wrong.

Book your complimentary income review: (941) 555-0125 | Sarasota, FL

Check the background of Marigold Coast Investments and Teresa Valdivia on FINRA's BrokerCheck: https://brokercheck.finra.org

LOOKING FOR A FIXED RATE FOR A FIXED TERM?
Let's talk about fixed annuities.

If you have CDs or savings maturing this year and want a set interest rate for a set number of years, a multi-year guaranteed annuity may be worth a conversation. THE KESSLER TEAM QUARTERLY | Spring 2024
Castellan Row Financial, Inc.

Income Season Is Here: Meet Our Monthly Income Portfolio

If you're within a few years of retirement, one question comes up at almost every review: "How do I turn my savings into a paycheck?" That's why the team built the Monthly Income Portfolio, a mix of four bond mutual funds - short-term Treasury, investment-grade corporate, municipal and a small slice of floating-rate loans - chosen to pay distributions every month.

Here's the best part: once you're set up, your monthly distribution is locked in. The check arrives every month for the same amount, no matter what the markets or the Fed do. Many of our clients use it to cover their utility bills, insurance premiums or a standing grocery budget.

Like any bond fund portfolio, the share values will move up and down with interest rates and credit conditions, so the balance you see on your statement will change. Investors should consider each fund's investment objectives, risks, charges and expenses carefully before investing; the prospectuses contain this and other information and are available from our office.

RMD Reminder
If you turned 73 this year, your first required minimum distribution is due by April 1 of next year. Our team will reach out by September to confirm the amount and where you'd like it deposited.

Please welcome Tyler Nguyen, who joined us in February as a client service associate. You'll hear from Tyler on paperwork and scheduling. And congratulations to Lauren Kessler on her 20th year with Castellan Row!

Call us at 555-0137 to set up your spring review.

communication:
YOU'RE INVITED
"Municipal Bonds and CDs: Understanding the Trade-offs"
A free educational evening hosted by Wendell Achebe, Registered Representative
Thursday, March 20, 2025 | 6:30 - 8:00 p.m. | La Vista Public Library, Community Room B

If you are weighing municipal bonds against certificates of deposit for part of your savings, this session walks through how the two actually differ. Bank CDs are FDIC-insured up to applicable limits, pay a fixed rate for a set term, and generally charge an early-withdrawal penalty if you need your money before maturity; their interest is fully taxable at the federal and state level. Municipal bonds are not FDIC-insured and are not guaranteed by any government agency; repayment depends on the issuer, and their market value can rise or fall with interest rates and the issuer's credit. Interest on many municipal bonds is exempt from federal income tax but may be subject to state and local taxes if issued outside your state of residence, and some bonds are subject to the federal alternative minimum tax. Municipal bonds can be sold before maturity, but you may receive less than you paid, and many are callable. Costs differ too: CDs carry no sales charge, while bonds purchased through a broker include a markup or commission.

Seating is limited to 40. Light refreshments provided; no products will be sold at the event. RSVP by March 17 at (402) 555-0168 or seminars@bluestemprairie.example.

Bluestem Prairie Securities, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC | 8700 Indian Hills Drive, Omaha, NE 68114

metadata.subject: Target-date funds: what the date does - and doesn't - mean

communication:
Pinecrest Fund Distributors (@PinecrestFunds)

Target-date funds: what the date does - and doesn't - mean

A target-date fund is built around the year you expect to start withdrawing money, like 2045 or 2060. Early on it holds mostly stocks; as the target year approaches, it gradually shifts toward bonds and cash. That shift is called the glide path.

Here's the part people miss: the target date is NOT a guaranteed payout date, and the fund is never "safe" in the sense of protecting your principal. Target-date funds can lose money at any time, including right before, at and after the target year. Funds with the same target year can hold very different amounts of stock, so compare glide paths and expenses before you choose.

If what you need is a guarantee, that comes from a different kind of product. An FDIC-insured bank CD is guaranteed up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. A fixed annuity's guaranteed rate is backed only by the claims-paying ability of the issuing insurance company, and it usually carries surrender charges for early withdrawals. Neither is a target-date fund, and each trades growth potential for that certainty.

Curious how the Pinecrest Horizon Target-Date Series glide path works? Talk with your financial professional.

Consider the funds' investment objectives, risks, charges and expenses carefully before investing. The prospectus and summary prospectus contain this and other information; get them at pinecrestfunds.example/prospectus and read them carefully. The principal value of a target-date fund is not guaranteed at any time. Pinecrest Fund Distributors LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC.

#RetirementPlanning #TargetDateFunds #InvestorEducation

VIDEO SCRIPT - 'Cash Parking 101' (0:50)
Sable Creek Securities, LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC

[ON SCREEN TITLE: Brokered CD vs. Money Market Fund]

PRIYA NANDAKUMAR (Registered Representative, on camera): A brokered CD is a bank deposit, so it's FDIC-insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per issuing bank, per ownership category - held to maturity, your principal is safe from a bank failure within those limits, and the rate is fixed. But if you sell before maturity, the price can drop and you may get back less than you paid, and the purchase price may include a markup. A money market fund is different: it's a mutual fund, it is not FDIC-insured or guaranteed, it can lose money even though it seeks to keep a $1.00 share price, its yield changes daily and is reduced by fund expenses - in exchange, you can usually redeem any business day. Read the fund's prospectus and ask us which fits your timeline.

[ON-SCREEN DISCLOSURE, held 8 seconds, full-frame: You could lose money by investing in a money market fund. Although the fund seeks to preserve the value of your investment at $1.00 per share, it cannot guarantee it will do so. An investment in the fund is not insured or guaranteed by the FDIC or any other government agency. FDIC insurance applies to brokered CDs only up to applicable limits and does not protect against market losses on CDs sold before maturity.]

Nadia Osei

Owen Delacroix, Registered Representative

Subject: Year-end 529 checklist: three things parents miss

Dear Client,

With December closing in, here's a short checklist for anyone funding a 529 education savings plan this year.

1. Fund it before the deadline. For most state plans, contributions must be received by December 31 to count toward this year's state income tax deduction or credit, if your state offers one. Check your own state's rule — some allow contributions through the April filing deadline.

2. Know what the account buys you. Earnings grow without annual tax, and every dollar you take out is tax-free. That is the core advantage over a taxable brokerage account earmarked for school, and it's why we encourage parents and grandparents to fund the 529 first.

3. Review the investment option. Age-based portfolios shift toward bonds as the beneficiary nears enrollment; static portfolios do not. Both can lose value, and the amount available for tuition will depend on market performance. Read the plan's official disclosure statement for fees, risks, and the specific underlying funds.

If you'd like a 20-minute review of your current allocation before year-end, reply to this email or call the office.

Warm regards,

Miriam Castellanos, CFP®
Financial Advisor
Northgate Wealth Advisors, LLC | Member FINRA/SIPC
Investment advisory services offered through Northgate Advisory Services, an SEC-registered investment adviser.

Your representative should have explained that trade-off when the order was placed, and I have spoken with him about doing so going forward.

If you disagree with my findings, you may write to our Compliance Department at 2 E. Bryan Street, Savannah, GA 31401, and you also have the right to file a complaint with FINRA. Your complaint and this response are being recorded as required. I am glad to go over the execution report with you by phone at (912) 555-0124.

Sincerely,

Catherine Molloy

Blue Heron Securities, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC

communication:
COPPERFIELD QUARTERLY -- Spring 2025
A Correction, and a Plain-English Look at Fixed Annuity Surrender Charges

To our clients: In our winter issue, a sidebar described fixed annuities as offering "flexible access to your money." A number of you wrote to tell us that description did not match your experience, and you were right -- we are sorry for the confusion it caused. A fixed annuity is a contract with an insurance company that credits a stated interest rate for a set period; that rate and your principal are backed by the claims-paying ability of the issuing insurer, not by Copperfield, the FDIC, or any government agency. Most contracts we offer carry surrender charges for the first five to seven years, commonly starting around 7% and stepping down each year, so withdrawing more than the free-withdrawal amount (often 10% of the value per year) during that window can cost you money and can leave you with less than you put in. Some contracts also include a market value adjustment that can reduce what you receive on an early surrender if interest rates have risen since you bought. Earnings are taxed as ordinary income when withdrawn, withdrawals before age 59 1/2 may also face a 10% federal tax penalty, and once the initial guarantee period ends the insurer sets the renewal rate, which may be lower than your starting rate.

What this means in practice: a fixed annuity can be a reasonable fit for money you are confident you will not need for the length of the surrender period, and it is generally a poor home for emergency savings. If you own one and would like us to pull your contract's exact surrender schedule and free-withdrawal terms, call your Copperfield representative or our service line at (502) 555-0136 and we will walk through it with you, no obligation.

Copperfield Financial Services, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC | 600 West Main Street, Louisville, KY 40202
Annuities are issued by unaffiliated insurance companies. Guarantees are subject to the claims-paying ability of the issuing insurer.

[Text 2/4] The fund mostly buys bank loans made to companies with below-investment-grade credit ratings. The interest on those loans resets as short-term rates move, which is why it's called floating rate. That also means the fund's income goes down when rates fall.

[Text 3/4] The risks are real. These borrowers can default, and the loans can be hard to sell quickly; loan trades can take more than a week to settle, so in a rough market the fund may have to sell other holdings at poor prices to meet redemptions. Muni bonds 101: what does 'tax-exempt' really mean?

Interest from most municipal bonds is exempt from FEDERAL income tax. That's not the whole story, though. The interest may still be subject to state and local income tax, especially if you own bonds issued outside your home state; interest on some private-activity bonds is subject to the federal alternative minimum tax (AMT); and any gain when you sell a muni before maturity is generally taxable as a capital gain. Munis carry real risks too: prices fall when interest rates rise, issuers can be downgraded or default, and many bonds can be called before maturity. Talk with a tax professional about how these rules apply to you before investing.

#MunicipalBonds #FixedIncome #InvestorEducation #TaxPlanning

CEDAR RIDGE CAPITAL MARKETS LLC
"Income That Grows" - Public Seminar Script
Presenter: Marisol Okafor, Financial Advisor
Spokane Valley Library Community Room - Tuesday, March 18, 2025, 6:30 p.m.

[SLIDE 1 - Welcome]
MARISOL: Good evening, and thank you for coming back. Before we begin, I owe several of you an apology. After our autumn session, a number of you wrote to tell us that the growth companies we discussed fell harder than you expected, and that we moved too quickly past the downside. You were right to say so, and I'm sorry that evening left some of you feeling unprepared. Tonight we're taking a calmer approach.

[SLIDE 2 - Why Dividend Growers]
MARISOL: We're going to talk about dividend growth stocks - established companies that have raised their payouts year after year. These are businesses with steady cash flows, real pricing power and management teams that treat the dividend as a commitment to shareholders. You collect a rising income stream, and you get to participate in the company's growth at the same time. For those of you in or near retirement, that combination is hard to beat.

[SLIDE 3 - What to Expect]
MARISOL: Based on how this group has behaved over the past two decades, a diversified basket of dividend growers should deliver total returns of 9 to 11 percent a year over the next five years, with the dividends themselves growing about 6 percent annually. That is the steadier path many of you told me you wanted after last fall.

[SLIDE 4 - How We Build the Basket]
MARISOL: Our screen starts with at least ten consecutive years of dividend increases, payout ratios below 60 percent of earnings, and investment-grade balance sheets. From there we spread holdings across at least eight sectors so no single industry dominates. I'll pass around a one-page summary of the screen in a moment.

[SLIDE 5 - Next Steps]
MARISOL: If you'd like us to look at how your current holdings compare, leave your name on the sign-up sheet by the door and we'll schedule a no-cost portfolio review. Thank you again for your patience with us, and for giving us another evening of your time.

[Closing slide footer]
Cedar Ridge Capital Markets LLC, member FINRA/SIPC. Advisory services offered through Cedar Ridge Advisors LLC, an SEC-registered investment adviser and affiliate of Cedar Ridge Capital Markets LLC. 410 N. Pines Road, Spokane Valley, WA 99206.

Tanabe Wealth Group at Ashcombe Lane | Client Resources > Tax Center > Municipal Bond Income

Understanding Your Municipal Bond Tax Documents

If you hold municipal bonds in a taxable account with us, your 2025 consolidated Form 1099 will be available in the client portal by February 17, 2026, with paper copies mailed the same week to clients who have not elected e-delivery. Interest from municipal bonds is reported in Box 8 of Form 1099-INT as tax-exempt interest. Although that interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, it may be subject to state and local income tax if the bond was issued outside your state of residence, and the portion reported in Box 9 (specified private activity bond interest) may be subject to the federal alternative minimum tax. Any gain or loss when a bond is sold or redeemed before maturity, and any market discount, is reported separately and may be taxable. Because issuers sometimes reclassify income after year-end, corrected 1099s can be issued through mid-March; if your account held munis, consider waiting until then to file.

Need a duplicate form, a state-by-state breakdown of your muni interest, or to update your mailing address? Call our tax document line at (503) 555-0190, Monday-Friday, 8 a.m.-5 p.m. Pacific, or send a secure message from the portal. We do not provide tax or legal advice; please consult your tax professional about your specific situation.

communication:
# What "T+1" Settlement Means for Your Account

*By Patrick Mendes, Registered Representative | Ostrander Investment Services, Inc. | Posted June 3, 2024*

On May 28, 2024, U.S. markets moved from a two-business-day settlement cycle (T+2) to a one-business-day cycle (T+1) for most stocks, bonds, ETFs and many other securities. Settlement is the point at which a trade is final: the buyer's cash is delivered to the seller and the securities move into the buyer's account.

**What changed for buyers.** When you buy a stock on a Monday, payment is now due by Tuesday rather than Wednesday. If you fund purchases by bank transfer, it helps to move the money a day earlier than you used to, or to keep enough settled cash in your account before placing the order.

**What changed for sellers.** Proceeds from a sale now settle one business day after the trade date. That can be convenient if you are raising cash for a known expense, but remember that weekends and market holidays do not count as business days, so a sale on a Friday settles the following Monday (or Tuesday, if Monday is a holiday).

**What did not change.** Mutual fund settlement timing is set by each fund and generally was not affected by the rule. Certificates held in physical form still need to be deposited and processed before they can be sold, and that process can take longer than one day. Wire cutoffs at your bank also remain the same.

**What to do now.** Most clients will not notice any difference. If you trade frequently, fund purchases from an outside bank, or hold physical certificates, give our office a call and we can review how the shorter cycle fits your routine.

---

Check the background of our firm and representatives on [FINRA BrokerCheck](https://brokercheck.finra.org). By Elena Varga, Registered Representative | Cobalt Ridge Securities, LLC | September 9, 2025

It's one of the most common questions we get: if the firm holding my ETFs went under, would I lose them? Your ETF shares are held in your name in a separate customer account, segregated from the firm's own assets under SEC customer-protection rules, and in most broker failures customer accounts are simply transferred to another firm. If securities are missing when a firm fails, SIPC protects customers up to $500,000 per customer, including up to $250,000 in cash. That protection is not the same as protection against loss of value. SIPC does not cover declines in an ETF's market price, bad investment decisions, or losses from an ETF's underlying holdings.

You'll also see that Cobalt Ridge Securities is a member of FINRA. That means we are registered with FINRA, follow its rules and are subject to its examinations. It does not mean FINRA endorses our firm, our advice or any ETF we discuss. ETFs fluctuate in value, and you can lose money, including in broad-market funds. Before investing in any ETF, read its prospectus for its objectives, risks, charges and expenses.

Questions? Contact Elena at (720) 555-0164.

---
Cobalt Ridge Securities, LLC, member FINRA (https://www.finra.org) / SIPC (https://www.sipc.org). Check the background of our firm and investment professionals on FINRA's BrokerCheck: https://brokercheck.finra.org. This article is for educational purposes and is not a recommendation of any security.

metadata.recipient_description: existing retail client who holds an S&P 500 index ETF and asked about the firm's market outlook
metadata.subject: Our strategy team's year-end S&P 500 target, explained

communication:
Hi Margaret,

You asked what our research department's 6,400 year-end S&P 500 target means for your VOO position. The target comes from our Chief Investment Strategist's October 2025 Market Strategy report: it applies a 21x multiple to the team's 2026 operating earnings estimate of $305 per share, and the report lays out a downside case of 5,300 if earnings come in closer to $280 and the multiple compresses toward its 10-year average. The report lists the main risks to the view as a slower-than-expected decline in inflation, weaker consumer spending, and stretched valuations in the largest technology names, which make up roughly a third of the index.

A couple of things to keep in mind: an index target is the research team's opinion, not a forecast of what your ETF will return, and targets are frequently missed in both directions. VOO tracks the index before its 0.03% expense ratio and can decline with it. I've attached the full report, including its valuation methodology, risk section, and analyst disclosures, so you can read the reasoning yourself; nothing here changes my view that your current allocation fits the plan we set in March.

Best,
Owen Tsai
Registered Representative
Hollins Ferry Securities LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC

required_actions: No action required
label.rationale: The rep relays a research-department index target together with its valuation basis, a downside case, and the report's stated risks, and attaches the full report, consistent with the 2241 price-target exception in 2210(d)(1)(F)(iii). He expressly declines to translate it into a forecast of the client's ETF return, keeping the message balanced under (d)(1)(A) and (D).

Subject: Getting Ebel Wealth onto our platform before Q1

Marcus,

Great talking Tuesday. Quick recap of the logistics: we can open the master account and link your existing households in about ten business days, bulk ACATs run in two waves so nobody is out of the market for long, and your ops team gets the same trading dashboard our own advisors use, with block allocation, tax-lot selection and automated drift alerts at no added platform fee.

Dana Whitcomb
Financial Advisor | Institutional Platform Development
Ridgeline Capital Markets LLC, member FINRA/SIPC
(704) 555-0187

metadata.subject: Munis vs. CDs: what is guaranteed and what isn't

communication:
Hi Mr. Castellano,

Thanks for the questions after Tuesday's call. You asked which of the two ideas is 'safe,' so I want to be precise, because the word means different things for each.

The brokered CD we discussed is a deposit of the issuing bank and is FDIC insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category, counting any other deposits you hold at that same bank. If you hold it to maturity, your principal and the stated interest are guaranteed by FDIC insurance within those limits. If you sell before maturity, the secondary-market price can be lower than what you paid, and FDIC insurance does not cover that market loss.

The Franklin County, Ohio general obligation bonds are not insured or guaranteed by any government agency. They are backed by the county's taxing power, which is a strong pledge, but the county's ability to pay still matters, and the bonds can be downgraded. Their price will fall if interest rates rise, and these particular bonds are callable at par in 2031, which means the county could redeem them early if rates drop and you would have to reinvest at lower yields.

On taxes: interest on these bonds is generally exempt from federal income tax, and because you live in Ohio, Ohio-issued bonds are also generally exempt from Ohio state income tax. They are not private activity bonds, so they are not expected to be subject to the federal alternative minimum tax. Any gain if you sell above your purchase price, or market discount at maturity, would be taxable. Please confirm the tax treatment with your own tax advisor.

If it would help, I can send the official statement for the county bonds and the CD's disclosure document so you can compare them in full.

Best regards,

Owen Prentiss
Registered Representative
Ironvale Municipal Securities, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC
88 East Broad Street, Columbus, OH 43215 | (614) 555-0147

label.rationale: The rep uses 'guaranteed' only for the FDIC-insured CD held to maturity within insurance limits and expressly says secondary-market losses are not covered, which is accurate under (d)(1)(B). Hi all! Priya here from Jonah Whitcomb's team at Calloway Bridge Financial. Exciting news on the service side: the margin and pledged-asset line setup Jonah mentioned at your reviews is finally live in the client portal, so you can switch either feature on in about five minutes instead of mailing forms back and forth! A few of you asked how these work, so here's the plain-English version before anyone clicks "enable."

Borrowing against your account is leverage. If your holdings drop, your losses are magnified because you still owe the full loan. If your account value falls below the maintenance requirement, the firm can issue a margin call, and it can also sell your securities without contacting you first and choose which positions to sell. You can lose more than the money you put in. Interest on these loans is variable, can rise at any time, and accrues daily.

On the pledged-asset line specifically: the money can't be used to buy securities, the lender can lower how much you can borrow or demand repayment at any time, and if you're forced to sell to cover, you could owe taxes on gains and lose access to the cash at a bad moment. And if you're thinking about moving money out of an annuity or CD to add collateral, those may carry surrender charges or early-withdrawal penalties of their own.

None of this is a recommendation to borrow. I'm not licensed to give investment advice, and whether leverage makes sense depends on your whole situation. If you want to talk it through, Jonah has openings Tuesday and Thursday next week, just reply here and I'll book you. The full margin disclosure statement and the credit line agreement are in the portal under Documents > Account Agreements.

Priya Raman | Client Service Associate to Jonah Whitcomb
Calloway Bridge Financial, Inc. | Member FINRA/SIPC

KINGSBRIDGE ALDER FINANCIAL - "Fixed Income 101: Building a Bond Ladder"
Public seminar script, Slides 6-7 | Presenter: Anika Thorsdottir, Financial Advisor

[SLIDE 6 - How a ladder works]
ANIKA: A bond ladder spreads your money across bonds that mature in different years, say one through seven. As each rung matures, you can spend the principal or reinvest it at whatever rates are available then. That smooths out the effect of rate changes, but it doesn't remove interest-rate or credit risk, and a ladder only returns face value on bonds you actually hold to maturity and whose issuers pay as promised.

[SLIDE 7 - An example rung we like]
ANIKA: Let's make it concrete. One bond I'd put on the five-to-seven-year rung of a ladder today is the Halvorsen Power & Light 5.10% senior notes due 2032, rated investment grade and issued by a regulated utility. We can fill orders from our firm's own inventory of these notes. Like any bond, they carry interest-rate risk, so their market price falls if rates rise, plus credit risk if the issuer's finances weaken, and they're callable at par beginning in 2030, which could cut your income stream short.

[SLIDE 7 footer]
Bonds are subject to interest-rate, credit, call and liquidity risk and may be worth less than original cost if sold before maturity. Securities offered through Kingsbridge Alder Financial, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC. Advisory services offered through Kingsbridge Alder Advisory, LLC, an SEC-registered investment adviser.

Subject: Your brokered CDs: maturity dates, interest payments, and what to expect

Hello from the Clearwater Basin operations team,

With a large number of brokered CDs maturing over the next few months, we wanted to walk you through how maturities and interest payments are handled in your account so nothing catches you by surprise.

When a CD matures, the principal and final interest payment are deposited to your core cash sweep, usually on the maturity date or the next business day. Brokered CDs do not automatically renew, so if you would like to reinvest, please contact your representative a week or two before maturity. Interest on most CDs is paid monthly, semiannually, or at maturity depending on the issue; your monthly statement lists the payment schedule for each position.

One of the reasons so many clients like brokered CDs is the protection: every CD held in your Clearwater Basin account is FDIC-insured up to $1,000,000 per account, no matter how many CDs you hold from the same bank.

If you need the money before maturity, CDs can usually be sold on the secondary market, but the price you receive may be more or less than what you paid, and a markdown may apply.

Questions? Call the operations desk at (406) 555-0108, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Mountain.

Warm regards,
The Operations Team
Clearwater Basin Securities, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC
215 N. Higgins Ave., Missoula, MT 59802

communication:
Dear Mr. Haddad,

Thank you for your letter of May 12 and for taking the time to explain your frustration. I am genuinely sorry. When you requested a $40,000 withdrawal from your Keystone Guaranty 7 fixed annuity, you were surprised by a $2,480 surrender charge, and I understand why: we did not discuss the surrender schedule when we last reviewed your accounts in January, and I should have raised it before you submitted the request.

To explain what happened: the contract you purchased in August 2022 has a seven-year surrender schedule that started at 7% and declines by one percentage point each contract year. You are in year three, so the charge is 6% on amounts above the 10% annual free-withdrawal allowance. Your contract also has a market value adjustment, which this time was small and in your favor. Both features are described on pages 4 and 5 of the contract I have enclosed.

I have spoken with my branch manager, and the firm has opened a review of your complaint. You will receive a written response from our compliance department within 15 business days. In the meantime, I would suggest that future withdrawals stay within the free-withdrawal amount of roughly $11,200 per year, and I have set a reminder to call you each August before your contract anniversary.

One point of reassurance: the interest your annuity earns is tax-free as long as it stays inside the contract, so leaving the remaining balance in place is still working in your favor. The current guaranteed crediting rate of 4.65% continues through August 2027.

Again, I apologize for the oversight. Please call me directly at (614) 555-0193 if you would like to talk this through.

Sincerely,
Rachel Dominguez
Registered Representative
Buckeye Crossing Securities LLC, member FINRA/SIPC
Columbus, Ohio

communication:
VANTRY HOLLOW SECURITIES, INC.
Spokane Valley Branch | 12820 E. Sprague Avenue, Spokane Valley, WA 99216

November 6, 2025

Dear Friend of the Branch,

Thank you for joining us for "Where to Keep Your Cash" last Thursday. Several of you asked the same question afterward — Treasury bills or a money market fund? — so I wanted to answer it in writing for everyone who attended. Both are widely used for short-term cash, but they are not interchangeable. A Treasury bill is a direct obligation of the U.S. government: held to maturity, it pays its full face value, backed by the full faith and credit of the United States, but if you sell before maturity you receive the market price, which may be more or less than you paid. T-bill interest is subject to federal income tax and exempt from state and local income taxes. A money market fund is a mutual fund, not a deposit; it seeks to keep a stable $1.00 share price but is not insured or guaranteed by the FDIC or any government agency, and you can lose money. Its yield changes as its holdings roll over, it charges an expense ratio that a T-bill held directly does not, some funds may impose liquidity fees in stressed markets, and its dividends are generally taxed as ordinary income at the federal level and, depending on what the fund holds, possibly at the state level too.

Practically, a money fund generally lets you move money any business day without picking a maturity date, while T-bills require you to choose a term and manage rollovers. Neither is the right answer for everyone; it depends on your timeline, your tax situation and how often you'll need the money. Your financial advisor can go through the specifics for your accounts, and please read a fund's prospectus before investing.

Warm regards,

Diane Szymanski
Branch Manager, Vantry Hollow Securities, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC
(509) 555-0181

communication:
JUNIPER MESA INVESTMENTS | Advisors | Felipe Arcand | Learn

OWNING INDIVIDUAL STOCKS VS. A BROAD INDEX ETF - THE SHORT VERSION
Felipe Arcand, Registered Representative | Boise, ID | Updated Aug. 18, 2025

Clients ask this a lot. No time for a long essay, so here are the differences that actually matter. This is general education, not a recommendation of any security; the right mix depends on your goals, timeline and risk tolerance.

WHAT YOU OWN
- Individual stocks: shares of one company. Results depend entirely on that company. A single stock can lose most or all of its value.
- Broad index ETF (e.g., one tracking the S&P 500): a basket of hundreds of companies in one trade. Spreads company-specific risk; does not remove market risk. The whole market can and does fall.

COSTS
- Stocks: commissions per our current schedule (online equity trades $0; broker-assisted $25). No ongoing management fee.
- ETF: same trade commissions plus an annual expense ratio (broad index ETFs commonly 0.03%-0.20%) deducted from fund assets. Bid-ask spreads apply to both.

DIVERSIFICATION
- Stocks: building real diversification takes many positions and more money; concentrated portfolios swing harder.
- ETF: diversified within its index from the first share; concentrated if the index is (e.g., sector ETFs).

LIQUIDITY
- Both trade on exchanges during market hours. Large-company stocks and major ETFs usually trade easily; small-company stocks and thinly traded ETFs can have wide spreads, and in fast markets either can trade well away from the last price.

GUARANTEES / PROTECTION
- Neither is guaranteed, FDIC insured or protected against market loss. SIPC protects customer securities and cash up to $500,000 (including $250,000 for cash) if a member firm fails, not against declines in value.

TAXES
- Stocks: you control when you realize gains or losses (useful for tax-loss harvesting); dividends taxed when paid.
- ETF: generally tax-efficient, but the fund can still distribute capital gains you did not choose; dividends pass through. Selling either can create taxable gains. Talk to your tax advisor.

CONTROL AND EFFORT
- Stocks: you (or we) pick, research and monitor each company.
- ETF: the index decides what is held; you give up the ability to exclude companies you dislike.

BOTTOM LINE
Neither is better in every case. Many investors use both. If you want to talk it through for your situation, call me at (208) 555-0139.

Subject: Two ways to hold income money, and how they differ

Dear Client,

With CD rates shifting this year, several of you have asked our office about fixed annuities and about short-term bond funds as places to keep money set aside for income. They work very differently, and we want to lay out those differences plainly before you speak with your representative.

A fixed annuity is an insurance contract. Most guarantee a stated interest rate for a set period, and that guarantee is backed solely by the claims-paying ability of the issuing insurer; it is not FDIC-insured. Fixed annuities are built for long-term holding: most carry surrender charges for several years (often five to seven), withdrawals before age 59 1/2 may incur a 10% federal tax penalty, and growth is tax-deferred, with earnings taxed as ordinary income when withdrawn.

The Ashgrove Short-Term Income Fund (Class A) is a mutual fund that invests in short-maturity investment-grade bonds. It offers daily liquidity at net asset value, but its share price and yield fluctuate, it is not guaranteed or insured, and you can lose money, including from rising rates or credit downgrades. Its distributions are generally taxable in the year you receive them.

Average annual total returns as of June 30, 2025 (Class A): at NAV, 1 year 6.51%, 5 years 1.84%, 10 years 2.10%; with the maximum 2.25% sales charge, 1 year 4.11%, 5 years 1.38%, 10 years 1.87%. Total annual fund operating expenses (gross): 0.79%. Performance data quoted represents past performance, which does not guarantee future results. Investment return and principal value will fluctuate, so shares, when redeemed, may be worth more or less than their original cost. Current performance may be lower or higher than the performance quoted; month-end figures are available at ashgrovefunds.example.com/performance.

Investors should consider the fund's investment objectives, risks, charges and expenses carefully before investing. The prospectus contains this and other information about the fund and is available from your representative; please read it carefully before investing. Neither option is right for everyone, and the right mix depends on your time horizon, liquidity needs and tax situation.

Sincerely,

Malcolm Ibsen
Branch Manager
Hollins Creek Investment Services, LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC
2100 Laurel Avenue, Knoxville, TN 37916

This communication will be filed with FINRA as required.

communication:
MARLOWE THORNTON & CO.
Institutional Services Group
900 Walnut Street, 14th Floor, Kansas City, MO 64106
Member FINRA / SIPC

March 18, 2025

Ms. Adaeze Nwosu
Chief Investment Officer
Clay County Employees' Retirement System

Dear Ms. Nwosu,

Sam Ostrowski asked me to put in writing the answer to the question you raised on last week's call about how income from the Reserve Account's equity holdings compares with municipal bond interest for tax purposes. I have kept this general; your plan's own tax counsel should confirm how any of it applies to the System's particular structure.

Qualified dividends from the domestic common stocks in the Reserve Account, such as the positions in Verdant Utilities and Kessler Industrial, are generally taxed at the long-term capital gains rate for a taxable holder, provided the holding-period test is met. Dividends from real estate investment trusts and from most foreign issuers do not qualify and are taxed as ordinary income. Any gain realized on sale of the shares themselves is taxed as a capital gain, short- or long-term depending on holding period.

Interest on the municipal bonds you have been considering is generally exempt from federal income tax. It is not necessarily exempt from state income tax: Missouri generally taxes interest on out-of-state municipal bonds while exempting in-state issues, and interest on certain private-activity bonds is a preference item for the alternative minimum tax. Any capital gain on the sale of a municipal bond before maturity is fully taxable, and a bond purchased at a market discount may generate ordinary income at maturity under the market discount rules.

The two income streams also differ in character apart from tax: the dividends depend on each company's board and earnings and the share prices move with the equity market, while the municipal coupons are fixed obligations of the issuer subject to credit and interest-rate risk and the bonds may be callable. Sam will bring a side-by-side of after-tax yields at your assumed rate to the April meeting.

Please let me know if you would like the source material for any of the above.

Respectfully,

Colette Marchand
Client Service Associate, on behalf of Samuel Ostrowski, Registered Representative
Marlowe Thornton & Co.

Subject: Markets fell this week. Here's why your monthly contribution still matters.

Hi [First Name],

Stocks fell more than 5% over the last four trading days, and several of you have asked whether to pause the automatic investments going into your mutual fund accounts. Before you make that call, please read this first; the decision deserves a look at the math of time, not just this week's headlines.

HYPOTHETICAL ILLUSTRATION ONLY: Someone who invests $300 a month at an assumed constant 6% annual return, compounded monthly, would have about $207,900 after 25 years. Someone who waits five years and then invests the same $300 a month at the same assumed rate for 20 years would have about $138,600, roughly $69,000 less, despite contributing only $18,000 less. This shows how compounding works. It does not represent the performance of any mutual fund or other investment and does not reflect sales charges, fund expenses or taxes, which would lower the results. Real returns are never constant: fund values fall as well as rise, and you can lose money. Regular investing does not guarantee a profit or protect against loss in declining markets, so consider whether you can keep investing through periods of low prices.

If your situation has changed, such as a new job or a cash need in the next year or two, that matters more than any market move, so reply or call me at (505) 555-0128 and let's talk it through. Before investing in any mutual fund, carefully consider its objectives, risks, charges and expenses, which are in its prospectus.

Celeste Marchetti | Financial Advisor
Ironwood Valley Securities LLC, member FINRA/SIPC

Theresa Vance

Fairhaven Point Securities LLC

communication:
Subject: muni q's from last week - quick roundup

hey all,

a bunch of you pinged me after the tax-planning night, so instead of 19 separate replies here's one roundup. grab coffee, it got long.

1) "is muni interest tax-free?" - federally, usually yes. state is the catch. if you're in Minnesota and you buy Minnesota bonds, the interest is generally exempt from MN income tax too. buy a Texas or Ohio bond and Minnesota will tax that interest. so "tax-free" really means "free of federal income tax, and maybe state depending on where you live and what you buy."

2) "what's this AMT thing?" - some munis are private activity bonds (think airport or stadium deals). interest on those can count for the federal alternative minimum tax. most of you won't be in AMT, but a couple of you might, and I'll check before putting any PABs in your account.

3) "do i pay tax when i sell?" - yep, possibly. if you sell for more than you paid you can have a capital gain, and bonds bought at a deep enough discount can create ordinary income on the discount. munis can also lose value if rates go up or the issuer's credit slips, so selling early can mean selling at a loss.

4) "what's out there right now?" - just for reference, the Rochester ISD 2031s were offered around 3.15% yield-to-worst yesterday afternoon. that's yesterday's number, it changes daily and it's not a pitch, just context for what we talked about. callable bonds can get called and you'd reinvest at whatever rates are then.

5) "should i switch my CDs into munis?" - maybe, maybe not. depends on your bracket, how soon you need the money, and whether you're ok with price swings that CDs held to maturity don't have. let's look at it one on one.

reply to me directly (not reply-all, please!) if you want to set up time.

- Jonah
Jonah Feldkamp | Registered Representative
Northwoods Crossing Securities, member FINRA/SIPC
Duluth, MN | 218-555-0177

Generally you have four options: (1) leave it in your former employer's plan if the balance allows, (2) roll it into your new employer's plan if that plan accepts rollovers, (3) roll it into an IRA, or (4) take a cash distribution, which is usually taxable and may carry a 10% penalty if you're under 59 1/2. Each one has tradeoffs: employer plans sometimes have lower-cost institutional share classes and stronger creditor protection, while an IRA usually gives you a wider menu of investments but may cost more depending on what you hold and how the account is set up. If you do roll over, a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer avoids the mandatory 20% withholding that comes with a check made out to you.

None of these is right for everyone, and I'd want to compare your old plan's fees and fund lineup before suggesting anything. Reply here and we'll set up 20 minutes.

Dana Whitcomb, CFP | Wealth Advisor | (614) 555-0182

metadata.subject: A note on Calder Industrial's spring swing

communication:
FENWICK HOLLOW SECURITIES, INC. | Member FINRA/SIPC
215 Commerce Street, Chattanooga, TN 37402

June 2, 2026

Dear Friends,

Several of you have asked me about Calder Industrial (CLDR) after its wild spring. In March the shares fell about 31% over three weeks when the company disclosed a supply problem at its Monterrey plant, and by mid-May they had recovered almost all of that ground once the plant was back at full output. If you held on, your position today looks much like it did in February.

I want to be careful about what that episode does and does not tell us. A quick recovery last time is not evidence of a quick recovery next time: this rebound depended on a specific fix that happened to work, and a different kind of problem - a lost customer, an accounting issue, a weak cycle - could keep the stock down for much longer or permanently. For most of you CLDR is between 5% and 9% of your portfolio, and I'd like to revisit whether that size still matches what you can tolerate. I'll be calling each of you over the next two weeks.

Warm regards,

Angela Mbeki
Registered Representative
Fenwick Hollow Securities, Inc.

required_actions: No action required

Hey gang,

After our last round of reviews, a bunch of you asked what I'm actually excited about for the next few years, and honestly the answer keeps coming back to automation and robotics. Warehouses, surgery, cars, farming - it's showing up everywhere you look.

The way I'd play it is the Coldwater Robotics & Automation ETF (CWRB). Here's what I like about it: it holds about 60 companies across the US, Japan and Europe, so you're not betting the farm on one stock. The expense ratio is 0.45%, which is reasonable for a specialty fund. It trades like a stock, so you can buy or sell any time the market's open, and you get the whole robotics wave in one ticker without having to pick winners yourself.

I'm thinking a 5-10% slice for most of you, funded from cash or by trimming whatever's run up the most. If you want in, just reply 'robots' and I'll put together a trade for you to OK. If you'd rather talk it over first, grab time on my calendar at the link below.

Also - reminder that the office is closed the 27th and 28th for Thanksgiving. Hope you all have a great one!

Cheers,
Sam

Samantha Ortiz
Registered Representative
Bluewillow Securities LLC, member FINRA/SIPC
Book time: bluewillowsec.com/sam

metadata.subject: Margin call follow-up

communication:
Hi Mr. Castellanos, it's Dana Whitfield at Ridgeline Capital Securities (member FINRA/SIPC). I'm sorry the margin call on Friday caught you off guard - you're right that I should have walked you through it more carefully when we set up margin. Plainly, here's how it works: you borrowed against your Halcyon Biotherapeutics shares, so when the stock fell 38% after the trial readout, your account lost more than the stock's drop alone, and once your equity fell below the 30% maintenance level the firm had to ask for more cash or sell shares - and it can sell without waiting for you if the deadline passes.

Two other risks worth saying out loud: about 70% of your account is in that one stock, so a single company's news drives your whole balance, and as a small biotech it can gap up or down overnight with no chance to sell in between. I can't tell you where the stock goes from here. I've asked my branch manager to review how margin was explained at account opening, and she'll call you this week; if you want to talk about reducing the loan or the concentration, I'm free after 3 today.

THE GRANITE FORK MUNI LETTER | Spring 2025

First, an apology. Several of you called after our winter issue to point out that the yield table on page 2 showed tax-equivalent yields at a 37% federal bracket without saying so, and that the figures ignored state taxes. You were right, we should have been clearer, and a corrected table with the bracket and assumptions spelled out is enclosed as a separate insert. We're sorry for the confusion it caused.

With that cleared up, many of you asked how a laddered municipal portfolio has behaved over time. We ran our Granite Fork Ten-Rung Muni Ladder model back over 2015-2024 using historical index yields, and it produced an annualized total return of 3.9% with no down calendar year. That backtest is a good guide to what a ladder built today can deliver over the next decade, which is why we think this spring is a great time to start one. Interest on most municipal bonds is exempt from federal income tax but may be subject to state and local income taxes and, for some investors, the federal alternative minimum tax. Bonds carry interest rate, credit and call risk, and you may receive less than you invested if you sell before maturity.

Call your Granite Fork advisor to talk about whether a ladder makes sense for you.

Granite Fork Securities, member FINRA/SIPC | 88 Marion Street, Lexington, KY 40507

Subject: Follow-up: how target-date funds work

Dear Investor,

Thank you for attending the "Retirement Basics" webinar on September 16 and for submitting your questions. Several of you asked similar things about target-date funds, so the internal sales desk is answering them together here. This message is educational and is not a recommendation that any particular fund is right for you; your Kestrel Bay representative can help with that.

A target-date fund is a mutual fund that holds a mix of stock, bond and sometimes cash investments and gradually shifts toward a more conservative mix as its target year approaches. That shift is called the glide path. Two funds with the same target year can have very different glide paths: some reach their most conservative mix at the target date ("to" glide paths), while others keep adjusting for many years afterward ("through" glide paths) and may hold substantially more stock at the target date. Comparing the glide path and the stock allocation at the target year is more informative than comparing the year in the fund's name.

Target-date funds still carry the risks of the stocks and bonds they hold, including market, interest-rate, credit and inflation risk. The principal value is not guaranteed at any time, including at or after the target date, and you can lose money. Fees vary widely between fund families and share classes, and some funds also bear the expenses of the underlying funds they invest in. Before investing, consider each fund's objectives, risks, charges and expenses, which are described in its prospectus; your representative can provide one.

A few of you asked about account protection. Kestrel Bay Securities, Inc. is a member of FINRA and SIPC. SIPC protects the securities and cash in a customer's brokerage account up to $500,000 (including up to $250,000 for cash) if a member firm fails financially. SIPC does not protect against a decline in the value of your investments, and neither SIPC nor FINRA membership means that either organization endorses or approves Kestrel Bay or any fund we offer. More information is available at sipc.org and finra.org.

If you would like to review a specific fund's glide path, please reply to this email or call the desk at (617) 555-0185.

Kind regards,

Jonah Whitfield
Internal Sales Desk
Kestrel Bay Securities, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC
One Federal Street, 22nd Floor, Boston, MA 02110
