Subject: The Fed cut rates today - what it means for your fixed-rate savings

Dear Friends,

The Federal Reserve lowered its benchmark rate by a quarter point this afternoon, September 17, 2025. My view is direct: if you have savings you won't need for at least five years and they've been sitting in a money market account, this is the week to have a real conversation about a multi-year guaranteed annuity (MYGA). Here's my basis. Of the eight insurers on our approved list, six have already reduced their 5-year MYGA rates at least once since July, and two told us this week that further changes are under review. Money market yields generally move with the Fed's rate. I can't tell you where rates go from here - nobody can - but the rates insurers are offering today are known, and they can change without notice.

Before you call, please weigh the trade-offs. A MYGA ties up your money: most carry surrender charges of 6% to 8% in the early years, and many include a market value adjustment that can reduce what you receive if you leave early. The guarantee depends on the claims-paying ability of the issuing insurer; annuities are not bank deposits and are not FDIC insured. Interest grows tax-deferred, but it is taxed as ordinary income when withdrawn, and withdrawals before age 59 1/2 may also face a 10% federal tax penalty. If you may need the money sooner, an annuity is probably the wrong tool. Reply or call (515) 555-0129 and we'll look at your situation.

Warm regards,
Meredith Haugland, CFP(R)
Larkspur Ridge Financial, member FINRA/SIPC
Annuities are issued by insurance companies and offered through Larkspur Ridge Insurance Agency, LLC, an affiliate of Larkspur Ridge Financial. Guarantees are subject to the financial strength and claims-paying ability of the issuing insurer.

Subject: Today's selloff and your 2030 target-date fund

Hi all,

With the S&P 500 down about 4% this morning on the tariff headlines, a few of you have already called, so I wanted to get the same information to everyone who is close to retirement and holds a 2030 target-date fund. These funds shift toward bonds as the target year approaches, but they still hold a meaningful stock allocation and they are not guaranteed at any point, including at or after the target date. Your balance can and will move with markets, and some of you will see that on today's statements.

If part of your money needs to be there on a specific date regardless of markets, one option we can talk through is a brokered CD. Brokered CDs are FDIC-insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per issuing bank, per ownership category, and the issuing bank, not Copperline, is obligated to repay principal and stated interest at maturity. That guarantee only holds if you keep the CD to maturity: if you sell early in the secondary market, the price can be below what you paid, and the yield will generally be lower than the long-run return potential of a stock-and-bond fund. Call me at 614-555-0122 before making any changes so we can look at your full picture first.

Best,
Marisol Ventura
Registered Representative
Copperline Investment Services, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC
Columbus, OH

THE LANTERN PEAK LETTER - May 2025
By Teresa Vukovich, Registered Representative

Why I'm Leaning Into Utilities - and What Could Go Wrong

I'll be blunt: I think utilities are one of the most interesting corners of the market right now, and I've been adding a utilities sector ETF (XLU) to client portfolios where it fits. My reasoning: U.S. electricity demand is growing again after roughly two decades of being nearly flat, driven by data centers and new manufacturing, according to U.S. Energy Information Administration data, and regulated utilities can earn approved returns on the grid investment that demand requires. The sector also tends to pay higher dividends than the broad market. But this is not a sure thing. Utilities are sensitive to interest rates - when rates rise, their shares often fall - regulators can deny rate increases, big capital projects can run over budget, and dividends can be cut. A single-sector ETF is far less diversified than a total-market fund and can lose value, so I'd treat it as a slice of a portfolio, not the core. My view could prove wrong, and past sector trends do not guarantee future results.

If you'd like to talk about whether a utilities position fits your plan, call me at (412) 555-0133. Investors should consider an ETF's investment objectives, risks, charges and expenses before investing; the prospectus contains this and other information. Ask me for one and read it carefully.

Lantern Peak Securities, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC | 600 Grant Street, Pittsburgh, PA 15219

COPPERFIELD & HAINES SECURITIES, LLC
14 Abercorn Street, Savannah, GA 31401 | (912) 555-0186
Member FINRA/SIPC

April 22, 2024

Dear Client,

I'm writing to let you know about an industry-wide change that takes effect on Tuesday, May 28, 2024. On that date, the standard settlement cycle for most U.S. stock, bond and ETF trades shortens from two business days after the trade date ("T+2") to one business day ("T+1"). In practical terms, when you sell, the proceeds will be available in your account one business day after the trade instead of two; when you buy, payment will be due one business day after the trade. If you keep cash in your account's sweep, purchases will continue to settle automatically and you don't need to do anything. If you usually mail a check to cover a purchase, please call me before you place the order so we can make sure the funds arrive in time.

The change is a matter of market plumbing set by the SEC, and it does not affect the value of anything you own. Mutual fund purchases and redemptions follow each fund's own schedule, which is unchanged. If you hold paper stock certificates, please give me a call, since those generally need to be deposited before a sale under the shorter timeline.

Warm regards,

Odessa Pruitt
Registered Representative
Copperfield & Haines Securities, LLC

I'm writing to a few of you who keep larger cash balances at outside banks, since several of you called after this morning's news that Pinecrest Regional Bank was placed into FDIC receivership. Step three: if you want me to handle the purchase, reply with "OK to sweep" and the amount, and I'll place the trade the day the funds post. You'll get a trade confirmation that evening.

Marcus Feld

- $2.0MM Cedar Falls Community School District GO, 4.00% due 06/01/2034, callable 06/01/2031 @ par; offered at 3.38% yield-to-call / 3.61% yield-to-maturity. Underlying rating Aa2.

The Connecticut issue would not be exempt for an Iowa-domiciled bank, and Iowa franchise tax treatment of the in-state issues should be confirmed by your tax advisor. Prices move inversely with rates.

If useful, I can run a tax-equivalent yield comparison using the bank's actual marginal rate and cost of funds rather than a generic assumption. Let me know by Thursday if you'd like to hold any of these; offerings typically turn over within a day or two.

Best,
Caleb Andersen

Many of you have asked what to do with a 401(k) from a former employer. We appreciate the trust you place in us.

Sincerely,

Walter Ingersoll
Branch Manager
Kensington Harbor Securities, Inc.

Subject: SPY vs. VTI: the question several of you asked after the webinar

Hi everyone,

A few of you asked after last Thursday's call whether there's a real difference between SPY and VTI, so here's one answer for the group (BCC'd for privacy). Both are exchange-traded funds that hold U.S. stocks, but they don't track the same thing: SPY follows the S&P 500, roughly 500 large companies, while VTI follows the CRSP US Total Market Index, which includes several thousand stocks across large, mid, small and micro caps, so VTI carries more exposure to smaller companies, which have historically been more volatile. Their structures differ too: SPY is organized as a unit investment trust, so it can't reinvest dividends between payouts or lend its securities, while VTI is an ETF share class of an open-end fund. Both have low expense ratios, but the ratios are not identical, and the two differ in daily trading volume and bid-ask spreads, which matter more to frequent traders than to long-term holders. Neither is insured or guaranteed, both can lose value, and their returns will usually be close but not the same.

I've attached each fund's current prospectus and fact sheet so you can see the expense ratio, holdings and standardized performance directly. Which one fits depends on what else you own, so let's talk it through at your next review rather than switching anything based on this note.

Best,
Gabriel Fontaine
Registered Representative
Silverlake Crossing Securities, LLC, member FINRA/SIPC
(608) 555-0177

communication:
Subject: Following up on our chat about the bond side of your portfolio

Hi Theo,

Great talking with you Tuesday - and congratulations again on the promotion! You asked me why I keep bringing up the intermediate bond position, so I wanted to put my thinking in writing.

You'll remember 2022 was a rough year for bonds: the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index fell about 13%, its worst calendar year in decades, because rates rose so fast. Then in late 2023, when rates pulled back, the same index had one of its sharpest two-month rallies on record. I'm not bringing that up because I think it's about to repeat - it may not, and rates could just as easily stay higher or rise further. I'm bringing it up because it shows how sensitive bond prices are to rate moves in both directions, and because your portfolio is currently about 92% stocks and cash, which leaves you with very little ballast if equities have a bad stretch.

That's why I'd like you to seriously consider moving about $40,000 of your cash into the Brightwater Intermediate Bond Fund (Class A). I really like this fund for your situation: it holds mostly investment-grade government and corporate bonds with an average duration of around six years. The trade-offs matter, though. If rates rise, the fund's share price will fall - roughly 6% for each 1% rise in rates, based on that duration - and it carries credit risk on its corporate holdings. It's not FDIC insured and you can lose money. Class A shares carry a front-end sales charge of up to 3.75% (which drops at breakpoints starting at $50,000) and an expense ratio of 0.71%, so if you think you'll need this money within a couple of years, a CD or Treasury bill may be a better fit, and I'm happy to show you those too.

I've attached the prospectus - please give it a read, particularly the risks section, before we decide anything. I'd love to get 30 minutes on your calendar next week to go through it together and make sure it fits your goals and timeline.

Talk soon,

Priya Venkataraman
Registered Representative
Lockhaven Securities Corp., Member FINRA/SIPC
455 Grand Avenue, Suite 1210, Des Moines, IA 50309
(515) 555-0186

communication:
Hi Mrs. Delacroix,

You asked how a new-issue municipal bond like the Granville Local School District 4.00% general obligation bonds due 2041 gets to market, so here's the short version. The district hires an underwriter, bond counsel issues an opinion on the tax status, and the official statement lays out the district's finances, the property-tax pledge behind the bonds, and the call schedule (these are callable at par starting in 2034, which means you could get your principal back early if rates fall). Interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and because these are Ohio bonds and you're an Ohio resident, it is generally exempt from Ohio state income tax too. It may be subject to the federal alternative minimum tax depending on your situation, and any gain if you sell before maturity is taxable.

One thing that should give you comfort: every bond our desk offers has been reviewed and approved by FINRA and the MSRB before it's allowed onto our inventory, so the credit work has effectively been double-checked by the regulators. And frankly, our municipal trading desk is the best in the Midwest at finding value in school district paper; nobody prices these tighter. Let me know if you'd like to go through the official statement together before the retail order period closes Thursday.

Warm regards,
Ethan Sorensen
Registered Representative
Buckeye Crossing Securities, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC
Columbus, OH | 614-555-0182

Subject: About last Tuesday's sell orders in GTBX

Hi all,

I owe each of you an apology. When I placed market orders to sell part of your Granite 0-3 Month Treasury Bill ETF (GTBX) positions during last Tuesday's opening volatility, several of you received prices noticeably below the fund's net asset value, and I should have used limit orders. Unlike a mutual fund, an ETF's market price is required by law to stay within a few cents of its NAV, so what happened Tuesday was a one-time glitch rather than a real risk of owning the fund. For the GTBX you still own, you will not lose a dollar on this fund as long as you hold it through quarter-end - I'll make sure of it.

As always, call me directly with any questions.

Best,
Owen Castellano
Registered Representative

(512) 555-0193

communication:
Reinvest it or spend it? A little math on bond and CD interest

When a bond or CD pays interest, you have a choice: take the cash, or put it back to work. Over time that choice makes a bigger difference than most people expect, and here is a simple way to see it.

HYPOTHETICAL EXAMPLE: Imagine $10,000 earning an assumed 4% per year for 10 years. If the interest is spent each year, the original $10,000 is still $10,000 at the end, and you have collected $4,000 along the way, a total of $14,000. If instead every interest payment is reinvested at that same assumed 4% and compounds annually, the balance grows to about $14,802. The roughly $802 difference is the effect of earning interest on interest.

This illustration is hypothetical and shows only a mathematical principle. It is not a projection of the return of any bond, CD or other investment, and it does not reflect taxes, fees or commissions. Real-world rates change: when you reinvest, you may have to accept a lower rate than you started with (reinvestment risk). Bond prices fall when interest rates rise, issuers can default, and bonds or brokered CDs sold before maturity may be worth less than you paid.

Want to talk through how you handle interest in your own accounts? Reach out to a Westmark Harbor financial professional at (843) 555-0102.

Westmark Harbor Securities LLC, member FINRA/SIPC. Brokered CDs are FDIC-insured up to applicable limits only when held to maturity at an FDIC-member bank.
#CompoundInterest #FixedIncome #FinancialLiteracy

THE LONG VIEW LEDGER
Investing basics, minus the jargon

What a "Quality" ETF Actually Owns
By the Long View Ledger editorial team | July 22, 2025

"Quality" is one of the most popular labels in the ETF world, but it means something specific. Quality-factor ETFs typically screen for companies with high return on equity, low debt relative to earnings, and steady earnings growth, then weight the survivors by size or by their quality score. Take the Summit Quality Factor ETF (ticker SQFX), the quality fund our advisors discuss most often with clients: it returned 22.6% in 2024 and 58.3% cumulatively over the past three years, beating the S&P 500 in both periods. That kind of record is why the factor has drawn so much attention.

Before you buy, know what you are getting. Factor ETFs can trail the broad market for long stretches, quality screens tend to favor large technology and health care names, which adds concentration, and every ETF charges an expense ratio that comes out of your return. Quality stocks fall in broad selloffs too. Read the prospectus, and talk to an advisor about whether a factor fund fits your plan.

Securities offered through a registered broker-dealer, member FINRA/SIPC. This article is for educational purposes only and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security.

metadata.recipient_description: Eight retail clients who asked about covered call income ETFs, sent as a broadcast on the firm's approved messaging platform
metadata.subject: Covered call ETFs vs a plain S&P 500 fund

communication:
[Brightwater Mill secure messaging - broadcast to 8 recipients]

hey all - a few of you asked about those 'monthly income' covered call ETFs after the ads everyone keeps seeing. quick side by side vs a plain S&P 500 fund like SPY so you have the full picture before we talk 1:1

the covered call kind (a fund that owns the S&P and sells calls on it every month) pays a much bigger distribution. BUT that cash comes from selling away upside. when the market rips it lags badly because gains are capped. when the market drops you still take most of the drop, the option premium only cushions a little. so it's not a 'safer' S&P, more like trading future growth for income today. and the distribution changes month to month, it isn't a fixed yield

costs + taxes: covered call ETFs usually run about 0.35-0.60% a year vs 0.0945% for SPY. a lot of the covered call payout is taxed as ordinary income or comes back as return of capital (which lowers your cost basis), while SPY's dividends are mostly qualified. inside an IRA the tax piece matters less, in a taxable account it matters a lot

both trade all day on the exchange, both can lose money, neither is guaranteed. read the prospectus before buying either one, I can send links

happy to look at whether either fits your situation, just send me a time that works

- Leo Castellanos, Financial Advisor
Brightwater Mill Securities, LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC | advisory services through Brightwater Mill Advisors, LLC

required_actions: No action required

communication:
Subject: Curve un-inversion: what history shows (from Marcus Delgado)

Hi Hannah,

Marcus asked me to send along this note following your conversation last week about the Treasury curve. He's traveling and will follow up on Thursday.

"Hannah, as we discussed, the 2-year/10-year Treasury spread turned positive again in September after more than two years inverted, the longest stretch on record. Investors often treat the inversion itself as the recession signal, but historically the more informative moment has been the un-inversion, when short rates fall back below long rates as the Fed begins cutting. Looking at the eight un-inversions since 1978, the S&P 500 was higher twelve months later in six of them, with a median 12-month gain of 9.8%.* The intuition is that by the time the curve normalizes, policy is easing and markets have typically started to look through the slowdown. None of this is a forecast, and we'd treat it as one input among several when you set equity risk budgets for 2025."

Best,
Paige Whitlock
Client Service Associate, on behalf of Marcus Delgado, Managing Director
Thornquist Capital Markets, LLC, member FINRA/SIPC
200 Clarendon Street, Boston, MA 02116

This communication is intended solely for institutional investors.

*In five of the eight cycles a recession began within 18 months of the un-inversion, and in three of them the S&P 500 fell more than 20% at some point during the following 12 months; the 12-month figures are point-to-point and do not reflect interim declines. Source: Thornquist Capital Markets analysis of Federal Reserve and S&P Dow Jones Indices data, 1978-2024.

Subject: Why part of your cash reserve is now in a short-term bond fund

Hi all,

A few of you asked after our reviews last month why I moved part of your emergency reserve out of the money market sweep and into the Crestline Short-Duration Bond Fund (Class I), so I'm sending one note to everyone who asked. Short-duration bond funds own bonds that mature in roughly one to three years. Because those bonds roll over quickly, the fund can pick up higher rates sooner than a longer bond fund, and it typically pays more income than a sweep account. You can sell shares on any business day and the cash is in your account the next day.

Think of it as the next step up from cash: same daily access, more income. For money you want to keep reachable but working a little harder, it's a sensible home. If you'd like me to move more of your reserve over, just reply and I'll set it up.

Best,
Daniel Okafor

[Tamarind Point Securities, Inc. - text message, Thu 12/05/2024 4:42 PM]

Hi Gabriela, Owen Castellanos here at Tamarind Point. Following up on your question at lunch about the small-cap move. Sharing for your firm's internal research only, not for your clients - please don't forward this thread.

Recap of what happened: the Russell 2000 rose a little under 6% on Nov 6, the day after the election, and the big small-cap index ETFs (IWM and peers) tracked it. Most of the jump came from rate-sensitive regional banks and domestic industrials. By the end of the month part of that had already faded as the 10-year Treasury yield backed up.

Why I'm not reading much into it: one-day moves like that were driven by a specific event and a big repositioning of short bets. Small caps have had several sharp rallies over the last 3 years that reversed within weeks, so I wouldn't treat Nov 6 as a signal of what comes next or as a pattern. Index ETFs also carry the same concentration as the index - right now a sizable chunk is unprofitable companies, which cuts both ways when financing costs move.

If useful, I can send our desk's factor breakdown of the move and a holdings comparison across the three largest small-cap ETFs (expense ratios, tracking difference, number of holdings). Happy to set up 20 min next week.

Owen Castellanos | Tamarind Point Securities, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC | (480) 555-0129

A few of you pointed out that I called the 2-year brokered CD and the 2-year Treasury note 'basically the same,' and that wasn't a fair way to put it. Corrected side-by-side: the CD (Lindqvist Bank, 4.05% APY, matures 6/2027) is FDIC-insured up to $250,000 per depositor per bank, counting any other deposits you already hold at Lindqvist. It isn't callable, but the secondary market is thin, so if you sell before maturity you could get less than you paid. Its interest is taxed federally and by your state. The Treasury (4.00% coupon, matures 5/31/2027) is backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government and trades in a deep market, so it's easier to sell early, though its price also moves with rates before maturity. Its interest is federally taxable but exempt from state and local income tax. Both are bought with a markup built into the price, which will show on your trade confirmation. Neither one is better for everyone; it depends on your state tax bracket and whether you might need the money early. Sorry again for the shorthand. - Priya Natarajan, Pellham & Rowe Securities, member FINRA/SIPC

required_actions: No action required
label.rationale: As correspondence to ten clients, the comparison is judged under (d)(1)(A) rather than (d)(2), and it discloses the material differences anyway: FDIC limits versus government backing, liquidity, price fluctuation, tax treatment and markups. The apology corrects the earlier oversimplification without making new claims.

communication:
Subject: Re: what happened with the bond ETF??

Hey Marisol,

Totally hear you, and I'm sorry this one stung. You asked me straight up why the Larkspur Long Treasury ETF is down about 14% since you bought it in February, so here's the straight answer: the fund holds Treasuries maturing 20+ years out, which makes it really sensitive to interest rates. When long-term yields climbed from roughly 4.2% to 4.9% this spring, prices on those bonds dropped and the ETF dropped with them. Subject: RE: Harlow Floating Rate Income Fund

Ken -

Short answer: I can place it, but read this first.

- At your size it'd be C shares. 1% back-end charge (CDSC) if you sell within 12 months. Ongoing expenses 1.74%/yr, about 0.75% more per year than the A shares, which adds up if you hold longer than ~6 years.

- It is not a money market fund or a cash substitute. You can lose principal.

Prospectus attached. If after reading it you still want it as roughly 5% of the account, reply and I'll enter the order. Glad to talk A vs C shares first.

J. Okonkwo

Title: Market Hours and Holidays: What to Know for 2026

[SCENE 1 - Cairnfield Securities logo over city skyline]
NARRATOR: Welcome to Cairnfield Securities' client education series. Today we'll cover when U.S. stock markets are open, when they're closed, and how that affects your orders and settlement dates.

[SCENE 2 - On-screen text: "Regular session: 9:30 AM - 4:00 PM ET"]
NARRATOR: The regular trading session for major U.S. stock exchanges runs from 9:30 in the morning to 4:00 in the afternoon, Eastern time, Monday through Friday. Those sessions typically have fewer participants, which can mean wider price spreads and larger price swings, so ask your representative how extended-hours orders work before using them.

[SCENE 3 - Calendar graphic listing holidays]
NARRATOR: In 2026, the stock markets are scheduled to be closed on New Year's Day, Martin Luther King Jr. Day on January 19, Presidents' Day on February 16, Good Friday on April 3, Memorial Day on May 25, Juneteenth on June 19, Independence Day observed on Friday, July 3, Labor Day on September 7, Thanksgiving on November 26, and Christmas Day. Some days before or after holidays have early closes, so check the exchange calendar posted on our website.

[SCENE 4 - On-screen text: "Bond market schedules can differ"]
NARRATOR: The bond market follows its own recommended calendar, so on a few days, such as Columbus Day and Veterans Day, bond trading may be closed or shortened while stock markets remain open. Holidays also push back settlement: most stock trades settle one business day after the trade date, and a holiday adds a day.

[SCENE 5 - Closing card]
NARRATOR: Questions about a specific order or settlement date? Contact your Cairnfield representative or our client service team at 1-800-555-0177.

VIDEO SCRIPT - "Markets Just Dropped. Your Kid Starts College Next Fall. Now What?" (approx. 90 seconds)

[ON SCREEN: Nadia Ferreira, Registered Representative, Calloway Bridge Securities, Inc.]

NADIA: If you watched the market slide this week and your first thought was your child's 529 account, you're not alone - our phones have been ringing since Monday. Here's what to know right now, before you make any moves.

NADIA: Most 529 plans offer age-based portfolios that gradually shift toward bonds and cash-like investments as the enrollment date gets closer. That can soften a downturn, but it doesn't eliminate it: a portfolio built for a fall 2026 freshman can still lose value, and nothing in a 529 is guaranteed or FDIC-insured unless you've chosen a specific bank-deposit option. Before selling in a down market, ask when you'll actually need the money - tuition is usually paid a semester at a time, so not every dollar is due next fall.

NADIA: Keep the rules in mind, too. Withdrawals for non-qualified expenses are subject to income tax plus a 10% additional federal tax on earnings, and every plan charges fees that reduce returns. If you're weighing plans, check whether your home state offers tax benefits only for its own plan. If you want a second set of eyes on your timeline, call our office at (503) 555-0134.

[ON-SCREEN DISCLOSURE, held 8 seconds and read aloud]
NARRATOR: Before investing, consider the plan's investment objectives, risks, charges and expenses, found in the plan's official statement; ask us for a copy and read it carefully. Calloway Bridge Securities, Inc. is a member of FINRA and SIPC. Membership does not mean that FINRA or SIPC endorses our firm or any investment. SIPC protects securities and cash held at a member firm up to $500,000, including a $250,000 limit for cash, if the firm fails; it does not protect against market losses. Investing involves risk, including possible loss of principal.

410 Delancey Avenue, Hartford, CT 06103

March 3, 2025

Dear Valued Client,

On February 24, a connectivity failure at one of our order-routing vendors delayed the handling of market orders entered between 9:41 and 10:28 AM ET. Many of these orders were in Vantor Biotech (VNTB), which was moving sharply that morning after its trial announcement. We apologize for the disruption and for the calls that went unanswered while our service desk worked through the backlog.

We have completed a full review. Every delayed order was filled within the national best bid and offer at the moment it was executed, and every fill was confirmed to you the same day. Accordingly, no client was disadvantaged by the 47-minute delay, and no price adjustments are required. We have since added a second routing vendor so a single outage cannot hold up orders again. If you have questions, please call our client service team at (860) 555-0119.

Sincerely,
Annelise Ward
Branch Manager and Registered Representative
Silverbirch Investment Services, Inc.

Because the plan's holdings far exceed SIPC limits, I've attached our summary of the firm's excess-of-SIPC coverage, including its aggregate limits.

What membership does and does not mean: being a FINRA member means we are subject to FINRA's rules, examinations and oversight. It does not mean FINRA or SIPC endorses our firm, guarantees your assets, or has approved any investment in your portfolio.

I'll be at my desk all day. If the committee wants a call with our CFO or treasurer, I can set it up on short notice.

Priya Raman

Granite Meridian Securities LLC | Member FINRA/SIPC
200 W. Adams Street, Chicago, IL 60606

Dear Client,

Several of you have asked about utility bonds after this winter's rate moves, so I want to share the conclusions of Lindqvist Research's February 3, 2026 report on Calder Valley Power Co. 5.25% senior notes due 2034 (rated BBB+/Baa1). The report sets a 12-month price target of 98.00 versus a price of 94.10 on February 2, based on a relative-value spread analysis that assumes the notes' spread over Treasuries narrows by about 35 basis points toward comparable BBB+ regulated utilities once the company's pending rate case is resolved. The report identifies the risks to that target: rising Treasury yields, an unfavorable rate-case decision, wildfire or storm liability that could lead to a downgrade, limited secondary-market liquidity, and a make-whole call provision. A price target is not a guarantee and the notes may trade well below it. Lindqvist Research may act as a market maker in these notes and co-managed the issuer's March 2025 bond offering; the full report, including its valuation methodology, ratings history and disclosures, is available on request.

Best regards,
Celeste Arnaud, Registered Representative
Lindqvist & Moore Securities LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC

VIDEO SCRIPT - 'A Correction on Rollovers, and One Stock for IRA Income' | Presenter: Daniel Mwangi, CFP® | Juniper Shoals Financial, LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC | Recording date: October 2, 2025

[ON CAMERA, desk setting]
DANIEL: Before anything else, I owe some of you an apology. Several viewers wrote in after last month's video on 401(k) rollovers, and they were right: I talked about the benefits of rolling into an IRA and didn't spend enough time on the reasons to stay put. So let me fix that.

[GRAPHIC: 'Reasons to leave money in your 401(k)']
DANIEL: Your plan may offer institutional share classes with lower expenses than you'd pay in an IRA. Assets in an ERISA plan generally have stronger protection from creditors. If you leave your job in or after the year you turn 55, you can usually take withdrawals from that plan without the 10% early-withdrawal penalty, which you can't do from an IRA until 59½. And an IRA with an advisor like me involves fees that your plan may not charge. A rollover can still make sense for consolidation or wider investment choice, but it's a trade-off, not a no-brainer.

[GRAPHIC: ticker card 'Halbrook Water & Power Co. (NYSE: HWP) - $47.85, closing price October 1, 2025']
DANIEL: Now, for those who have already rolled over and want income inside the IRA, one stock I am recommending is Halbrook Water & Power. It's a regulated utility with a current dividend yield of about 4.1%, and its rate case approvals over the past three years give it a reasonable basis for steady cash flow. The risks are real: utilities are sensitive to interest rates, regulators can deny rate increases, and the dividend can be cut. This is a single stock and shouldn't be a large share of anyone's retirement savings.

[ON-SCREEN DISCLOSURE, held 10 seconds, read aloud]
DANIEL: Some required disclosures. Juniper Shoals Financial makes a market in Halbrook Water & Power. I personally own shares of HWP, and the firm holds HWP in its proprietary trading account. Juniper Shoals Financial co-managed a public offering of Halbrook's common stock in March 2025. Supporting information for this recommendation is available on request; just use the contact link below.

[CLOSING]
DANIEL: Past performance doesn't guarantee future results, and nothing in this video is a promise about returns. If you want to talk through your own rollover decision, book a call through the link. Thanks for holding me to a higher standard.

[END CARD: Juniper Shoals Financial, LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC | Advisory services offered through Juniper Shoals Advisory, LLC, an SEC-registered investment adviser and affiliate | BrokerCheck: brokercheck.finra.org]

communication:
From: Renata Oyelaran <royelaran@wexcombeRidgeFin.com>
Subject: Your CDs are maturing - here's a way to keep the safety and get more income

Hi there,

If you're like a lot of our clients, you've had money parked in bank CDs over the last two years, and many of those CDs are coming due this spring as banks trim their rates. I've had more conversations about "what now?" in the past month than in all of last year, so I wanted to share how we're thinking about it.

One approach we've been building for clients is a five-year ladder of investment-grade corporate bonds: we buy bonds that mature in each of the next five years, and as each one comes due you can spend the principal or roll it to the far end of the ladder. Think of it as a CD ladder that simply pays more. Current yields on the ladders we've built this month range from about 4.6% to 5.1%, compared with the 3.4% to 3.9% we're seeing on bank CDs of similar terms.

The best part is that the math doesn't change when markets get bumpy. Hold each bond to maturity and you get every dollar of principal back, no matter what rates or the stock market do in between - the same peace of mind you've had with your CDs, just with a bigger interest check.

Ladders also give you flexibility. Because a rung matures every year, you're never more than twelve months away from fresh cash, and if rates rise you'll be reinvesting at the higher levels. We typically suggest a minimum of $50,000 so each rung can hold several issuers.

If you have a CD maturing in the next 90 days, reply to this email or call our office and we'll put together a sample ladder using today's offerings so you can see it side by side with your bank's renewal rate.

All the best,

Renata Oyelaran, CFP
Financial Advisor
Wexcombe Ridge Financial, member FINRA/SIPC
1550 Carondelet Street, Suite 300, New Orleans, LA 70130 | (504) 555-0128

Group note, everyone is BCC'd since several of you messaged this morning. Stocks are down about 3% at midday after the jobs report, and a few of you asked where to park cash you don't want in the market for the next 6-12 months. Three common choices, and they are not interchangeable: (1) Bank CD: FDIC-insured up to $250,000 per depositor per bank and a fixed rate, but you usually pay a penalty to cash out early, and if it's a brokered CD from us you can sell it before maturity but possibly for less than you paid. (2) 6-month Treasury bill: backed by the U.S. government if held to maturity, interest is subject to federal income tax but exempt from state and local income tax, and selling early means taking the market price, which could be a gain or a loss. (3) Government money market fund: daily liquidity, but it is not FDIC-insured or guaranteed, its yield moves with rates, it has an expense ratio that comes out of what you earn, and although it seeks to hold a $1.00 share price you could lose money.

None of these is a substitute for long-term growth money, and today's drop doesn't tell us where stocks go from here. Rates on all three change daily so I'm not quoting numbers in a group message. Reply here and I'll pull live quotes for your account and we can talk about which, if any, fits.
Rafael Ostrowski, Registered Representative, Fennimore Gate Securities LLC, member FINRA/SIPC

SEMINAR SCRIPT - "Getting Paid to Wait: Bonds in 2026"
Juniper Row Investments, LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC
Presenter: Victor Almeida, Registered Representative | Script prepared by Hannah Pruitt, Client Service Associate, for principal review

[SLIDE 4 - Why bonds deserve a second look]
VICTOR: After the last few years, a lot of you have cash sitting in savings and you're asking whether bonds finally make sense again. I think this is one of the more interesting moments for bond investors in a long time, and I want to show you one fund we use for clients who want income without picking individual bonds themselves - the Bayfront Intermediate Bond Fund.

[SLIDE 5 - Bayfront Intermediate Bond Fund, Class A: average annual total returns as of September 30, 2025]
VICTOR: Here are the fund's standardized numbers, and I want you to look at both rows. At net asset value, the fund returned 3.12% over one year, 0.48% a year over five years and 1.91% a year over ten years. Including the maximum 3.75% front-end sales charge, those figures are -0.75%, -0.29% and 1.52%. Yes, two of those are negative - the five-year period includes 2022, when rising rates pushed bond prices down sharply, and that's exactly the kind of risk you take on in a bond fund. The fund's total annual operating expense ratio is 0.82% gross, 0.74% net after a fee waiver the adviser has agreed to through April 30, 2026.

[SLIDE 5 footer, same type size as the table]
Performance data quoted represents past performance, which does not guarantee future results. Investment return and principal value will fluctuate, so shares, when redeemed, may be worth more or less than their original cost. Current performance may be lower or higher; call 1-800-555-0119 for performance as of the most recent month-end. Without the fee waiver, returns would have been lower.

[SLIDE 6 - What can go wrong]
VICTOR: Bond funds are not CDs. They are not FDIC-insured, the share price moves when interest rates move - if rates rise, the price falls - and the fund can lose value if issuers it owns are downgraded or default. There is no maturity date when you're promised your money back. If you need every dollar on a specific date, a CD or an individual Treasury might be the better tool, and I'm happy to talk about those too.

AN UPDATE TO THIS PAGE
Several readers told us the earlier version of this page was hard to follow and made its chart look like a forecast for municipal bonds. They were right, and we apologize for the confusion. We have rewritten the example below so that it shows only the arithmetic of compounding.

HYPOTHETICAL ILLUSTRATION: REINVESTING VERSUS SPENDING INTEREST
Assume $50,000 earns a constant 3% per year for 20 years. If every interest payment is spent, you would receive $30,000 of interest and still hold the original $50,000, for $80,000 in total. If every payment is instead reinvested at the same 3%, the balance would grow to about $90,306. This is a hypothetical illustration of a mathematical principle only. It does not represent the performance of any municipal bond, fund or account offered by Fairmont Ridge Investments, it assumes a constant rate that no actual investment provides, and it ignores fees and taxes. In practice, reinvestment rates change, bond prices fall when interest rates rise, issuers can default or call bonds before maturity, and you may receive less than you paid if you sell before maturity. Interest on municipal bonds is generally exempt from federal income tax but may be subject to state and local income taxes and the federal alternative minimum tax, and any capital gains are taxable.

Questions? Call our fixed income desk at (608) 555-0193.

Subject: quick annuity note before the holidays

Hey all -

Hope everyone's doing good! A few of you asked me at the client breakfast last week about parking some cash somewhere steadier than the market, so I figured I'd just shoot one email to the group instead of playing phone tag. You're BCC'd so nobody sees anybody else's info, don't worry.

The product I keep pointing people to right now is the Prairie Mutual SureRate 5 fixed annuity. It's paying 5.15% for the first 5 years, which is locked in by the contract for that term. Best part - it's FDIC insured just like your checking account, so your principal is covered by the government no matter what happens. Honestly that's why I like it for the money you can't afford to see bounce around.

Couple of things to know so nobody's surprised: there's a surrender charge if you pull out more than 10% a year during the first 5 years (starts at 7% and steps down 1% a year), and if you take money out before 59 1/2 the IRS can hit you with a 10% penalty on the earnings on top of regular income tax. After year 5 the rate resets to whatever Prairie Mutual is offering then, which could be lower.

If you want to look at it, text or call me and we'll sit down - takes about 30 minutes and I'll bring the contract and the disclosure doc so you can read through the whole thing. No pressure at all, I know it's not for everybody.

Have a great Thanksgiving!

Rhonda Pfeiffer
Branch Manager
Tidewater Crest Financial, LLC | Member FINRA/SIPC
418 W. Idaho St., Boise, ID 83702 | 208-555-0147

metadata.recipient_description: Trust officers at a regional bank's trust department evaluating 529 accounts for trust assets
metadata.subject: 529 options for the education trusts - quick rundown

communication:
Hey Marcus, Dee, Alan,

Good seeing you all Tuesday. Here's the rundown on the 529 question for the education trusts you administer, where the bank as trustee would be the account owner.

The Vermillion State 529 Plan has three buckets that matter for you. The age-based portfolios are mutual-fund-based and move from stocks toward bonds as the beneficiary nears college. Those are NOT guaranteed by anybody and can lose value, including close to enrollment.

The Stable Principal portfolio is the one people call 'guaranteed', and that's fair only with a caveat: it's backed by a funding agreement with Calloway Mutual Life, so the principal and declared crediting rate are guaranteed by that insurer and depend on its claims-paying ability. It is not FDIC-insured and not guaranteed by the state, the plan or us. The current crediting rate is 3.15% and resets each January.

The FDIC-Insured Savings option holds deposits at Brenner Federal Savings Bank. That one is genuinely FDIC-insured, up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category, so you'd want to check aggregation with any other deposits the trusts hold at Brenner. The rate is variable and lower than the stable option right now.

On costs: age-based portfolios run 0.22%-0.41% all-in, the stable option has no explicit fee (the insurer's spread is built into the rate), and the savings option has none. Non-qualified withdrawals pay ordinary income tax plus a 10% penalty on earnings, which matters if a beneficiary skips college. Happy to sit down with the trust committee. This is for your internal review and not for distribution to trust beneficiaries.

Best,
Jess Mahoney, CFP
Financial Advisor
Larkspur Ridge Securities LLC, member FINRA/SIPC | Investment advisory services through Larkspur Ridge Advisors LLC

communication:
SABLE CREEK WEALTH PARTNERS - CLIENT NOTES | October 2025
From the desk of Imogen Tsai, CFP(R)

The Four Dates Behind Every Dividend

Ever bought a stock the day before a dividend was paid and wondered why you didn't receive it? It comes down to a few dates. The declaration date is when a company's board announces the dividend. The record date is when the company checks its books to see who is entitled to it. The ex-dividend date is the cutoff for buyers: purchase on or after the ex-date and the dividend goes to the seller; purchase before it and it goes to you. Since U.S. stock trades moved to one-business-day (T+1) settlement in May 2024, the ex-date and record date usually fall on the same day. On the ex-date, a stock's price typically opens lower by roughly the dividend amount, so there is no free money in buying just beforehand.

The last date, the payable date, is when cash actually lands, often several weeks later. That's why a dividend can show as "pending" in your account for a while. If you have dividend reinvestment turned on, shares are bought on the payable date. Questions about how dividends post, or whether reinvestment is set up on your account? Call our service team at 919-555-0148.

Sable Creek Wealth Partners | Securities offered through Sable Creek Wealth Partners, member FINRA/SIPC. Advisory services offered through Sable Creek Advisors LLC, an SEC-registered investment adviser and affiliate of Sable Creek Wealth Partners.

metadata.subject: re: the muni thing we talked about at Jen's bbq

communication:
Hey Sam!

Great chatting Saturday, and sorry it took me a few days to circle back. You asked whether munis make sense since you're in a high bracket here in California, so here's the honest rundown.

Short version on taxes: interest on most municipal bonds is exempt from federal income tax. If the bond is from a California issuer, the interest is generally exempt from CA income tax too; bonds from other states usually aren't, so CA would tax that interest. A couple of catches: interest on some private-activity bonds counts for the federal AMT, if you sell a bond for more than you paid you owe capital gains tax like anything else, and muni interest still gets added back when figuring how much of Social Security is taxable and your Medicare premium bracket.

They aren't risk-free either. Prices drop when rates go up, so if you need to sell before maturity you could get back less than you paid. Issuers can get downgraded or, rarely, default, a lot of bonds can be called early when rates fall, and smaller issues can be hard to sell quickly.

To compare a muni with a taxable bond people use the taxable-equivalent yield. Purely as math, not a quote on anything: a 3.6% tax-exempt yield works out to about 5.54% for someone in a 35% federal bracket (3.6 / 0.65), before state taxes, and the number changes with your actual bracket.

If it's useful I can pull a few California GO bonds so you can see real yields, ratings and call dates, and you should run it by your CPA too. No pressure at all.

Derek

Derek Szabo | Registered Representative
Marigold Bay Securities, LLC, member FINRA/SIPC
(415) 555-0129

metadata.subject: Active vs. index: the two options we discussed

communication:
Hi all,

Following up on last week's workshop: several of you asked me to put the two core U.S. stock options we discussed side by side, and honestly I'm excited about both of them for different reasons. Here's the straight comparison.

The Mariposa Large Cap Opportunities Fund (Class A) is actively managed: a team picks about 45 stocks it believes can outgrow the market, which means it can lag or beat the S&P 500 by a wide margin in any year. It carries a front-end sales charge of up to 5.50% and a gross expense ratio of 0.82%, and because the managers trade more, it tends to distribute more taxable capital gains in a regular account. The S&P 500 index fund we offer simply holds the whole index, aims only to match it (less fees), has no sales charge and costs 0.05% a year, and usually distributes fewer capital gains. Both are fully invested in stocks, both can lose money, neither is guaranteed or insured, and both can be sold on any business day at that day's price. If you want a shot at beating the market and are comfortable paying more for it, the active fund is a great fit; if low cost and matching the market matter most, the index fund is hard to argue with. Read both prospectuses and give me a call at (805) 555-0179 so we can pick what fits your goals.

Luis Ferreira, Registered Representative
Mariposa Bay Securities, Member FINRA/SIPC | San Luis Obispo, CA

metadata.subject: Follow-up chat: what is actually guaranteed

communication:
[Firm chat - Copperfield Investment Services LLC]

Devin Reyes 2:07 PM: Happy to unpack this, Priya. You asked which of the things we talked about are actually 'safe' or 'guaranteed', and it's a fair question because those words get thrown around loosely.

Devin Reyes 2:08 PM: Brokered CDs: these are bank CDs you buy through a brokerage account. Principal and interest are FDIC-insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category - so the guarantee comes from the FDIC, not from us, and only within those limits. Held to maturity, you get your principal back from the issuing bank (or the FDIC if the bank fails). The catch: if you need to sell early, you sell on the secondary market, and the price can be below what you paid if rates have risen. Most brokered CDs can't simply be 'broken' like a branch CD, and some are callable by the bank.

Devin Reyes 2:10 PM: Fixed annuities: the guaranteed rate and principal protection are real, but they're guaranteed by the insurance company that issues the contract and depend on its claims-paying ability. They are not FDIC-insured and not backed by Copperfield or any government agency. They usually carry surrender charges for the first several years if you take out more than the free-withdrawal amount, and withdrawals before 59 1/2 can bring a 10% IRS penalty on top of ordinary income tax on the gains.

Devin Reyes 2:11 PM: Everything else we touched on - the stock and bond funds, the ETF model - is not guaranteed by anyone and can lose value, including the money you put in. That's the trade-off for the higher long-term growth potential.

Devin Reyes 2:12 PM: If it helps, I can send you the FDIC's deposit insurance page and a sample annuity contract summary so you can see the exact terms before we talk Thursday. No pressure either way.

Devin Reyes | Registered Representative | Copperfield Investment Services LLC, member FINRA/SIPC

Devin Reyes 2:07 PM: Happy to unpack this, Priya. You asked which of the things we talked about are actually 'safe' or 'guaranteed', and it's a fair question because those words get thrown around loosely.

Devin Reyes 2:08 PM: Brokered CDs: these are bank CDs you buy through a brokerage account. Principal and interest are FDIC-insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category - so the guarantee comes from the FDIC, not from us, and only within those limits. Held to maturity, you get your principal back from the issuing bank (or the FDIC if the bank fails). The catch: if you need to sell early, you sell on the secondary market, and the price can be below what you paid if rates have risen. Most brokered CDs can't simply be 'broken' like a branch CD, and some are callable by the bank.

Devin Reyes 2:10 PM: Fixed annuities: the guaranteed rate and principal protection are real, but they're guaranteed by the insurance company that issues the contract and depend on its claims-paying ability. They are not FDIC-insured and not backed by Copperfield or any government agency. They usually carry surrender charges for the first several years if you take out more than the free-withdrawal amount, and withdrawals before 59 1/2 can bring a 10% IRS penalty on top of ordinary income tax on the gains.

Devin Reyes 2:11 PM: Everything else we touched on - the stock and bond funds, the ETF model - is not guaranteed by anyone and can lose value, including the money you put in. That's the trade-off for the higher long-term growth potential.

Devin Reyes | Registered Representative | Copperfield Investment Services LLC, member FINRA/SIPC

communication:
GREYSTONE HOLLOW FINANCIAL, LLC
Member FINRA/SIPC
88 Harbor Lane, Portland, ME 04101

March 18, 2025

Dear Valued Client,

I owe you an apology. The year-end IRA review packet I mailed you in February included a one-page summary of the Ashbury Balanced Income Fund, the fund many of you selected when we rolled your 401(k) assets into your IRA. That page showed the fund's 2024 calendar-year return at the NAV without the sales charge and did not show the longer-term figures you are entitled to see. Several of you called to ask why the number did not match your statement, and you were right to ask. I am sorry for the confusion, and I want to give you the complete picture.

Ashbury Balanced Income Fund, Class A (ABIAX). Average annual total returns as of December 31, 2024, reflecting the maximum 4.75% front-end sales charge: 1 year 3.92%; 5 years 5.41%; 10 years 5.86%. Without the sales charge, the same periods were 8.86%, 6.44% and 6.38%. The fund's total annual operating expense ratio, before any waivers, is 0.97% (net 0.89% after a contractual waiver through April 30, 2026). The figures represent past performance, which does not guarantee future results. Investment return and principal value will fluctuate, so your shares, when redeemed, may be worth more or less than their original cost, and current performance may be lower or higher than shown. Month-end performance is available by calling Ashbury Funds at (800) 555-0162 or from me directly.

Because these accounts are rollover IRAs, I also want to restate what we discussed at the time of the rollover: the fund holds both stocks and bonds and can lose value; IRA assets grow tax-deferred, not tax-free, and withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income and may be subject to a 10% additional tax before age 59 1/2. Your former employer's plan may have offered lower-cost institutional share classes, which was one of the trade-offs we reviewed together.

Please read the fund's prospectus, which I have enclosed again, carefully before making any further investment decisions; it contains the fund's objectives, risks, charges and expenses. I have asked our operations team to review how these summaries are prepared so that this does not recur. If you would like to go over your account, call me at (207) 555-0139.

With my apologies and thanks,

Lillian Marchetti
Registered Representative
Greystone Hollow Financial, LLC

January 8, 2026

Dear Valued Client,

As we begin 2026, I want to share our perspective on the year just ended and the environment ahead. 2025 brought real volatility, including a sharp drawdown in April, followed by a recovery that carried major U.S. stock indexes to new highs later in the year. Bond yields remained elevated relative to most of the past decade, which has improved the income available from high-quality fixed income.

Several risks deserve your attention. Valuations on large U.S. technology companies are high by historical standards, trade policy remains uncertain, and the path of inflation could keep interest rates higher than many investors expect. Diversification does not ensure a profit or protect against loss in a declining market.

That said, with earnings growth broadening beyond a handful of mega-cap names and the Federal Reserve having room to ease further, we believe the stage is set for U.S. equities to deliver another year of double-digit gains in 2026, and we expect balanced portfolios to finish the year comfortably ahead of where they started.

We will hold annual reviews throughout February and March. My assistant, Joel, will reach out to schedule yours, or you can call the office at any time. Thank you for the trust you place in us.

Sincerely,

Renata Solberg

communication:
What a Target-Date Fund's Glide Path Is Doing While You Aren't Looking
by Owen Castellano, Ember Street Financial | February 3, 2026

A target-date fund is a single mutual fund that holds a mix of stock and bond funds and shifts that mix as the year in its name approaches: more stocks when the date is decades away, more bonds and cash as it gets close. The shift is called the glide path, and it is the main thing you are buying. Two funds with the same year can have very different glide paths, and some keep shifting for years after the target date. The fund does not know your situation; it only knows the calendar. Fees, the underlying funds, and how aggressive the path is are the things to compare, and all of them are in the prospectus.

Why do people use them for long horizons? Mostly because of time, and time is arithmetic rather than prediction. Here is a purely hypothetical illustration of compounding: $300 contributed every month for 30 years is $108,000 of contributions. At an assumed 4% annual rate of return, compounded monthly, that grows to about $208,000; at an assumed 6%, about $301,000. These figures are math only. They are not the past or expected performance of any target-date fund or any other investment, they do not reflect fees, expenses or taxes, which would reduce the results, and the assumed rates are not guaranteed. Real returns vary from year to year and can be negative, and you can lose money in a target-date fund, including near or after the target date.

Ember Street Financial, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC. Target-date funds are subject to the risks of their underlying investments; the principal value is not guaranteed at any time, including at the target date. Read the prospectus before investing.

Dear Mrs. Okonkwo-Reyes,

I'm sorry. You're right to be frustrated, and I should have been clearer when we bought the Maumee Valley (Ohio) Water Authority revenue bonds in your account last year. Interest on those bonds is exempt from federal income tax, but because you live in California, it is subject to California state income tax; California exempts only interest on bonds issued within California. That is why your 2024 Form 1099-INT led to the state tax your preparer flagged. The bonds are not private activity bonds, so the interest is not subject to the federal alternative minimum tax, and if you sell them before maturity any gain or loss would be taxable.

Going forward, I've put together a short list of California general obligation and revenue bonds whose interest would be exempt from both federal and California income tax, along with their after-tax yields for your bracket so you can compare. California issues often yield less, so the in-state choice isn't automatically better; we can go through it on Thursday's call. I've also logged your complaint in our file as our procedures require and shared it with my branch manager, Lena Fairbanks, in case you'd like to speak with her directly.

Sincerely,
Owen Castellanos, CFP
Financial Advisor
Bellhaven Ridge Financial Services, LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC

February 3, 2026

Dear Friends,

Many of you have told me you're tired of watching cash sit idle while the headlines swing from one extreme to the next, so I want to put two options squarely on your radar before more of the attractive rates we've seen disappear. First, brokered CDs: the deposits are FDIC insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category, which makes them about as safe as it gets for money you can leave alone until maturity. The fine print matters, though: if you need to sell before maturity, you sell on the secondary market at whatever price is available, which can be less than you paid, and that market loss is not covered by FDIC insurance. Second, for money earmarked for retirement, a fixed annuity offers a guaranteed rate for a set term, with the guarantee backed solely by the financial strength and claims-paying ability of the issuing insurance company, not by the FDIC or any government agency; most also carry surrender charges for several years if you withdraw more than the free amount.

Neither is right for every dollar or every person, and the rates available change weekly. Call me at (303) 555-0114 and let's look at which, if either, fits your timeline.

Warm regards,

Lucinda Abernathy-Ruiz
Financial Advisor
Hollis & Vanterpool Financial, Inc.; annuities offered through Hollis & Vanterpool Insurance Agency, LLC

communication:
ok, hot take: T-bills are the most underrated thing in your portfolio right now
Jess Calloway | Lantern Hill Securities, LLC | Nov 3, 2023

real talk. as of friday's close the 3-month Treasury bill yielded about 5.4% and the 2-year note about 4.9% (source: U.S. Treasury daily yield curve, 11/3/2023). that's the most cash-like stuff has paid since 2007. for the part of your money that has to be there next year — tuition, a down payment, your emergency fund — I think it's hard to argue with. backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government if held to maturity, and the interest is exempt from state and local income tax (it IS subject to federal income tax, so don't call it tax-free).

now the part nobody tweets. a 5.4% bill is a 3-month promise, not a 5-year one — if the Fed cuts, you reinvest at whatever's on offer then, which might be a lot less. inflation ran about 3.7% at the last reading, so your real return is closer to 1.5%. and if you sell a note before maturity, you get the market price, which can be below what you paid. none of this is a recommendation for your specific situation — a Treasury that's perfect for your tuition money is the wrong place for money you won't touch for 20 years.

questions? DM me or hit the office. Lantern Hill Securities, LLC, member FINRA/SIPC. opinions are mine as of the date above and can change.

By Thomas Reinholt, Registered Representative

We are writing promptly because you placed an online order yesterday, April 7, during the period when U.S. exchanges paused trading under the market-wide circuit breaker. We want you to know exactly where that order stands and what, if anything, you need to do.

Your scheduled automatic transfers and next month's statement are not affected.

Please review the order history in your portal and contact us at (402) 555-0190 if anything does not match your records. A copy of this letter will be retained with your account file.

Sincerely,

Marguerite Oyelaran
Client Operations Supervisor
Stonebridge Lane Securities, LLC

metadata.subject: Your old 401(k): choices and trade-offs before you roll over

communication:
WESTFALL & BRIGGS SECURITIES, LLC
Member FINRA/SIPC
410 Commerce Street, Suite 300, Chattanooga, TN 37402

April 14, 2025

Dear [Client Name],

Because you recently told me you are leaving, or have left, your employer, I want to lay out your choices for your old 401(k) before you sign any paperwork. You generally have four: leave the money in the old plan, move it to a new employer's plan if that plan accepts rollovers, roll it to an IRA, or cash it out. Cashing out usually means ordinary income tax and, if you are under 59 1/2, a 10% additional tax. An IRA typically offers more investment choices, but it may cost more than an institutionally priced 401(k) once account fees, fund expenses and any advisory fee are added up. 401(k) assets generally have broad federal protection from creditors, while IRA protection outside of bankruptcy depends on state law. And if you separate from service in or after the year you turn 55, your plan may allow penalty-free withdrawals that an IRA would not.

If anyone, including me, suggests putting rollover money into a variable or fixed indexed annuity inside the IRA, understand what you would be giving up: those contracts usually carry surrender charges of 6% to 8% in the early years that decline over 7 to 10 years, so taking money out early can cost you real dollars, and the tax deferral an IRA already provides is not an added benefit of the annuity. Some IRA strategies also use margin or leveraged ETFs; borrowing magnifies losses as well as gains, and a leveraged ETF that resets daily can lose value over time even if its index ends roughly flat. None of these choices is right for everyone. I am glad to compare your plan's actual costs and options side by side with you before you decide; please call me at (423) 555-0189.

Sincerely,

Priya Venkataraman
Registered Representative
Westfall & Briggs Securities, LLC

communication:
A few reflections on building portfolios with exchange-traded funds

Over the past several years, I have increasingly used broad-market ETFs as the core holdings in client portfolios. Their transparency, intraday liquidity, and typically modest expense ratios make them a practical building block for long-term investors who want diversified exposure without paying for security selection they may not need.

That said, ETFs are not a shortcut around market risk. An ETF that tracks the S&P 500 will decline when the S&P 500 declines, and sector or thematic ETFs can be considerably more volatile than the overall market. Shares may trade at a premium or discount to net asset value, and brokerage commissions and bid-ask spreads can affect results. Investors can lose money, including principal.

I was grateful to receive this note from a client last month, and with his permission I am sharing it here:

"Before I started working with Elena, my retirement money was scattered across eleven funds I didn't understand. She rebuilt everything around a handful of low-cost ETFs, and my account has grown more in the last three years than in the decade before. Best financial decision I've made." - Robert T., Sacramento

If you would like to talk through whether an ETF-based approach fits your goals, time horizon, and tolerance for risk, my door is open. Please read a fund's prospectus carefully before investing; it contains information about investment objectives, risks, charges and expenses.

Elena Vasquez | Registered Representative
Coastal Meridian Securities, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC

#ETFs #RetirementPlanning #LongTermInvesting #FinancialAdvisor

metadata.subject: Follow-up on moving to an ETF core

communication:
HALCYON BRIDGE FINANCIAL, INC.
Member FINRA/SIPC | SEC-registered investment adviser
600 Grand Avenue, Suite 1400, Des Moines, IA 50309

March 3, 2026

Ms. Ines Castellanos
4127 Ingersoll Avenue
Des Moines, IA 50312

Dear Ines,

Thank you for the thoughtful questions at our meeting last week about moving part of your portfolio from actively managed mutual funds into a core of broad-market ETFs. I promised a written follow-up, so here it is.

How ETFs differ from the mutual funds you own. Like a mutual fund, an ETF pools investors' money into a portfolio of securities. Unlike a mutual fund, ETF shares trade on an exchange throughout the day at market prices, which can be slightly above or below the value of the underlying holdings (the net asset value). You pay a bid-ask spread when you buy or sell, and a commission may apply depending on your account type. Index ETFs often carry lower expense ratios than actively managed funds, and their structure can reduce capital gains distributions, but neither of those is guaranteed. An index ETF follows its index down as well as up, can lose money, and is not FDIC-insured.

What changing would actually involve. The largest cost of a switch is likely to be taxes, not fees. Several of your funds in the taxable account have sizable unrealized gains, and selling them would generate capital gains tax this year. One way to manage that is to make the transition gradually over two or more tax years, or to begin only with the IRA, where sales do not trigger current tax. I would also want to confirm that any ETFs we consider fit your allocation targets and do not duplicate holdings you already own.

You asked whether other clients have been through this. With his permission, here is what one client, Walter Haddad, wrote to me after we made a similar transition in 2024:

"I was nervous about selling funds I'd owned for twenty years. Daniel walked me through the tax cost of every sale before we made it, and we spread the changes over two tax years to keep the bill manageable. I finally understand what I own and what I'm paying for it."

Please keep a few things in mind about Walter's comments. His experience may not be representative of the experience of other clients, and it is not a guarantee of future performance or success. Walter is a current client, and he was not paid or otherwise compensated for his statement.

Before our next meeting, I will prepare a lot-by-lot estimate of the tax cost of each possible sale so we can decide together whether, and how quickly, to proceed. Prospectuses for any ETFs we discuss will come with that estimate; please read them carefully, as they describe each fund's objectives, risks, charges and expenses.

Warm regards,

Daniel Aoki
Financial Advisor
Halcyon Bridge Financial, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC

Bond Basics for 2025: what I tell new investors

Bonds are loans. When you buy a bond, you lend money to a company or government, and in return you receive interest and, if the issuer pays as promised, your principal back at maturity. Two numbers matter most. Duration tells you roughly how much a bond's price may move when rates change; a bond with a duration of 6 could lose about 6% of its value if rates rise one percentage point. Credit quality tells you how likely the issuer is to pay you back, and lower-rated bonds pay more because they carry more default risk.

For investors who want a professionally managed approach, the Ironbridge Short Duration Bond Fund is ranked #1 in its category by FundGauge, which is one reason I use it as a core holding for many conservative clients. Bond funds do not mature like individual bonds, so their value can go up and down indefinitely with rates.

If you prefer to own individual bonds, my current favorite is the Calloway Industries 5.25% senior notes due 2031. I like the business, the coupon is well above Treasuries, and we have them available right now through our desk. Message me for an allocation before they are gone.

All bonds carry interest rate, credit, call and liquidity risk, and you can lose money. Read a fund's prospectus before investing.

Malik Durant | Financial Advisor | Stonegate Ridge Brokerage LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC | Fort Wayne, IN

communication:
Dear Ms. Achterberg,

You're right that our March 4 trade summary for the Federal Home Loan Bank step-up notes did not explain the call feature clearly enough, and I apologize; your team should not have learned about the call from the custodian's notice. Here is the plain-English version we should have sent up front. These notes are callable by the issuer at par on any quarterly coupon date after the first year. Issuers tend to call when rates fall, which is exactly when reinvesting is least attractive, so the higher "step-up" coupons later in the schedule may never be paid. The notes trade in a thinner secondary market than Treasuries, so selling before maturity usually means a wider bid/ask spread and, if rates have risen, a price below par. They are joint and several obligations of the FHLBanks and are not guaranteed by the U.S. government. There is no leverage inside the notes themselves.

Going forward, every new-issue summary we send your team will include the full call schedule and yield-to-worst alongside yield-to-maturity. I have also forwarded your complaint to our compliance department, and you will receive a written acknowledgment from them. If it would help, I can walk your investment committee through the remaining callable positions in the portfolio on Thursday.

Sincerely,
Gabriel Moreau
Registered Representative, Institutional Fixed Income
Carraway Point Securities LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC

Dear Ms. Okafor,

Thank you for your time on Tuesday's call regarding the transition of the Halvorsen Family Trust and two related accounts from Calloway Ridge Securities to your custodian. I am writing to confirm the logistics we discussed so that your operations team and ours are working from the same checklist.

As agreed, the transfer will move in kind through ACATS. The accounts currently hold 14 individual equity positions, three of which include fractional shares. Fractional shares cannot move through ACATS; they will be liquidated and delivered as cash, which may produce a small taxable gain or loss for the trust. To start the process we will need the receiving firm's transfer initiation form signed by both co-trustees, a trust certification dated within the last 12 months, confirmation of the receiving account numbers, and a current Form W-9 for the trust.

Subject: Our apology for the delayed trade confirmations in March

Dear Clients,

I am writing personally to apologize. Between March 4 and March 15, 2025, trade confirmations for mutual fund purchases, exchanges and redemptions placed through our Fort Collins branch were delayed by up to nine business days. The cause was a processing error during our conversion to a new confirmation vendor, and it was our mistake, not yours.

Every order was executed on the day it was received at that day's closing net asset value, and your account balances on the client portal have been accurate throughout. Thank you for your patience and for the trust you place in our team.

Sincerely,

Raymond Tillotson

communication:
Subject: Year-end rollover deadlines and paperwork checklist

Hi {FirstName},

A number of you have asked about timing for 401(k) rollovers before December 31, so here are the practical details. If you have already decided to move money from a former employer's plan to an IRA with us, our operations team needs completed paperwork by Friday, December 12, 2025 to request the distribution in time for year-end processing. Plans set their own processing times, and some take three to four weeks, so we cannot control when your former plan releases the funds. A direct rollover, where the check or wire goes straight to the IRA custodian, avoids the mandatory 20% federal withholding that applies when a plan pays you directly. If you take an indirect rollover, you have 60 days to deposit the full amount, including the 20% that was withheld, or the shortfall is generally treated as a taxable distribution and may also be subject to a 10% additional tax if you are under 59 1/2. Required minimum distributions cannot be rolled over.

If you haven't decided, that's fine: there is no year-end deadline to roll over. Leaving assets in your former plan, moving them to a new employer's plan, or taking a distribution are also options, and each comes with different fees, investment choices, services and legal protections. I'm happy to walk through those differences with you before you decide anything. Please consult your tax advisor about your own situation; we do not provide tax advice.

Warm regards,
Keisha Montgomery
Registered Representative
Oakmere Securities Group, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC
318 Harbor Blvd, Suite 200, Norfolk, VA 23510

metadata.subject: Your brokered CD matures on May 15 - what happens next

communication:
Subject: Your brokered CD matures on May 15 - what happens next

Hello,

You're receiving this note because each of you holds a brokered CD in your Pinecrest Harbor account that matures on Thursday, May 15, 2025. I've sent it to the small group of clients in the same position (addresses are blind-copied for privacy), and I wanted to walk through the mechanics so nothing about maturity day comes as a surprise.

On the maturity date, the issuing bank pays the CD's face amount plus the final interest payment to our clearing firm, and the cash typically appears in your account's cash sweep the same day or the next business day. Nothing is reinvested automatically - brokered CDs don't roll over the way a CD at your local bank might - so the money will sit in your sweep until you tell us what you'd like to do with it.

If you'd like to talk through your options, reply to this email or call the office and we'll set up a time. If you'd rather the cash simply be sent to your linked bank account, we can do that too; for a transfer to an outside account we'll need a signed distribution request, which I can send through DocuSign.

On taxes: interest you've received this year, including the final payment, will be reported on your 2025 Form 1099-INT, which our clearing firm mails by mid-February 2026. For those holding the CD in an IRA, the maturity proceeds stay inside the IRA and there's nothing to report unless you take a distribution.

Thanks, and send me any questions.

Best,
Elena Marchetti, CFP(R)
Financial Advisor
Pinecrest Harbor Financial, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC
Investment advisory services offered through Pinecrest Harbor Advisors, LLC, an SEC-registered investment adviser and affiliate of Pinecrest Harbor Financial, Inc.
(503) 555-0161 | Portland, OR

Okay, fixed income nerd moment. 🤓 I get asked this at least twice a week: "Should I buy a CD or a Treasury bill?" Both can make sense for cash you don't need for a while, but they are NOT the same thing. Here's the honest rundown.

🏦 Brokered CDs: issued by banks and FDIC-insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, and that covers the bank failing, not the price. If you sell before maturity, you sell on the secondary market and can get back less than you paid (or there may be few buyers). Some CDs are callable, so the bank can end your rate early if rates drop. Interest is taxable at the federal AND state level.

🇺🇸 Treasury bills: backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government, with no $250k cap. They trade in a deep market, but prices still move with rates if you sell before maturity. The interest is subject to federal income tax but exempt from state and local income tax, which can matter a lot in high-tax states.

💵 Costs and yield: either one may include a markup or commission when you buy through a broker, so compare the yield AFTER costs. And rates on both change constantly; what's available today may not be there next month.

Bottom line: the right pick depends on your timeline, your state taxes, and how much you're holding at any one bank. Happy to walk through your situation. DM me or call the office.

Tomas Reyes, Registered Representative | Saguaro Peak Securities, LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC | Tucson, AZ
#FixedIncome #CDs #TreasuryBills #PersonalFinance
