communication:
DRIFTWOOD VALLEY FINANCIAL, INC. | Member FINRA/SIPC
Quarterly Client Letter, Winter 2025

Leaving an Employer: Your 401(k) and an IRA Compared

When you change jobs or retire, you generally may leave your savings in your former employer's plan, move them to a new employer's plan, roll them to an IRA, or take a cash distribution, which is generally taxable and may carry a 10% additional tax before age 59 1/2. The choices differ in material ways. Costs: employer plans may offer institutional share classes and the employer may pay some administrative expenses, while an IRA may involve commissions, advisory fees or account fees that can make it more expensive overall. Investment choices: an IRA usually offers a far broader range of investments, while a plan offers a limited menu that may include a stable value fund whose guarantee is provided by an insurance company or bank and depends on that issuer's ability to pay. Access to money: if you leave your job in or after the year you turn 55, the plan may permit penalty-free withdrawals that would not be available from an IRA until 59 1/2. Protection from creditors: assets in ERISA-covered plans generally have unlimited federal protection, while IRA assets are protected in bankruptcy only up to a periodically adjusted cap of roughly $1.7 million and outside bankruptcy depend on state law. Taxes: both defer taxes until withdrawal, withdrawals of pre-tax money are taxed as ordinary income, and employer stock held in a plan may qualify for net unrealized appreciation treatment that is lost if the shares are rolled into an IRA.

Neither option is right for everyone, and the best choice depends on your fees, investment needs, age and tax situation. Please also know that our representatives may earn compensation if you roll assets into an IRA with us, which is a conflict of interest we are glad to discuss. To review your own situation, call our Bend office at (541) 555-0126.

Wendell Haraway, Registered Representative
Driftwood Valley Financial, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC | 1100 NW Wall Street, Bend, OR 97703

Sincerely,

Renata Duarte, CFP(R)
Financial Advisor
Securities offered through Pembrook Securities LLC, member FINRA/SIPC. Advisory services offered through Pembrook Advisory LLC, a registered investment adviser and affiliate of Pembrook Securities LLC.

communication:
Small Caps: The Setup Is Here
By Erin Valdes, Registered Representative | Kestrel Point Securities LLC | September 9, 2025

Short version: the Fed's first cut is the starting gun for small caps.

Small companies carry more floating-rate debt than large caps, so every quarter-point the Fed takes off flows more directly to their bottom line. By forward P/E, they're also the cheapest relative to the S&P 500 in about two decades. Put those together and the Russell 2000 should outrun the S&P 500 by double digits over the next 12-18 months.

I've tracked rate cycles since 2008, and this indicator has never once failed to call the turn. Small caps can be volatile and can lag for long stretches, so size positions accordingly.

Kestrel Point Securities LLC, member FINRA/SIPC. This article is for informational purposes only and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security. Opinions are the author's as of the date above.

Subject: Follow-up: target-date lineup review and your SIPC question

Hi Andrea,

Thanks again for having me at Tuesday's retirement committee meeting. As promised, attached is the side-by-side of the three target-date series we discussed for the Greystone Fabrication 401(k) Plan (roughly 640 participants): equity allocation at the target date, to- versus through-retirement glide paths, expense ratios by share class, and the underlying asset-class exposures. This analysis is for the committee's evaluation and isn't designed for participants; if the committee decides to change the QDIA, we'll prepare a separate participant notice that goes through our firm's review process.

On your question about whether our FINRA and SIPC membership protects the plan if the target-date funds lose value: it doesn't, and I want to be precise about it. Hollis Bay Advisors & Securities is a FINRA member broker-dealer, which means we're subject to FINRA's rules and examinations, not that FINRA has approved or endorses us or any fund we offer. SIPC protects customers' securities and cash held at a member firm up to $500,000 (including up to $250,000 for cash) if the firm fails financially; it does not cover declines in the market value of investments. Target-date funds can lose money, including at and after the target date.

Happy to walk through the analysis with you before the December 9 vote.

Best,
Priya Ramanathan, CFP(R)
Financial Advisor | Hollis Bay Advisors & Securities, LLC
Securities offered through Hollis Bay Advisors & Securities, LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC. Advisory services offered through Hollis Bay Advisors & Securities, LLC, an SEC-registered investment adviser.

Hi Beth,

Thanks for coming in on Tuesday. It was great to hear about the move to Salem and about Ava starting at Oregon State this fall. I promised you a written recap of what we covered, so here it is.

Emergency reserve: we agreed to keep six months of expenses, about $38,000, in the bank money market sweep. That money stays out of the market so you aren't forced to sell anything if the roof or the car needs attention.

Income sleeve: as we discussed, we'll move $60,000 from the taxable intermediate bond fund into the Pinecrest National Municipal Income Fund (Class A). Beneficiaries: the IRA beneficiary form still lists your former address. I've included a pre-filled update form; please sign and return it in the envelope provided, or use the e-signature link I'll send separately.

As always, call or email with any questions. I'll check in again in April once your tax return is filed.

Warm regards,

Ian Castellanos

Glenmoor Financial Services, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC

Sincerely,

Gwendolyn Pratt
Registered Representative
Ashby & Thorne Securities

[VIDEO SCRIPT - "Before You Move Your 401(k) in a Volatile Market" - 2:10 runtime]

[ON CAMERA: Isaac Ferreira, Registered Representative, office setting]

ISAAC: Markets dropped hard this week, and my phone has been ringing. If you're thinking about rolling your 401(k) into something that promises protection - or something that promises to make it all back fast - please slow down for two minutes.

[GRAPHIC: "Annuities: what 'protection' costs"]

ISAAC: A lot of people are being pitched annuities right now. Some have real guarantees, backed by the insurance company's ability to pay, not by the government. But many lock up your money for seven to ten years. Take it out early and you can pay a surrender charge of 7% or more in the first years, on top of annual fees that can run 2% to 3% once you add riders.

[GRAPHIC: "Leveraged ETFs: built for a day, not a decade"]

ISAAC: On the other end, some folks want to roll into a 2x or 3x leveraged ETF to recover faster. Those funds reset daily. Over weeks or months, especially in choppy markets, they can lose money even if the index ends up flat - and they can lose much more than the index on the way down.

[GRAPHIC: "Your options"]

ISAAC: You can leave your 401(k) where it is, move it to a new employer's plan, roll it to an IRA, or cash out, which usually means taxes and possibly a 10% penalty. Your plan may have lower costs and creditor protections an IRA doesn't. Look at all of it before you decide, and don't let a scary week make the decision for you.

[END CARD: Isaac Ferreira, Registered Representative | Granite Fold Securities, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC | Check our background at brokercheck.finra.org | This video is educational and not a recommendation to buy or sell any security or insurance product.]

metadata.subject: Are munis really tax-free?

communication:
Let's talk munis ☕ (long post, sorry not sorry)

I get this question at least once a week: 'Are muni bonds really tax-free?' Mostly yes, with some buts. Interest on most municipal bonds is exempt from federal income tax. Whether it's exempt from STATE income tax usually depends on where you live: in-state bonds are often exempt for residents, out-of-state bonds usually aren't. Some munis (private activity bonds) pay interest that can be subject to the federal alternative minimum tax. And if you sell a muni for more than you paid, that gain is taxable like any other capital gain.

Why people like them anyway: for someone in a higher bracket, a lower muni yield can compare well with a taxable bond after tax. Quick hypothetical math, not a quote on any actual bond: a 3.5% muni yield works out to about a 5.56% taxable-equivalent yield for someone in the 37% federal bracket (3.5 divided by 0.63), before any state tax. In lower brackets the advantage shrinks or disappears.

What people forget: munis are not risk-free. Prices drop when rates rise, some issuers do default, many bonds can be called early, and individual munis can trade thinly, so selling before maturity may mean taking a lower price.

If you want to figure out whether munis make sense for your situation, my DMs are open. Talk to your tax pro too; I'm not one.

J.R. Castellanos, Registered Representative
Dunmore Peak Financial, LLC, member FINRA/SIPC | finra.org | BrokerCheck: brokercheck.finra.org
#MuniBonds #TaxTalk #FixedIncome

MARCUS: People ask me for "safe" bonds. I don't sell safe. Every bond can lose value. What I can tell you is exactly what the words "insured" and "guaranteed" mean on a muni, and what they don't.

MARCUS: Taxes. Muni interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. Bonds from outside your home state are usually taxable by your state. Some munis are subject to the federal alternative minimum tax. Sell at a gain, and that gain is taxable.

ANNOUNCER: Ridgeline Municipal Securities, LLC. Member FINRA/SIPC. 1-888-555-0161. Investing involves risk, including loss of principal. Consult your tax advisor.

Subject: A plain-English note on leveraged and inverse ETFs

Several of you have asked about 2x and 3x ETFs after this spring's swings, so here is the short version: these funds reset their leverage every day, which means that over any period longer than a single day your result can differ sharply from 2x or 3x the index, losses are magnified exactly as gains are, and in a choppy market you can lose money even if the index ends the period flat. They also tend to carry higher expense ratios than plain index ETFs and are built for short-term trading, so they are not appropriate for most long-term investors; please read the prospectus and talk with your financial professional before buying one.

Colette Abernathy, Branch Manager
Mesa Arroyo Securities, Inc. | Member FINRA/SIPC

Subject: Kestrel Industrial block — apology and next steps

Dear Mr. Abernathy,

I want to begin by apologizing directly for the handling of the Kestrel Industrial Group sell order on Tuesday. The Fund's instruction to work 180,000 shares over the session reached our desk at 9:41 a.m. but was not released to the algorithm until 11:15 because of a routing configuration error on our side. During that window the stock fell from $46.20 to $43.85, and I understand that the delay cost the Carrow County Employees' Retirement System meaningful value on the portion executed later in the day.

Our trading supervisor has reviewed the timestamps, and we have opened a formal error review. Our operations group will deliver a written reconstruction of the order handling, including fill prices by time interval, by Friday. If the review confirms that the delay resulted from our error, we will handle any correction through our standard trade-error process, and I will walk your team through the results personally.

On the remaining 220,000 shares the Fund continues to hold, I know your investment committee is frustrated. I have spoken with our industrials analyst, and I can guarantee the stock will be back above $46 before your fiscal year-end on June 30, so there is no need to sell into this weakness. I would recommend the committee hold the position and let it recover.

Again, I am sorry for the disruption this has caused, and I appreciate your patience while we complete the review.

Respectfully,

Daniel Oyelaran
Institutional Sales, Registered Representative
Westbrook Quay Securities LLC, member FINRA/SIPC
(503) 555-0136

Dear Ms. Varga,

Thank you for stopping by our Eau Claire office last Tuesday. You asked a good question - what actually happens to a 401(k) when you leave an employer - so I wanted to lay out the basics in writing.

When you separate from service you generally have four choices: leave the money in the Halbrook plan, move it to a new employer's plan, roll it to an IRA, or take a cash distribution (which is taxable and, before age 59 1/2, usually subject to a 10% additional tax). A direct rollover to an IRA is not a taxable event, and an IRA gives you access to a much broader menu of stocks, bonds, ETFs and mutual funds than the 24 options in your current plan.

Looking at the statement you shared, your plan account - most of which sits in the Halbrook Stable Value Fund - earned 3.1% last year while the S&P 500 returned more than 24%. Your plan simply has not kept up, and our managed IRA portfolios are built to fix exactly that.

Using a 7% average annual return, which is in line with what our balanced managed portfolios target, your $386,000 should grow to roughly $760,000 by the time you turn 65 in 2034 - real money you would be leaving on the table by staying put.

A rollover also lets you consolidate everything in one place with one statement and one advisor who knows your full picture. I've attached our account application and a transfer form; once those are signed, we handle the paperwork with Halbrook's recordkeeper.

Warm regards,
Priya Lindqvist
Registered Representative
Arden Hollow Financial, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC
(715) 555-0129

Subject: An apology about the rollover delays this month

Dear clients,

I'm writing to each of you who had a 401(k)-to-IRA rollover in process during May, because several of those took far longer than they should have. Some of you waited three weeks for checks from your plan administrators to be deposited, and two of you had to call us repeatedly to get an answer. What happened: we changed our intake procedure in early May to add a second review of every rollover recommendation, including a side-by-side of your plan's fees and investment options against the proposed IRA. The new step slowed things down more than we anticipated, and we didn't communicate that well. We've since added staff to that review and are working to get turnaround back to our usual 5-7 business days.

I also want to reassure you about why we did this. Our rollover review process was examined by FINRA during our routine exam this spring and came through with no findings, so you can be confident it has the regulator's stamp of approval. Frankly, no firm in the Tri-State area puts more care into rollover recommendations than we do.

If your rollover is still pending, or if you'd like to talk through the comparison we prepared for you, call me directly at 201-555-0164. Thank you for your patience and for trusting us with your retirement savings.

Sincerely,

Anthony Mercer
Registered Representative
Palisade Ferry Investments, Inc.
Member FINRA/SIPC

BUILD YOUR CORE WITH MUTUAL FUNDS
One account. Hundreds of funds. Guidance from people who know your name.

Why mutual funds?
A single fund can hold hundreds of stocks or bonds, giving you instant diversification that would be hard to assemble on your own. Professional managers handle the research and trading, and you can start with as little as $250 and set up automatic monthly investments that fit your budget.

What you get with us
We offer more than 400 funds from 30+ fund families, including index funds, actively managed stock funds, and bond funds for income-focused investors. Your advisor will help you match funds to your timeline and comfort with risk, then review your mix with you at least once a year. Ready to get started? It takes about 15 minutes to open an account online.

Know before you invest
Mutual funds are not FDIC insured, are not bank guaranteed, and may lose value. Diversification does not ensure a profit or protect against loss in a declining market. Funds charge ongoing expenses, and some charge sales loads or redemption fees. Before investing, carefully consider a fund's investment objectives, risks, charges and expenses, which are found in its prospectus. Ask your advisor for a prospectus and read it carefully.

Talk to an advisor today: (480) 555-0160

Subject: Re: should I be worried?

hey Sam,

totally fair question after the week we just had. For context - in spring 2025 the S&P 500 fell almost 19% from its February high into early April, and VTI (your biggest holding) dropped right along with it. By late June the index was back above where it started. I bring that up because it's what actually happened, not because it's a playbook. Sometimes markets bounce in weeks, sometimes it takes years (after the 2000 peak it took about seven to get back to even), and there's no way to know which kind of drop we're in while we're in it.

What I'd focus on is what we can control: you've got about 14 months of expenses in the money market and the short-term bond ETF, so you're not forced to sell VTI at a bad price to pay bills. If this dip is keeping you up at night, that's real info and we can talk about dialing the stock side down a bit - just know that selling after a drop locks in the loss and you could miss a recovery if one comes. Want to hop on a call Thursday?

Jordan

Jordan Whitlock, Financial Advisor
Juniper Coast Financial LLC, member FINRA/SIPC
Advisory services through Juniper Coast Advisors LLC, a registered investment adviser

Andrew Kessler, Institutional Equity Sales

metadata.subject: Re: Your question about SIPC and the Brightwell Robotics loss

communication:
Dear Mr. Haddad,

I'm sorry, both for the loss in your Brightwell Robotics position and for the confusion my assistant caused when she told you on the phone that "SIPC has you covered." That was wrong, and I apologize. Redwater Bay Financial is a member of FINRA and SIPC, but SIPC protection applies only if a member brokerage firm fails and customer securities or cash are missing, up to $500,000 per customer including $250,000 for cash. It does not cover a drop in a stock's market value, which is what happened when Brightwell fell after its earnings report last month. Likewise, our FINRA membership means we are subject to FINRA's rules and examinations; it is not an endorsement of our firm or of any stock we discuss.

I've shared your letter with our Chief Compliance Officer, Lena Ostrowski, and she will follow up with you separately. If you'd like, I'm glad to sit down and review whether Brightwell still fits your goals or whether trimming it makes sense, and you are also free to contact FINRA's Investor Complaint Center through finra.org. Again, I'm sorry for the mixed message.

Sincerely,
Grant Whitfield, CFP(R)
Financial Advisor
Redwater Bay Financial, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC | Advisory services through Redwater Bay Advisors LLC
2100 Commerce Drive, Green Bay, WI 54304

required_actions: No action required
label.rationale: The response corrects an earlier oral misstatement by accurately describing what SIPC does and does not protect and states that FINRA membership is not an endorsement, consistent with 2210(e) and (d)(1)(B). The complaint is routed to compliance, and the offer to review the position contains no claim or promise.

Subject: After this week's selloff - time to revisit the plan's QDIA

Ray,

With the S&P down almost 9% since Monday, I'd like to get in front of the committee before the next quarterly meeting rather than wait until November. I think it's time to move the plan's QDIA from the current 'through' series to the Northgate LifePath To-Retirement series.

The case is straightforward: the To series glides down to a 30% equity allocation at the target date and stays there, versus 55% in your current series, so participants within five years of retirement would have far less riding on stocks during a week like this one. The blended expense ratio is also about 6 bps lower. Northgate has been managing glide paths since 2006 and the series has close to $40 billion in assets. I can have a fiduciary memo and transition timeline to you by Friday so the committee can act quickly.

Best,
Elliot Saunders
Financial Advisor, Retirement Plan Services
Birchmont Advisory Securities, LLC, member FINRA/SIPC

Subject: Your beneficiary change on the Clearwater Life fixed annuity - my apologies

Dear Mrs. Abernathy,

Thank you for your call on Tuesday, and please accept my sincere apology. You were right to be frustrated. You submitted the beneficiary change for your Clearwater Life fixed annuity contract on August 2, and it should have gone to the insurance company that same week. Instead it sat in our office's pending queue because page 3 was missing the second signature, and no one on our team called to tell you. That is on us, not you.

Here is what I have done since we spoke. I called Clearwater Life's service center on Wednesday and confirmed they will accept a corrected page 3 by fax. I prepared a new copy with the signature line flagged; it is attached to this email, and I also mailed a paper copy to your Elmwood Drive address in case that is easier.

Once you sign and return it - by email, by mail, or by stopping into the office - I will fax it to Clearwater Life the same day and forward you the fax confirmation. The insurer tells me processing takes 7 to 10 business days, after which they mail a written confirmation directly to you. I will also call you as soon as I see it posted on their system.

I have asked our operations manager to change how incomplete forms are tracked so that a missing signature triggers a phone call to the client within two business days. If you would like to discuss this further with my branch manager, Paul Henley, he can be reached at (608) 555-0126.

Again, I am sorry for the delay and the worry it caused.

Sincerely,
Renata Osei, CFP
Financial Advisor
Stillwater Grove Securities, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC
Stillwater Grove Advisory, LLC, an affiliated registered investment adviser
Madison, WI

Subject: About the clean energy ETF - and where we go from here

Dear Clients,

I'm writing to each of you who has called or emailed over the past few weeks about the decline in the Solstice Clean Power ETF. You trusted my judgment when we added it to your accounts last spring, and I understand why you're upset. I've read every message, and I want to respond to all of you directly rather than let this sit.

Looking back, I gave too much weight to the policy tailwinds for the sector and not enough to how sensitive these companies are to interest rates and subsidy uncertainty. When rates stayed higher for longer, that concentration hurt. That's on me, and I've changed how I size thematic positions as a result.

Going forward, I'd like to discuss moving those proceeds into the Granite Shoals Dividend Leaders ETF. It's everything the clean energy fund wasn't: a steady stream of quarterly income, lower volatility, and broad diversification across more than 100 established, dividend-paying companies. For clients who want to stay invested but sleep better, I think it's the natural next step.

Nothing will be traded without your approval. I'll be calling each of you over the next week to talk through your account and whether this change makes sense for you, and if you'd prefer a different approach, we'll find it together.

Sincerely,

Graham Osei
Registered Representative
Cobblestone Point Securities LLC, member FINRA/SIPC
(608) 555-0172

COPPER BASIN SECURITIES BLOG | Client Education

Trading halts during a fast market: what happens to your stock orders
By Naomi Feld, Director of Trading Operations | April 8, 2025

With stocks falling sharply over the past three sessions, several clients have asked what happens if trading stops. U.S. exchanges use market-wide circuit breakers tied to the S&P 500: a 7% decline (Level 1) or 13% decline (Level 2) before 3:25 p.m. Eastern pauses all stock trading for 15 minutes, and a 20% decline (Level 3) halts trading for the rest of the day. Individual stocks can also pause for five minutes under limit up-limit down bands when they move too far, too fast. Open orders are generally not cancelled by a halt, but when trading resumes, a market order will execute at the next available price, which can be far from the last price you saw. Many investors prefer limit orders during volatile periods for that reason, though a limit order may not be filled at all. This post is about order mechanics only; it is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security, and we are not predicting where prices go next.

Questions about an open order? Call our trade desk at (520) 555-0110.

Copper Basin Securities, Inc. is a member of FINRA (www.finra.org) and SIPC (www.sipc.org). Research our firm and our financial professionals on FINRA BrokerCheck: brokercheck.finra.org.

Individual stocks can also pause for five minutes under limit up-limit down bands when they move too far, too fast. Open orders are generally not cancelled by a halt, but when trading resumes, a market order will execute at the next available price, which can be far from the last price you saw. Many investors prefer limit orders during volatile periods for that reason, though a limit order may not be filled at all. This post is about order mechanics only; it is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security, and we are not predicting where prices go next.

Questions about an open order? Call our trade desk at (520) 555-0110.

Copper Basin Securities, Inc. is a member of FINRA (www.finra.org) and SIPC (www.sipc.org). Research our firm and our financial professionals on FINRA BrokerCheck: brokercheck.finra.org.
---

LANTERNFIELD SECURITIES, LLC

April 9, 2025

Mr. Desmond Yarrow, Chief Investment Officer

310 Grand Avenue, St. Paul, MN 55102

Dear Desmond,

Thanks for having me at your investment committee meeting last week. You asked for the fee-drag math we sketched on the whiteboard, so here it is in writing for your committee's internal use; please don't pass it along to clients as is, since it was prepared for an institutional audience and isn't designed as client material. HYPOTHETICAL ILLUSTRATION: assume $1,000,000 compounding at a constant 6.00% per year for 20 years, and the same amount compounding at 5.50%, which is the same assumed gross rate less an extra 0.50% in annual costs. After 20 years the first grows to about $3,207,000 and the second to about $2,918,000, a gap of roughly $289,000 attributable solely to the cost difference. The rates are arbitrary assumptions chosen to show how compounding magnifies small annual cost differences; they are not the return of any ETF, strategy or account we offer, actual returns vary from year to year and can be negative, and the illustration ignores taxes, trading costs and the sequence of returns.

I'm happy to walk through how this fits into your ETF due diligence on expense ratios and tracking difference when we meet in May.

Warm regards,

Helen Achterberg
Financial Advisor
Lanternfield Securities, LLC
For institutional use only. Not for distribution to retail investors.

With the S&P 500 down more than 12% in three weeks and the tariff headlines changing by the hour, my phone has not stopped ringing. communication:
Hi Jasmine,

Before you decide on the Westerly Floating Rate Income Fund, here's the plain-English version of what we covered on the phone. The fund buys senior bank loans, which pay interest that rises and falls with short-term rates; that helps when rates climb, but your income will drop if the Fed cuts. The loans are made to below-investment-grade companies, so defaults happen, and in a sharp selloff the loan market can fall fast (it dropped roughly 20% in a few weeks in March 2020). Bank loans can take a week or more to settle when the fund sells them, so in heavy redemptions the fund may have to sell what it can rather than what it wants, and it can borrow up to a third of its assets to meet those redemptions, which magnifies losses. On costs, you'd be buying C shares, which carry a 1% contingent deferred sales charge if you sell within 12 months and a gross annual expense ratio of 1.74%.

If after all that it still fits the income sleeve we talked about, I'm glad to place the order; if not, that's completely fine too. The prospectus is attached, and the "Principal Risks" section goes into these points in more detail.

Talk soon,
Andre Lindqvist
Registered Representative
Brookvale Ridge Securities, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC

The fund buys senior bank loans, which pay interest that rises and falls with short-term rates; that helps when rates climb, but your income will drop if the Fed cuts. Andre Lindqvist

communication:
Subject: RE: Should I move to the muni fund before the Fed meets?

Hi Helen,

Good question, and I would rather give you a useful answer than a confident one. I do not know what the Fed will do on Wednesday, and I will not guess what either the Brightwater Short-Term Bond Fund or the Brightwater Intermediate Municipal Fund will return afterward. Here is what I can lay out so you can decide with your eyes open.

The two funds are built for different jobs. The short-term fund holds taxable bonds with an average duration under two years, so its price moves relatively little when rates change, in either direction. The intermediate muni fund runs a duration closer to five years, so it is more sensitive to rate moves both up and down; that is simply how bond pricing works, not a prediction. The muni fund's income is generally exempt from federal income tax but may be subject to Ohio state income tax on out-of-state bonds and to the federal alternative minimum tax, and any capital gains distributions are taxable. The muni fund also carries a higher expense ratio (0.52% versus 0.31%) and different credit exposure, all of which is in the prospectuses I have attached. Whether the tax treatment helps you depends on your bracket, which we should run together rather than assume.

If you want to walk through it before Wednesday, I have time Tuesday at 11:00. If not, there is nothing that has to happen this week.

Best,
Tomas Reinholt
Registered Representative
Brightwater Securities Corp., member FINRA/SIPC
(614) 555-0190

Please consider each fund's investment objectives, risks, charges and expenses carefully before investing; the prospectus contains this and other information. Fund shares fluctuate in value and may be worth more or less than their original cost when redeemed.

The tax language correctly identifies state tax and AMT exposure under (d)(4), and no performance figures are presented.

metadata.recipient_description: Prospect who attended a library investing workshop
metadata.subject: Is 52 too late to start investing?

communication:
Hi Bettina,

Thanks for your question after the library workshop about whether it's too risky to start investing at 52. It's a fair worry, so here's how I think about it. Stock prices bounce around a lot in the short run, and 2008 and 2022 are good reminders of that, which is why money you'll need in the next few years usually belongs somewhere steadier. But the stock market rewards patience. If you invest in a diversified portfolio and leave it alone for at least 15 years, you are guaranteed to come out ahead; that is simply how the math works over long periods. Starting at 52 still gives you that runway before a typical retirement age.

If you'd like, we can sit down and map out how much belongs in a short-term bucket versus a long-term one. I'm in the Ann Arbor office Tuesdays through Fridays.

Warm regards,
Imani Castellanos
Registered Representative
Starling Gate Investments, member FINRA/SIPC
(734) 555-0158

metadata.recipient_description: Single existing retail client household (married couple)
metadata.subject: How reinvested dividends compound - a hypothetical illustration

communication:
RAVENNA SHORE SECURITIES, INC.
Member FINRA/SIPC
1120 Pacific Avenue, Suite 300, Tacoma, WA 98402

July 8, 2025

Mr. and Mrs. Luis Delgado
2714 North Proctor Street
Tacoma, WA 98407

Dear Luis and Carmen,

It was a pleasure seeing you both in June. At the end of our meeting, Carmen asked how reinvesting dividends can make a portfolio "snowball" over time, and I promised to put something on paper. The engine behind that snowball is compounding: when earnings are reinvested, the next year's growth is calculated on a larger base, so the dollar gains can grow even if the rate stays the same.

To show the math, here is a purely hypothetical example. Suppose $50,000 earned a constant rate every year for 20 years, with all earnings reinvested and nothing withdrawn:
  - at 4% per year: about $109,556
  - at 6% per year: about $160,357
  - at 8% per year: about $233,048

These figures illustrate a mathematical principle only. They do not represent the past or future performance of any stock you own, any stock I might suggest, or any other investment, and the rates were chosen simply to show how the gap widens over time.

Please keep a few important caveats in mind. Real investments do not earn a constant return; stock prices rise and fall, sometimes sharply, and a portfolio can lose money in any year, including the early years when losses have the greatest effect on the end result. Companies can reduce or eliminate their dividends at any time. The example also ignores taxes on dividends in your taxable account, trading costs and account fees, all of which would lower the results.

What the illustration does show is why we set up automatic dividend reinvestment in your joint account last year, and why time in the plan matters as much as any single year's results. If you'd like, we can review the reinvestment settings and your income needs together at our next meeting in October.

Warm regards,

Jasmine Thorvaldsen
Registered Representative
Ravenna Shore Securities, Inc.
(253) 555-0181

communication:
Re your q on the 2050 fund - can't tell you what it'll return, no one can. But here's the math you asked about, purely hypothetical: $500/mo at an assumed 6%/yr, compounded monthly, for 25 yrs = approx $346,500. Same $500/mo at an assumed 4% = approx $257,000. Not a projection for your fund or any investment; ignores fees and taxes, and real returns vary year to year and can be negative.

Point is just that time + steady contributions matter. Can walk thru the fund's actual glide path and expenses at your review on the 14th. - Dev Malhotra, Pinecrest Row Securities

As the year draws to a close, I write to share several observations regarding the Meridian Steady Income Fund (Class A), which a number of you hold in your accounts.

The Fund has paid a distribution every single month since its inception in March 2012, more than 160 consecutive payments without interruption. Its share price today stands within a few cents of where it opened 2025. In my judgment, these two facts together describe a holding that has done precisely what income investors ask of it.

Looking ahead, I expect the Fund to continue delivering this same dependable monthly income, with its share price holding steady, through whatever rate environment 2026 brings. I therefore see no reason for any of you to revisit your allocation at this time. Should you wish to discuss your account, I remain available at your convenience.

Respectfully,

Gregory Thale
Senior Portfolio Consultant
Thale Private Client Group
(503) 555-0186 | gthale@thalepcg.com

Subject: Roads, ports & power lines: why infrastructure is having a moment

Hey there,

Quick question: when's the last time you thought about who owns the toll road you drove on this morning? Probably never. But infrastructure, the unglamorous stuff like pipelines, cell towers, airports and power grids, has been one of the more talked-about corners of the market this summer, and we've been getting a lot of questions about it.

One way some investors get exposure is through the Brightwater Global Infrastructure ETF (ticker: BWGI). It holds about 120 companies across 22 countries that own or operate infrastructure assets, and it pays a quarterly distribution. And it's been on a run: BWGI is up 18.6% year to date and 27.2% over the past 12 months (market price, as of August 15, 2025). Not bad for "boring," right?

Now the honest part. Infrastructure companies often carry heavy debt, so their shares can be sensitive to interest rates and can drop when rates climb. About 55% of BWGI's holdings are outside the U.S., so currency swings and foreign political risk come with the territory. Regulated utilities can have their rates capped by governments. And like any ETF, BWGI trades at market price, which can be above or below its net asset value, and you can lose money.

If you want to see whether infrastructure fits your mix, or whether you already own more of it than you realize through your other funds, reply to this email or book 20 minutes with your Saltmarsh advisor. No pressure, we're always happy to talk shop.

Before investing, carefully consider the fund's investment objectives, risks, charges and expenses. This and other information is in the prospectus, available at saltmarshsecurities.com/prospectus or by calling (843) 555-0112. Read it carefully before investing.

Cheers,
The Saltmarsh Securities Team

BLUEWATER LEDGER SECURITIES -- BOISE BRANCH
Home | Our Team | Retirement Resources | Contact

How Target-Date Funds Work

Many employer retirement plans offer target-date funds, and clients often ask us what the year in a fund's name means. This page explains the basic terms you are likely to see in your plan materials.

The target date. The year in the fund name is the approximate year an investor expects to begin withdrawing money, usually around retirement. A fund labeled 2045 is designed for someone planning to retire around 2045.

The glide path. Each fund family sets a schedule for how its fund's mix of stocks, bonds and cash shifts over time. Glide paths differ between fund families, and some continue changing for years after the target date ('through' the date) while others stop at the target date ('to' the date). The fund's prospectus describes its glide path.

Costs and risks. Expenses vary by fund and share class. The principal value of a target-date fund is not guaranteed at any time, including at or after the target date, and the fund can lose money. Investors should consider a fund's investment objectives, risks, charges and expenses carefully before investing; the prospectus contains this and other information and should be read carefully.

Questions about the options in your own plan? Contact the Boise branch at 208-555-0126 or visit our office at 950 W. Bannock Street, Suite 400, Boise, ID 83702.

Carla Nunez, Branch Manager

Check the background of our firm and investment professionals on FINRA's BrokerCheck (https://brokercheck.finra.org).
Bluewater Ledger Securities, Inc., Member FINRA (https://www.finra.org) / SIPC (https://www.sipc.org).

46 Orchard Terrace

Dear Lucien and Ilse,

After our conversation about Pinebrook Bancorp, I wanted to put my view in writing: I think U.S. regional banks are among the most undervalued corners of the stock market right now, and I am recommending that you continue to hold your Pinebrook shares rather than sell at today's prices. My reasoning is that deposit outflows across the group have largely stabilized since the spring bank failures, Pinebrook's own deposits grew in the second quarter, and the stock trades near its tangible book value, well below its ten-year average of about 1.5 times book.

That said, this is a sector with real risks, and I don't want you to underweight them. Regional banks hold sizable commercial real estate loans, and office-loan losses could rise further; competition for deposits is squeezing lending margins; and if the economy slows, credit losses could grow and the stock could fall well below today's price. Pinebrook also represents about 12% of your portfolio, which is more concentrated than I would like, so if we do hold, I'd suggest we not add to it. I'm happy to send you the quarterly filings and the analysis I relied on, and we can revisit this at our November review.

Warm regards,

Graham Okonkwo-Bell
Registered Representative
Thornbury Hill Securities, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC
(802) 555-0114

Hi Denise,

Thanks for the quick turnaround on the authorized-signer forms; everything is in good order and the county's account is fully set up. For settlement on the 12-rung brokered CD ladder next Tuesday, we'll draw from the operating account at Mesa Valley Bank per the standing instruction you signed on the 3rd, and each CD will settle into the county's custody account here. Statements will show each issuing bank by name so your auditors can confirm coverage.

On your board's question about whether the principal is "safe": each CD is issued by a different FDIC-insured bank and capped at $245,000 so principal plus accrued interest stays within the coverage limit applicable to the county's public-unit deposits at each bank. FDIC insurance guarantees principal and interest up to that limit if an issuing bank fails, and is backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government. It does not protect against changes in market value: if the county sells a CD before maturity on the secondary market, it could receive less than it paid. I'll send the settlement confirmations once the trades clear. Let me know if your treasurer's office needs anything else for the file.

Best,
Owen Castellanos
Registered Representative, Public Finance Services
Juniper Gate Securities, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC

OLD MILL SECURITIES CORP. - COMMUNITY EDUCATION SERIES
Seminar Script: "Reading a Mutual Fund Prospectus Without the Headache"
Presenter: Priya Venkataraman, Financial Advisor
Venue: Lancaster Public Library, Duke Street Community Room | Run time: approx. 45 minutes

[SLIDE 1 - Title]
PRIYA: Good evening, and thank you for joining us. My name is Priya Venkataraman, and I am a financial advisor with Old Mill Securities Corp., member FINRA and SIPC. Tonight is purely educational. We will not be discussing or recommending any particular fund, and there is nothing to buy or sign this evening.

[SLIDE 2 - What is a prospectus?]
PRIYA: Every mutual fund must provide a prospectus, a legal document filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission that describes the fund's objective, strategies, risks, fees and how to buy and sell shares. Many funds also offer a shorter summary prospectus. Both are available free of charge from the fund company, usually on its website.

[SLIDE 3 - The fee table]
PRIYA: Near the front, you will find the fee table. It shows shareholder fees, such as any front-end sales charge, and annual fund operating expenses, expressed as a percentage of your investment. We will walk through what each line means and where to find breakpoint discounts that may lower a sales charge.

[SLIDE 4 - Principal risks]
PRIYA: The risk section explains what could cause the fund to lose value. Read it carefully, because it describes the specific risks of that fund's strategy, whether that is interest rate risk, credit risk, foreign market risk or something else.

[SLIDE 5 - Share classes and Q&A]
PRIYA: Finally, we will look at how share classes differ in sales charges and ongoing expenses. After that, I will open the floor for questions. Copies of tonight's slides are on the table by the door, and my contact information is on the last page if you would like to follow up individually.

Old Mill Securities Corp., member FINRA/SIPC. 120 N. Duke Street, Lancaster, PA 17602. This presentation is for educational purposes only.

YOU'RE INVITED
"Retirement on Autopilot? What Your Target-Date Fund Really Does"
A free evening workshop hosted by Thistle & Vane Financial Group

Tuesday, September 16, 2025 | 6:30 to 8:00 p.m.
Lakeview Community Center, Room B, 1200 Shoreline Drive, Madison, WI
Light dinner provided. Seats are limited, so reserve yours today!

Millions of Americans have their 401(k) on autopilot in a target-date fund. But do you really know what's under the hood? Join Jerome Whitfield, a registered representative with Thistle & Vane, for a no-jargon evening that will help you understand the fund you may be counting on for retirement.

Here's what we'll cover:
- How a glide path shifts your mix of stocks and bonds as you age
- Why two "2040" funds from different companies can hold very different investments and charge very different fees
- Good news for savers: every target-date fund in your 401(k) is required by law to be 100% in bonds and cash by your target retirement date, so your stock market exposure ends the year you retire
- What to ask before you roll a target-date fund into an IRA

Target-date funds are not guaranteed at any time, including at or after the target date. Their value will fluctuate, you can lose money, and fees and expenses vary from fund to fund. Consider each fund's investment objectives, risks, charges and expenses carefully before investing; the prospectus contains this and other information and should be read carefully.

RSVP by September 10: call (608) 555-0121 or visit thistlevane.example.com/workshop

Thistle & Vane Financial Group, Member FINRA/SIPC
No investment products will be sold at this event.

Subject: Re: Should I keep reinvesting the dividends?

Hi Mr. Lindqvist,

Good question, and it is mostly a question about math rather than about any particular stock. Here is a purely hypothetical illustration: if $10,000 grew at a constant 6% a year with every dollar of growth left invested, it would be about $32,071 after 20 years; at a constant 4% it would be about $21,911. The gap comes from compounding, gains earning their own gains, and it widens the longer money stays invested. These figures are hypothetical, are not a projection of how Ridgeway Foods, Calloway Rail or any other stock in your account will perform, and ignore taxes and commissions as well as the fact that real returns are uneven and can be negative in many years. Dividends are not guaranteed either; companies can cut or suspend them.

Whether reinvesting makes sense for you depends on whether you need the income now, how concentrated you already are in those two names, and your taxes, since reinvested dividends in a taxable account are still taxed in the year they are paid. Happy to go through it on our call Thursday.

Best,
Helena Brandt
Registered Representative
Marrowstone Point Securities LLC, member FINRA/SIPC

Subject: Bond fund vs. CD - the differences we discussed

Dear Ms. Achterberg,

Thank you for meeting with me on Tuesday. You asked how an intermediate-term bond mutual fund compares with the 3-year bank CD your credit union offered for the $80,000 from your home sale, so here are the material differences side by side rather than a recommendation.

Guarantees and safety: the CD is FDIC-insured up to $250,000 per depositor per bank, and you receive your principal back at maturity. A bond fund is not insured or guaranteed by anyone; its share price moves daily with interest rates and the credit of the bonds it holds, and you can lose money. Liquidity: you can redeem fund shares on any business day, but at that day's price, which may be below what you paid; the CD typically charges an early-withdrawal penalty (often several months of interest) if you cash out before maturity. Costs: the fund's prospectus lists a total annual operating expense ratio of 0.48% and no sales charge on the share class I would use, while the CD has no stated fees beyond the penalty. Income and taxes: CD interest is fixed for the term and taxed as ordinary income each year; fund distributions vary with the portfolio and are also generally taxed as ordinary income, and selling shares can create a capital gain or loss. Objectives: the CD suits money you need intact on a known date; the fund is designed for investors who can accept price swings in exchange for a diversified bond portfolio with no maturity date.

I have attached the fund's prospectus. Once you have had time to read it, I am happy to talk through which, if either, fits your timeline.

Kind regards,

Anjali Rao
Registered Representative
Oakhurst Lane Securities, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC
503-555-0181

Subject: Following up: the yield curve question

Hi Mr. Castellanos,

Thanks for stopping by our table at the Fresno home and garden expo on Saturday. You asked what people mean when they say the yield curve is "inverted," so here's the plain-English version. Normally, longer-term bonds pay higher yields than short-term ones because investors want to be paid for tying their money up longer. When short-term yields climb above long-term yields, the curve is called inverted. Some economists watch it as a possible recession signal, but its timing has been unreliable, and it isn't a reason on its own to buy or sell anything.

If you'd ever like to sit down and talk about your own situation, I'm happy to set up a no-cost meeting at your convenience.

Best regards,
Danielle Hsu, Registered Representative | 559-555-0107 | Fresno, CA

communication:
Three questions I ask before owning a dividend stock
Posted by Jordan Pike | March 18, 2026 | 5-minute read

A high dividend yield is the first thing many people notice, and it is often the least useful. When a stock yields 9% while its peers yield 3%, the market is usually telling you something: investors may expect a cut. So the first question I ask is how much of the company's earnings, and more importantly its free cash flow, goes out as dividends. A payout ratio creeping toward or above 100% means the dividend is being funded by something other than the business, often debt.

The second question is about the balance sheet: could the company keep paying through a bad year or two, or would it have to choose between its lenders and its shareholders? The third is about history and culture: has management held or raised the payout through past downturns, and do they talk about it as a commitment or an afterthought? None of these questions guarantees anything. Dividends can be reduced or eliminated at any time, and a stock can fall in price even while its dividend holds up. But asking them has kept many investors from chasing yield into a trap.

About the author: Jordan Pike is a registered representative based in Boise, Idaho, who works with families on retirement income planning. Contact: jordan@pikeplanning.example.com | (208) 555-0167

This article is for educational purposes only and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security. Investing involves risk, including loss of principal.

hey Priya!

ha, totally get it, watching three of your five stocks drop on the same day is no fun. short answer: no need for any snap decisions, but your question about swapping some of the individual names for a fund is a fair one and worth talking through.

Subject: Changing jobs? Your 401(k) choices, plus a look at one fund we use in rollover IRAs

Hi there,

Spring is when a lot of our clients change jobs or retire, and the question we hear most is what to do with an old 401(k). You generally have four choices: leave the money in your former employer's plan (if allowed), move it to your new employer's plan, roll it to an IRA, or cash it out. Cashing out usually triggers income tax and, before age 59 1/2, a 10% additional tax. Employer plans often have lower-cost institutional share classes, may allow penalty-free withdrawals if you leave your job at 55 or older, and receive federal ERISA creditor protection; an IRA offers a wider range of investments but may cost more depending on what you choose and how your account is structured. We'll walk through the fees and services of each option with you before you decide.

For clients who do roll to an IRA, one balanced fund we often discuss is the Sentinel Balanced Allocation Fund (Class A). Clearpath Fund Analytics ranked the fund's Class A shares in its Moderate Allocation category, based on total return without sales charges, as of March 31, 2025: 1-year, 211 of 742 funds (top 29%); 5-year, 98 of 668 funds (top 15%); 10-year, 71 of 541 funds (top 14%). Clearpath rankings are based solely on total return, assume reinvestment of distributions, and do not reflect sales charges; had sales charges been included, rankings may have been lower. Rankings for other share classes may differ. Past performance, including rankings, is no guarantee of future results.

Current performance may be lower or higher; call (402) 555-0172 for month-end performance. The fund invests in both stocks and bonds and is subject to market, interest-rate and credit risk.

Hi Adaeze,

You asked what the new price target in our analyst's note on Halvorsen Industrial Robotics (HIRB) actually means, so here is a plain-English summary. On February 3, 2026, Calloway Ridge's equity research team raised its 12-month price target to $64 from $55 and kept its Outperform rating; HIRB closed at $51.20 that day. A price target isn't a promise of where the stock will trade - it's the analyst's estimate of value, derived by applying a 24x multiple (roughly the average of four automation peers) to the team's 2027 earnings estimate of $2.67 per share. The analyst also notes the stock has been more volatile than the S&P 500 and that the target may not be reached within 12 months, or at all. Calloway Ridge makes a market in HIRB, and the full report (attached) lists the analyst certification and our other disclosures on page 9. Since HIRB is already about 6% of your portfolio, I'd suggest we talk before you add to it - I'm free Thursday afternoon.

Best,
Jonah Whitcombe

metadata.subject: A correction, and a fuller picture on 401(k) rollovers

communication:
Dear Clients and Friends,

Last month's mailer, 'Simplify Your Retirement with an IRA Rollover,' drew a fair complaint from several of you: it talked up the advantages of rolling over and said almost nothing about the reasons you might not. You were right, and I apologize. Here is the side-by-side I should have sent the first time.

Costs. Many large employer plans offer institutional share classes and negotiated recordkeeping fees that can be lower than what you would pay in an IRA. In an advisory IRA with us you would pay an annual advisory fee of up to 1.10% of assets plus the underlying fund expenses; a brokerage IRA carries commissions or sales charges instead. Your plan's annual fee disclosure shows what you pay today.

Investment choices and guarantees. A plan limits you to its menu; an IRA can hold a much wider range of stocks, bonds, funds and ETFs. Some plans offer a stable value fund or guaranteed account that can't be moved into an IRA, and nothing in an IRA carries a guarantee unless you buy a product backed by an insurer's claims-paying ability.

Access to your money. If you leave your employer in or after the year you turn 55, the plan generally lets you withdraw without the 10% early-withdrawal penalty; in an IRA the penalty-free age is generally 59 1/2. Some plans allow loans; IRAs do not.

Protection and taxes. Money in an ERISA plan has broad federal protection from creditors, while IRA protection outside bankruptcy depends on your state's law. A direct rollover is not taxable. If the plan mails the check to you instead, 20% is withheld and you have 60 days to redeposit the full amount to avoid tax and possible penalties. If you hold company stock in your plan, the 'net unrealized appreciation' rules may favor a different approach, so talk with your tax advisor first. Required minimum distributions apply to both, though a current employer's plan may let you delay them while you're still working there.

Whichever account you use, investments carry market risk, including possible loss of principal. Leaving the money where it is, moving it to a new employer's plan, or rolling it over can each be the right answer. If you'd like a line-by-line comparison of your own plan and an IRA, call our office at (505) 555-0128. We are paid when you roll assets to us, and we'll say so in the meeting, too.

With apologies and thanks,
Colleen Abernathy, Registered Representative
Halvorsen & Teague Securities, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC
6100 Uptown Blvd NE, Albuquerque, NM 87110

required_actions: Approve for use
label.rationale: The email compares staying in a 401(k) with rolling to an IRA and discloses the material differences (d)(2) requires: costs, investment options, guarantees, liquidity and penalty ages, creditor protection and tax treatment. communication:
Dear Ms. Okonkwo,

Thank you for your time on Monday. You asked me to explain the bond ladder in writing, so here it is in plain terms. A five-year ladder splits your money into five roughly equal pieces maturing one year apart; each year the maturing piece is reinvested in a new five-year bond, so you are never guessing where rates will be, you always have a rung coming due within twelve months, and the average yield drifts toward whatever the market is paying over time. The trade-off is that bond prices move with interest rates, so a rung sold before maturity can be worth less than you paid, and an issuer can default.

To show you what that looks like in practice, I ran our five-year investment-grade corporate ladder back through 2010 to 2024. Over that stretch it would have returned 4.3% a year with no down years. On your $300,000, that works out to roughly $12,900 of income per year, which is what you can expect from the strategy going forward. I can set the accounts up whenever you're ready.

Kind regards,
Hal Brennan
Registered Representative, Copperline Securities, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC
312-555-0160

communication:
Subject: Your old 401(k): the four choices, side by side

Hi everyone,

Several of you changed jobs this year and asked the same question at our reviews, so I'm sending one note to the five of you (you're BCC'd, so no one sees anyone else's address). This is general education, not a recommendation for your situation. Before I recommend anything, I'll go through your specific plan documents with you.

Option 1: Leave the money in your former employer's 401(k). Many large plans offer institutional share classes or collective trusts with expense ratios well below what an individual can buy on their own, and some include a stable value fund you won't find in an IRA. Federal law (ERISA) generally protects 401(k) assets from creditors. If you leave your employer in or after the year you turn 55, you can usually take withdrawals from that plan without the 10% early-withdrawal penalty, which an IRA does not allow until 59 1/2. Downsides: your menu is limited to what the plan offers, the plan may charge recordkeeping fees, and some plans restrict partial withdrawals.

Option 2: Roll it to an IRA with us. You'd have a much broader range of investments: individual stocks, bonds, CDs, ETFs and thousands of mutual funds, and we could look at all of your accounts together. But it is not free. Depending on the account type, you'd pay commissions on trades or an annual advisory fee (our advisory program runs 0.85% to 1.25% a year), plus the expenses of the funds you hold, which can add up to more than staying in the plan. IRA creditor protection depends on federal bankruptcy law and Michigan law rather than ERISA, you lose the age-55 rule, and you can't take a loan from an IRA the way some plans allow.

Options 3 and 4: Roll into your new employer's plan if it accepts rollovers (similar trade-offs to Option 1, with that plan's menu and fees), or cash out, which is usually the most expensive choice because the whole amount is taxed as ordinary income and may carry the 10% penalty.

A few points apply no matter what. None of these options is guaranteed: stocks, bonds and funds can lose value in a plan or an IRA, and a stable value fund depends on the issuer's contracts. If you hold your employer's stock in the plan, ask me about net unrealized appreciation before moving it, because rolling it to an IRA can forfeit that tax treatment. A direct rollover (check payable to the new custodian) is not taxable. If the plan pays you instead, it must withhold 20% for federal tax, and you have 60 days to deposit the full amount, including the withheld 20% from your own pocket, or the shortfall is taxed as a distribution.

If you'd like, bring your former plan's annual fee disclosure (the "404a-5" notice) to our next meeting and we'll put the numbers side by side for you specifically.

Best,
Gabriel Feliciano
Registered Representative
Tidewater Lane Securities, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC
118 E. Front Street, Traverse City, MI 49684 | (231) 555-0182

A quarterly newsletter from Kevin Lindqvist, Bayfront Municipal & Equity Services, Inc.

Why municipal bonds deserve a look this fall

Municipal bonds pay interest that is generally exempt from federal income tax. Subject: About the August 5 market open: what happened to some ETF stop orders

Dear Client,

Many of you contacted us after the volatile open on Monday, August 5, 2024, when several ETFs briefly traded well below the value of their underlying holdings and some stop orders executed at prices far from the prior close. We want to explain plainly what happened. When a stop order's trigger price is reached, it becomes a market order and fills at the next available price, which in a fast market can be significantly below the stop price. Larkspur routed these orders as they were entered, and our Trading Supervision group is reviewing each affected execution against our best-execution obligations; we cannot say in advance what the outcome of any individual review will be. If you believe an order in your account was handled improperly, please contact your representative or write to our Compliance Department at 1180 Grand Avenue, Des Moines, IA 50309 (compliance@larkspurcm.example), and you will receive a written response.

Please review any open stop orders with your representative today. A stop-limit order will not fill below your limit price, but it may not fill at all if the price moves through your limit, so neither order type protects you in every market. ETF market prices can also differ from their net asset value, especially near the open and during periods of heavy volatility.

Larkspur Capital Markets, Inc., member FINRA/SIPC
1180 Grand Avenue, Des Moines, IA 50309 | 515-555-0122

Retain with the related complaint files and best-execution review records

Next step would be a 45-minute planning session where we go over your timeline, the cash you want to keep liquid, and your comfort with ups and downs. I've attached our Form CRS and our firm brochure. Let me know a couple of times that work for you next week.

All the best,
Dev Malhotra

PARKED CASH EARNING NEXT TO NOTHING?
Put it to work. Compare two short-term choices side by side.

Brokered CDs and U.S. Treasury bills both offer short maturities and a fixed rate if you hold to maturity. They are not the same product, and the differences matter:

- Protection: Brokered CDs are FDIC-insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category; amounts above that limit are not insured. Treasury bills are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government and are not FDIC-insured.

SLIDE 6 -- YOUR 401(k) OPTIONS WHEN YOU LEAVE AN EMPLOYER
Speaker script (Andrea Kowalczyk, Registered Representative, Pemberton Ridge Securities, member FINRA/SIPC)

When you separate from an employer, you generally have four choices: leave the money in your former employer's plan if the plan allows it, roll it into a new employer's plan, roll it into an Individual Retirement Account, or take a cash distribution, which is generally taxable and may carry a 10% additional tax if you are under 59 1/2. Each choice involves trade-offs in investment options, fees and expenses, services, creditor protection and required minimum distributions, and an IRA will often cost more than an institutionally priced 401(k). One point many of you in this room will care about: if you leave your job in or after the year you turn 55, rolling your balance into a Pemberton Ridge IRA preserves your ability to take penalty-free withdrawals before 59 1/2, just as you could from the plan. We'll walk through a side-by-side worksheet on the next slide so you can compare your own plan's costs against an IRA before deciding.

SLIDE 6 FOOTER: Pemberton Ridge Securities does not provide tax or legal advice. Consult your tax professional regarding your situation.

violations.explanation: The age-55 separation-from-service exception to the 10% additional tax applies to distributions from the employer plan, not from an IRA, so rolling over forfeits rather than preserves it.

Subject: Our view on midstream infrastructure ETFs

Hi Corinne,

Great catching up in Denver. As promised, here is why I keep pushing midstream energy infrastructure ETFs onto your model committee's agenda. We think the sector is one of the more compelling income opportunities in the market today: most pipeline and storage revenue comes from long-term, fee-based contracts rather than commodity prices, distribution coverage across the larger operators has improved since 2020, and balance-sheet leverage is lower than it was a decade ago. For a model that needs yield without adding more rate-sensitive bonds, we think it deserves a serious look.

The risks are real and your committee should weigh them: volumes still fall when production drops, the group is concentrated in a few dozen issuers, prices can be volatile and have fallen sharply in past energy downturns, and funds structured as C-corporations can carry a deferred tax liability that drags on returns, while MLP-based structures may issue K-1s. Regulatory and permitting changes can also affect new projects. I'm happy to send our desk's sector primer and a side-by-side of the main ETF structures.

Best,

Adrian Feldkamp

Blackwater Crossing Securities, Inc., Member FINRA/SIPC
For institutional use only. Not for distribution to retail investors.

THORNBURY PARK SECURITIES LLC - VIDEO SCRIPT
Title: "Understanding Mutual Fund Share Classes"
Runtime: approx. 2:40 | Presenter: Evelyn Marsh, Registered Representative
Distribution: firm YouTube channel and website education library

[OPEN - Evelyn seated at her desk. Lower third: "Evelyn Marsh, Registered Representative, Thornbury Park Securities LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC"]

EVELYN: Good afternoon. Many investors are surprised to learn that a single mutual fund often offers several share classes. The underlying portfolio is the same; what differs is how you pay for the fund. Today I will walk through the two classes most retail investors encounter.

[ON-SCREEN GRAPHIC: "Class A shares"]

EVELYN: Class A shares typically charge a front-end sales charge when you buy, often in the range of 3 to 5.75 percent for stock funds. That charge is reduced at certain investment levels, known as breakpoints, and the ongoing annual expenses of A shares are generally lower than those of other classes. A shares are often more economical for larger investments held over long periods.

[ON-SCREEN GRAPHIC: "Class C shares"]

EVELYN: Class C shares are different. With C shares, there are no sales charges of any kind, at purchase or at redemption, so every dollar you invest goes to work from day one and you are free to sell whenever you choose. The trade-off is a higher annual expense ratio, which over a long holding period can cost more than the A-share front-end charge.

EVELYN: Which class is appropriate depends on how much you invest, how long you expect to hold the fund, and whether you qualify for breakpoints. Those are questions worth discussing with your financial professional before you invest.

[ON-SCREEN TEXT: "Mutual funds are subject to market risk, including possible loss of principal. Fees and expenses vary by fund and share class."]

EVELYN: Before investing, carefully consider a fund's investment objectives, risks, charges and expenses. That information, including the specific fees for each share class, is in the fund's prospectus, which you can obtain from your financial professional. Please read it carefully before investing.

[CLOSE - Logo card: "Thornbury Park Securities LLC, Member FINRA/SIPC | 1100 Main Street, Kansas City, MO 64105 | 816-555-0124"]

QUARRY HILL SECURITIES
Elliot Danvers, Registered Representative | Louisville, KY
Home | About Elliot | Retirement Planning | Contact | BrokerCheck

Why We Use Target-Date Funds for Some Retirement Savers, and How to Read a Fund Ranking

For clients who want one diversified holding that adjusts over time, I sometimes use target-date funds. A target-date fund holds a mix of stock and bond funds and gradually shifts toward bonds as its target year approaches. That shift is designed to reduce volatility, not eliminate it: target-date funds can lose money at any time, including near and after the target date, and they do not guarantee income in retirement. Funds with the same target year can have very different stock allocations and glide paths, so the date alone doesn't tell you how much risk you're taking.

One fund I discuss with clients is the Hollow Creek Target 2045 Fund (Class A). You may have seen that it was recognized by Meridian Fund Analytics, an independent ranking firm whose rankings are generally published to subscribers and in financial media. Here is the full picture behind that ranking.

Meridian Fund Analytics Rankings, Target Date 2041-2045 Category (as of June 30, 2025)
- 1-year: ranked 61 of 218 funds
- 5-year: ranked 19 of 187 funds
- 10-year: ranked 24 of 131 funds
Rankings are based on total return for each period, with distributions reinvested, and do not take sales charges into account; if sales charges were included, the rankings might have been lower. Rankings for other share classes may differ. Fee waivers were in effect for part of the 5- and 10-year periods; without them, total returns and rankings would have been lower. Past rankings are no guarantee of future rankings or results.

Standardized Performance, Hollow Creek Target 2045 Fund, Class A (average annual total returns as of June 30, 2025)
Without sales charge: 1-year 11.42% | 5-year 8.95% | 10-year 7.61%
With maximum 5.50% sales charge: 1-year 5.29% | 5-year 7.72% | 10-year 7.00%
Total annual fund operating expenses (gross): 0.88%; net after contractual fee waiver through April 30, 2026: 0.79%
Performance data quoted represents past performance, which does not guarantee future results. Investment return and principal value will fluctuate, so shares, when redeemed, may be worth more or less than their original cost. Current performance may be lower or higher than the performance quoted. For performance current to the most recent month-end, call (502) 555-0148 or visit hollowcreekfunds.example.com.

A ranking is one data point. When I help a client choose a target-date fund, we also look at the glide path, the fund's expenses, and whether the target year matches when you'll actually need the money.

Before investing, carefully consider the fund's investment objectives, risks, charges and expenses. This and other information is in the prospectus, available from me or at hollowcreekfunds.example.com; please read it carefully before investing.

metadata.subject: Your CD and Treasuries - what this morning's bank news means for you

communication:
Hi Margaret,

I know you saw the headlines this morning about Pacific Crest Bank being closed by regulators, and I wanted to reach you before you had to call me. The facts on your account: you hold one brokered CD issued by that bank, $95,000 face, maturing August 2026, plus $180,000 in Treasury notes. Your CD is within the FDIC's $250,000 per-depositor, per-bank, per-ownership-category limit, so the FDIC will either transfer it to an acquiring bank or pay out principal plus interest accrued through the closing date. Payouts have typically come within days, though that timing isn't guaranteed. Your Treasuries are obligations of the U.S. government, not the bank, and are unaffected; their market prices still move with rates, but principal and interest are backed by the U.S. government if held to maturity.

You also asked last month about SIPC. Westbrook Capital Markets is a member of FINRA and SIPC. SIPC is a different protection: if a brokerage firm fails and customer securities or cash are missing, SIPC protects up to $500,000 per customer, including up to $250,000 in cash. It does not cover drops in market value, and neither FINRA nor SIPC endorses or vouches for any particular investment. I'll call you at 2 p.m. to walk through options for reinvesting the CD proceeds if it's paid out early.

Simone Achebe
Financial Advisor
Westbrook Capital Markets LLC, member FINRA/SIPC
San Diego, CA

CHANGING JOBS? LET'S LOOK AT WHAT TO DO WITH YOUR OLD 401(k).

When you leave an employer, you generally have four choices for your workplace retirement savings: leave the money in your former employer's plan (if the plan allows it), move it into your new employer's plan (if that plan accepts rollovers), roll it into an Individual Retirement Account (IRA), or cash it out. Each has trade-offs, and the right answer depends on your situation.

Things worth comparing before you decide
- Costs. Employer plans may offer institutional share classes and lower administrative fees than an IRA. An IRA with us may involve commissions or an advisory fee and fund expenses that are higher than what you pay in your plan.
- Investment choices. An IRA usually offers a wider range of investments; your plan may offer fewer options, but they are selected and monitored by a plan fiduciary.
- Protections. Assets in ERISA plans generally have strong federal protection from creditors; IRA protection depends on state law.
- Withdrawals and taxes. If you leave your job in or after the year you turn 55, you may be able to take withdrawals from your plan without the 10% additional tax that would apply to IRA withdrawals before 59 1/2. Cashing out generally triggers income tax and may trigger that additional tax.
- Employer stock. If your plan holds your employer's stock, special tax treatment (net unrealized appreciation) may be lost in a standard rollover.

How I work with you
I'll gather your plan's fee disclosure and investment menu, lay the options side by side, and put my recommendation and the reasons for it in writing. If staying in your plan is the better fit, I'll tell you. I am paid when assets are rolled into an account at Larkspur Ridge, which is a conflict of interest; our Form CRS and Regulation Best Interest disclosure explain how.

In a client's words
"I had three old 401(k)s and no idea what any of them cost. Elena pulled the fee statements for all three, showed me that one plan was actually cheaper than an IRA, and helped me roll the other two. For the first time, I understand what I own." - Patricia N., client since 2021

This testimonial was given by a current client. It may not be representative of the experience of other clients and is no guarantee of future performance or success. Patricia was not paid or otherwise compensated for her statement.

communication:
Subject: re: savings acct vs t-bills

Hi Andre,

Good seeing you at the Eastside food bank thing Saturday! Re your question - no wrong answer here, they just do different jobs. Quick rundown:

High-yield savings at your bank: FDIC-insured up to $250k, you can pull money out any day at full value, no fees at most online banks. Downside is the rate can change whenever the bank decides, and the interest is taxed federal + state.

T-bills (say 3- or 6-month): backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government, and the interest is exempt from state and local income tax (still federally taxable), which matters in Minnesota. We don't charge a commission to buy new T-bills at auction, but if you need the cash before they mature you'd have to sell at the market price, which could be a bit more or less than you paid, plus a small markdown. And they're not FDIC-insured - different kind of backing.

So for the first few months of expenses I'd usually want that in savings you can grab instantly; anything you know you won't touch for a while is where T-bills can make sense. Happy to grab coffee if you want to go through your numbers - no pressure either way.

Cheers,
Leah Bjornstad
Registered Representative
Juniper Hill Securities LLC | Member FINRA/SIPC
Minneapolis, MN | (612) 555-0147

T-bills (say 3- or 6-month): backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government, and the interest is exempt from state and local income tax (still federally taxable), which matters in Minnesota. We don't charge a commission to buy new T-bills at auction, but if you need the cash before they mature you'd have to sell at the market price, which could be a bit more or less than you paid, plus a small markdown. And they're not FDIC-insured - different kind of backing.

So for the first few months of expenses I'd usually want that in savings you can grab instantly; anything you know you won't touch for a while is where T-bills can make sense. Happy to grab coffee if you want to go through your numbers - no pressure either way.

The full report, including the valuation methodology, risk factors and required research disclosures, is available on request.

Member FINRA/SIPC | 300 Granby Street, Norfolk, VA 23510

November 2025

Dear Client,

On behalf of Russell Kimura, I'm writing to share some information about where to keep cash you won't need for the next few years. Many of you have bank CDs coming due this winter, and Russell wanted every client to understand an alternative he often discusses in review meetings.

The Harborline Short-Term Income Fund is a mutual fund that invests in short-maturity, investment-grade corporate and government bonds. Compared with a bank CD, it pays a higher yield, you can redeem shares on any business day instead of waiting for a maturity date, and there is no early-withdrawal penalty. For most clients it simply does the same job as a CD, only better.

How does a short-term bond fund work? Rather than holding one deposit at one bank, the fund owns hundreds of individual bonds chosen by a professional management team. As those bonds pay interest, the fund distributes income to shareholders monthly, which you can take in cash or reinvest.

Russell has reviewed dozens of short-term funds over his career, and Harborline is the best cash alternative available anywhere today. If you would like to discuss moving a maturing CD into the fund, please call our office at (757) 555-0164 to schedule a time with him.

Investors should consider the fund's investment objectives, risks, charges and expenses carefully before investing. The prospectus contains this and other information; please request one and read it carefully before investing.

Sincerely,

Theresa Ngata
Client Service Associate, on behalf of Russell Kimura, Registered Representative
Fairhaven Brokerage, Inc.
